title: 10 In-Demand Skills to Build for a Career in Cybersecurity
dek: From vulnerability scanning to incident write-ups, this guide maps the skills security job postings ask for and how long each one realistically takes.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
Cybersecurity hiring is driven by a short list of repeatable tasks: watching networks for breaches, patching what scanners find, keeping firewalls and encryption current, and writing up incidents so other people can act on them (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Build the skills behind those tasks and you are building what employers are actually buying.

This guide covers ten skill areas, the tools employers name in postings, a sequenced learning plan with milestones, and an honest comparison of self-study, certification, bootcamp, apprenticeship and degree routes. Costs change constantly, so it tells you where to check current prices rather than quoting numbers that go stale.

Key takeaways

  • Start with network and operating-system monitoring — spotting and explaining anomalous traffic underpins almost every other security skill, and it is the first duty BLS lists for information security analysts (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • Plan 6-18 months of consistent part-time study to reach entry-level competency from an IT background, and 18-36 months if you are starting with no technical experience.
  • Certification is usually requested, not legally required: BLS lists a bachelor's degree as typical entry-level education (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), while CyberSeek's heat map tracks how many postings ask for each certification versus how many people hold it (CyberSeek, CompTIA and Lightcast, 2025).

The Skills Landscape

Three data sources tell you what to learn, and they agree more than they disagree.

First, the federal occupational data. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics puts 2025 median pay for information security analysts at $129,180 a year ($62.11 an hour) and projects employment to grow much faster than average between 2025 and 2035, with openings projected each year on average across the decade (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). BLS also describes the work concretely: monitoring networks for breaches, maintaining firewalls and encryption software, checking for vulnerabilities, researching security trends, preparing incident reports, and developing security standards (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Those six duties are your syllabus.

Second, the tool-level data. ONET flags Tenable Nessus as an "In Demand" technology skill for this occupation, meaning it appears frequently in employer job postings (ONET OnLine, 2026). Its wider technology list for the role names Metasploit, PortSwigger Burp Suite, HP WebInspect, Rapid7 Nexpose, Symantec Endpoint Protection and McAfee VirusScan (O*NET OnLine, 2026). Learning a scanner and a web proxy is not a hobby detour; it is listed vocabulary.

Third, the certification market. CyberSeek, built by CompTIA and Lightcast with support from NIST NICE, publishes a chart comparing holders of common cybersecurity certifications against openings requesting each one (CyberSeek, 2025), and figures sourced from that heat map show more CISSP openings than certified individuals nationally (Thorteaches, citing cyberseek.org). State-level breakdowns show which certifications employers in your state actually ask for (WorkingNation), which matters because demand is uneven by employer type — most analysts work for computer companies, consulting firms, or business and financial companies (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2021).

ONET classifies the occupation as Job Zone Four, "Considerable Preparation Needed": most jobs in this zone require a four-year degree, but some do not (ONET OnLine, 2026). Read that as: skills and evidence can substitute for credentials with some employers, not all.

Core Skills to Learn

Each skill below lists why employers ask for it, one concrete way to practise it, and a part-time learning estimate (roughly 8-10 hours a week). Check current prices directly with the vendor or training provider before committing.

  • Network and system monitoring for breaches. The first duty BLS lists for the role (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Build a home lab with two or three virtual machines, generate traffic, and practise identifying what is abnormal. 2-4 months to basic competence.
  • Vulnerability scanning. Tenable Nessus is flagged as an "In Demand" skill for this occupation, meaning it shows up frequently in postings (ONET OnLine, 2026). Install the free-tier scanner against your own lab, then repeat with Rapid7 Nexpose, also named for the role (ONET OnLine, 2026). 4-8 weeks.
  • Patch and remediation prioritisation. Scanning produces hundreds of findings; employers pay for the judgement about which five get fixed first. Practise by writing a one-page remediation plan after each lab scan. 4-6 weeks, layered on the skill above.
  • Firewall and encryption administration. Named explicitly in the BLS duty list (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Configure host and network firewall rules in your lab and set up certificate-based encryption for a test service. 1-3 months.
  • Web application testing. PortSwigger Burp Suite and HP WebInspect both appear on ONET's technology list for the occupation (ONET OnLine, 2026). Work through a deliberately vulnerable practice application with Burp's community edition. 2-4 months.
  • Exploitation fundamentals. Metasploit is listed for the role (ONET OnLine, 2026). You do not need to be a penetration tester, but understanding how a finding becomes an incident changes how you triage. 3-6 months.*
  • Endpoint protection. Symantec Endpoint Protection and McAfee VirusScan appear on the same ONET list (ONET OnLine, 2026). Learn deployment, policy tuning and alert triage on any mainstream endpoint product — the concepts transfer. 4-6 weeks.
  • Incident reporting and written communication. BLS lists preparing incident reports as a core duty (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Write a timeline, impact statement and recommendation for every lab exercise; keep them as portfolio evidence. Ongoing; 4-8 weeks to a usable template.
  • Security standards and policy drafting. BLS lists developing and recommending security standards among the duties (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Draft an access-control and patching standard for a hypothetical 50-person company. 2-3 months alongside other study.
  • Baseline certification knowledge. CompTIA Security+ is described as confirming the baseline skills needed for core security functions and as a global benchmark for network and operational security practice (Cybersecurity Guide). A Security+ purchase bundle includes an exam voucher, one retake, a 12-month CertMaster Learn licence and a 12-month CertMaster Labs licence (TechTarget); CompTIA publishes current pricing. 8-16 weeks of part-time study.

Building a Learning Plan

  1. Weeks 1-6: fix the foundations. 8-10 hours a week on networking basics, Linux and Windows administration, and scripting. Milestone: you can build a three-machine virtual lab from scratch, move traffic between the machines, and explain what each port is doing.
  2. Weeks 7-18: tools before theory. 8-10 hours a week running Nessus and Nexpose scans against your lab and working through a vulnerable web app with Burp Suite — all three named in ONET's technology list for the occupation (ONET OnLine, 2026). Milestone: three written scan reports, each ending with a prioritised fix list a non-technical manager could follow.
  3. Months 5-7: certify the baseline. 6-8 hours a week on Security+ material, which covers core security functions and is positioned as a benchmark for network and operational security practice (Cybersecurity Guide). Before you book, check CyberSeek's state-level data on which certifications employers in your state request (WorkingNation). Milestone: consistent passing scores on practice exams, then the exam itself.
  4. Months 8-11: build the evidence file. 5-6 hours a week turning lab work into a portfolio: incident reports, a draft security standard, and a remediation plan — mirroring duties BLS lists for the role (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Milestone: a public repository or PDF pack of six artefacts you can hand to an interviewer.
  5. Months 10-14: get supervised reps. Apply for internal transfers, help-desk-to-security moves, or a U.S. Department of Labor-approved Registered Apprenticeship — approved titles for this occupation include Cyber Defense Analyst, Cyber Security Support Technician and Cybersecurity Analyst (NOF) (ONET OnLine, 2026). Milestone:* you are handling real alerts under supervision, not lab alerts.
  6. Months 12-18: target the applications. 4-5 hours a week matching your evidence to posting language. Search under the job titles ONET records for this occupation — Information Security Officer, Information Systems Security Analyst, Information Systems Security Officer, IT Security Analyst, Network Security Analyst (ONET OnLine, 2026) — not just "cybersecurity." Milestone: interviews, and a record of which skill gaps each rejection exposed.

Comparing Learning Paths

Prices change by provider, state and year, and no single public dataset reports completion or placement rates across all four routes. Treat the outcome column as what is documented, not as a guarantee.

PathTypical durationCost: where to checkWhat is documented about outcomes
Self-study plus home lab6-18 months part-timeTool vendors publish free community tiers and paid tiers; budget for hardware onlyNo central completion data. Evidence is your portfolio against the duties BLS lists for the role (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Certification track (e.g. CompTIA Security+)8-16 weeks part-timeCompTIA publishes current bundle pricing; the purchase includes an exam voucher, one retake, and 12-month CertMaster Learn and CertMaster Labs licences (TechTarget)CyberSeek charts holders of each certification against openings requesting it (CyberSeek, 2025); figures from that heat map show more CISSP openings than certified individuals nationally (Thorteaches, citing cyberseek.org)
BootcampCommonly 3-9 months, full- or part-timeAsk each provider for current tuition and its published outcomes report before enrollingProviders self-report placement; there is no single federal dataset verifying bootcamp hiring outcomes for this occupation
Registered ApprenticeshipTypically 1-4 years, paid and on the jobEarn while training; check sponsor termsU.S. Department of Labor-approved titles for this occupation include Cyber Defense Analyst, Cyber Security Support Technician and Cybersecurity Analyst (NOF) (O*NET OnLine, 2026)
Bachelor's degree4 years full-timeCheck the institution's published tuition and feesBLS lists a bachelor's degree as typical entry-level education, with under 5 years of related experience and no on-the-job training required (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025); ONET places the role in Job Zone Four, where most occupations require a four-year degree but some do not (ONET OnLine, 2026)

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a degree to get hired in cybersecurity?+

BLS lists a bachelor's degree as the typical entry-level education for information security analysts, along with less than 5 years of related work experience and no on-the-job training required (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). O*NET places the occupation in Job Zone Four, where most jobs require a four-year degree but some do not (O*NET OnLine, 2026). In practice: a degree widens the pool of employers who will screen you in, and Registered Apprenticeship routes such as Cyber Defense Analyst and Cyber Security Support Technician exist as alternatives (O*NET OnLine, 2026).

Does a certification actually improve my hiring odds?+

It depends which one and where. CyberSeek publishes a chart comparing the number of people holding each common cybersecurity certification against the number of openings requesting it (CyberSeek, CompTIA and Lightcast, 2025), and figures drawn from that heat map show more CISSP openings than certified individuals nationally (Thorteaches, citing cyberseek.org). State-level breakdowns show which certifications employers in your state request (WorkingNation). Check your own state's data before paying for an exam, rather than assuming national demand applies locally.

How much does this cost to get started?+

The cheapest viable start is free: community or free-tier versions of the scanning and testing tools named for this occupation — Nessus, Nexpose, Burp Suite, Metasploit (O*NET OnLine, 2026) — running on a laptop. Paid steps come later. A CompTIA Security+ bundle includes an exam voucher, one retake, and 12-month CertMaster Learn and CertMaster Labs licences (TechTarget); CompTIA publishes current pricing, and bootcamp and degree costs vary by provider and state. Get a written price before you commit to any of them.

How long until I am employable?+

From an existing IT or help-desk role, plan 6-18 months of part-time study using the plan above. With no technical background, 18-36 months is more realistic, because the first 6 months go on networking and operating-system fundamentals before any security tooling. Those are preparation ranges, not hiring promises — no study plan guarantees an offer.

Is the job market actually growing, or is that marketing?+

BLS projects employment of information security analysts to grow much faster than average from 2025 to 2035, with openings projected each year on average over the decade, and reports 2025 median pay of $129,180 a year, or $62.11 an hour (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). CyberSeek tracks national online cybersecurity openings using job demand data from Lightcast (formerly Burning Glass) combined with BLS supply data and figures from certification bodies (NIST, 2016; CyberSeek, 2025).

Which single skill should I learn first if my time is limited?+

Vulnerability scanning, closely followed by writing up what you found. Nessus is flagged as an "In Demand" technology skill for this occupation because it appears frequently in employer postings (O*NET OnLine, 2026), and preparing incident reports and recommending security standards are listed duties (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Four to eight weeks of focused practice gives you a scan-and-report artefact you can show in an interview.

Sources

  1. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Information Security Analysts : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025)
  2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Information Security Analysts Occupational Outlook Handbook (archived PDF) (2021)
  3. O*NET OnLine — 15-1212.00 - Information Security Analysts (2026)
  4. O*NET OnLine — Technology Skills: Information Security Analysts (2026)
  5. CyberSeek (CompTIA and Lightcast, supported by NIST NICE) — Cybersecurity Supply And Demand Heat Map (2025)
  6. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) — NIST Announces CyberSeek, an Interactive Resource for Cybersecurity Career Development (2016-11)
  7. Thorteaches (citing cyberseek.org/heatmap.html) — IT Security – from Cyberseek.org: 'More open CISSP job openings, than the total number CISSP certified individuals in the US'
  8. WorkingNation — Cybersecurity jobs are everywhere. Here's how to find them
  9. TechTarget — What is CompTIA Security+? An introduction to Security+ certification
  10. Cybersecurity Guide (cybersecurityguide.org) — An Overview of the CompTIA Security+ Certification Process

title: 10 Job Search Strategies That Actually Work
dek: Ten concrete moves — weekly outreach counts, posting-age filters, a tracker column that forces a next step — and how to run three of them in one week.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
Most job search advice fails because it names a category of effort rather than an action you can start on a Tuesday. The strategies below each have a trigger, a cadence and a number you can count at the end of the week, so you can tell the difference between a search that's working and one that's just busy.

None of them guarantees an interview, and the mix that works depends on your field, your location and whether the roles you want are posted publicly at all. Pick three, run them for two weeks, and keep the ones that produce conversations.

Key takeaways

  • Send 5 informational interview requests a week — and log replies, not sends
  • Apply to postings under 48 hours old using the date-posted filter
  • Run one mock interview a week on the employer's video platform

The Strategies

1. Send 5 informational interview requests a week

Pick one target job title or company, find two or three people doing that work, and contact them by call or email explaining your purpose and proposing a couple of times — then confirm the date, time and format once they reply (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). The point is not to ask for a job: it's to learn about the work environment and trends in the field, get a read on whether the company fits you, and meet people who may offer guidance or leads later (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Signal of success: two completed conversations a week, measured by calls held, not messages sent.

2. Message 3 alumni from your school each week through LinkedIn's alumni tool

On LinkedIn, go to your school's university page and open the Alumni section, which lets you filter graduates by where they live, where they work and what they do. Shortlist three whose current title matches the job you want, and send a short note referencing the specific thing you want to learn. Signal of success: a reply rate you can actually track — count replies out of messages sent each week and watch whether rewording the first line moves it.

3. Apply to postings under 48 hours old using the date-posted filter

Both LinkedIn and Indeed let you narrow job search results by how recently a job was posted (LinkedIn offers a "Past 24 hours" option; Indeed has a "Date posted" filter). Spend your first applying block of the day only on fresh postings, and leave older ones for a weekly sweep. Signal of success: at least 70% of the applications you logged this week came from postings less than two days old — the ratio of applications to interviews varies enormously by field and is never a fixed number, so measure your own.

4. Build a requirements-versus-qualifications table before every application

Write down each requirement listed in the posting and, next to it, what you have against it — this shows you where you may be lacking and lets you plan how to address the gap during the interview (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Do this before you write anything, because the gaps tell you what the cover letter has to answer. Signal of success: every application in your tracker has a completed table with at least one planned answer for the weakest row.

5. Rewrite your resume's top third to match the posting's job title and three keywords

Tailoring is not a vague instruction: change the headline title to the exact title in the posting where it's honest to do so, and make sure three terms the posting repeats appear in your summary or first role, with a number attached to at least one. Keep a master version and save each tailored copy under the employer name. Signal of success: you can point at three specific edits per application and say which line of the posting each one answers.

6. Write a 30-second elevator pitch and rehearse it out loud ten times

CareerOneStop advises preparing an elevator pitch, saying it helps you feel more confident when networking and get better results (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Cover what you do, what you're looking for, and one concrete example — then say it aloud until you stop reading it. Signal of success: you can deliver it in under 30 seconds, from memory, without a filler sentence at the start.

7. Set three saved searches with daily email alerts and triage them in one 20-minute block

Indeed and LinkedIn both let you save a search and receive email alerts when new matching jobs appear. Create three — one for your exact title, one for an adjacent title, one for a skill or tool you want to use — and open them all in a single scheduled block instead of refreshing all day. Signal of success: inbox to shortlist in 20 minutes, with five saved roles a week worth a full application.

8. Keep a one-tab tracker with a "next action date" column

Columns: company, role, date applied, source, contact name, status, next action, next action date. The next-action column is what turns a list into a system, because it tells you what today's work is without re-reading everything. Signal of success: zero rows with a next action date in the past at the end of each week.

9. Run one mock interview a week with a friend on the employer's video platform

CareerOneStop's tips for virtual interviews are to be tech-ready by checking your computer, camera and microphone and practicing on the employer's video platform; research the employer and job description; set up a quiet, uncluttered, professional-looking space; and do a practice run by asking a friend for a mock interview (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Use the friend's feedback to improve your answers, eye contact and engagement before the real thing (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Signal of success: one recorded or reviewed practice run per week, with two specific changes noted.

10. Follow up seven calendar days after applying, to a named person

Put the follow-up date in your tracker when you apply, find the hiring manager or recruiter by name, and send one short message. Personalize every line of the template below before you send it — as written it will read like a form letter, which is the one thing it must not do.

Follow-up note — edit before sending

Subject: [Job title] — application from [your name]

Hi [first name], I applied for the [job title] role on [date] and wanted to add one thing: [one specific, relevant result or project that matches a requirement in the posting]. If it's useful, I'm happy to walk through how I'd approach [specific challenge named in the posting]. Either way, thanks for your time.

Signal of success: a follow-up sent on schedule for every application that has a named contact, and a count of how many produce a human reply.

Putting It Together

Don't run all ten. In a first week, combine Set three saved searches with daily email alerts and triage them in one 20-minute block with Apply to postings under 48 hours old using the date-posted filter. The alerts do the finding overnight; your morning block does the sorting. Everything you shortlist goes straight into the tracker from Keep a one-tab tracker with a "next action date" column, with the follow-up date filled in on the day you apply rather than later.

Attach Build a requirements-versus-qualifications table before every application to each shortlisted role, and let it drive Rewrite your resume's top third to match the posting's job title and three keywords. The table tells you which requirements you meet cleanly — those are the keywords worth putting near the top — and which ones you'll need to address in conversation. Two thorough applications built this way will usually take the same time as six skimmed ones.

For the people side, pair Send 5 informational interview requests a week with Write a 30-second elevator pitch and rehearse it out loud ten times, because the pitch is what you'll need the moment someone says yes. Block one hour early in the week for outreach and one slot later for whatever conversations land. If interviews start coming in, add Run one mock interview a week with a friend on the employer's video platform and drop the volume of applications rather than the preparation — at that point, conversion matters more than count.

Frequently asked questions

How much time a week does this take?+

A workable version is about six to eight hours: one 20-minute triage block most weekdays, two longer blocks for tailored applications, and one hour for outreach. If you're employed full time, run the alert triage and tracker daily and keep outreach to a single evening slot rather than trying to do everything.

Do informational interviews work if I'm changing careers?+

They tend to be more useful for career changers than for people staying put, because you're buying information you don't have — how the work actually runs, which of your existing skills translate, and what the field's trends look like. Be direct that you're exploring a move, and ask about the path people took rather than asking for a referral in the first conversation.

Is following up after an application worth it, or does it annoy recruiters?+

One short, specific message a week after applying is normal professional behaviour; repeated chasing is not. Response rates vary by employer size, hiring volume and whether applications route through a shared inbox, so treat silence as information about the process rather than about you.

Do I need paid tools or a premium subscription?+

No. Saved searches, email job alerts, date-posted filters and school alumni directories are free features on the major job boards and on LinkedIn, and a spreadsheet does everything a paid tracker does. Check what your state's public workforce agency or local library offers before paying for anything, since availability differs by state.

Sources

  1. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — How to network
  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Informational interviews
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Interview tips
  4. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Virtual interviews
  5. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Master Virtual Job Interviews with These 4 Tips video

title: 12 Habits That Help New Employees Thrive at Work
dek: From a standing buddy chat to a written recap after every briefing, the small routines of your first 90 days decide how fast people trust your work.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
Starting a new job is less about talent than about the handful of routines you set up in your first few weeks. Gallup reported in 2021 that only 12% of U.S. employees say their company does a good job of onboarding, and only 29% of new hires feel fully prepared and supported to excel after it — which means most people have to build their own structure rather than wait for one to arrive.

The habits below are specific: a phrase to say, a slot in the calendar, a note to keep. They work whether your employer runs a formal 30- to 90-day programme or hands you a laptop and wishes you luck. What varies by employer, country and team is the formality — scripts that sound normal in one office read as pushy in another, so adjust the wording and keep the mechanism.

Key takeaways

  • Meet your onboarding buddy repeatedly, not once: SHRM reported in 2022 that 86 percent of new hires who met a buddy four to eight times in their first 90 days said it made them more productive.
  • Keep one running question list and bring it to your weekly 1:1 instead of pinging colleagues all day — you stop interrupting people and you get fuller answers in one sitting.
  • Send a short recap after every briefing ("here's what I understood — correct me if I've got it wrong") so wrong assumptions surface in week one, not at the deadline.

The Habits

  1. Book a recurring chat with your onboarding buddy in week one. SHRM reported in 2022 that 56 percent of new hires who met their buddy at least once in their first 90 days said it helped them become productive quickly, rising to 73 percent for two to three meetings, 86 percent for four to eight, and 97 percent for more than eight — frequency is the whole point. On day two, message whoever was assigned to you (or a colleague who has been there a year or more, which NYU Wasserman's programme lead Mendez suggests as the minimum for a useful buddy) and say: "Could we put 20 minutes in the diary every Tuesday for my first three months? I'd rather save my questions for you than interrupt people all day."
  1. Keep one running question list instead of asking as you go. Batching turns ten small interruptions into one conversation where the person can give you context, not just an answer. Open a single note on your first morning titled "Questions — [team name]", add to it all week, and bring the list to your 1:1; the one exception is anything that blocks you for more than 30 minutes, which you ask immediately.
  1. Send a recap after every briefing for your first month. Writing back what you heard exposes the thing you misunderstood while it still costs nothing to fix. Within an hour of any handover meeting, send four or five lines: "Thanks — here's what I took away: 1) the draft goes to Priya first, 2) deadline is the 14th, 3) I own the data pull but not the slides. Correct me if I've got any of that wrong."
  1. Write your own version of the job description in week one. Gallup has found that only 43% of employees strongly agree they have a clear job description, and new starters are the most exposed to that fog. Draft a single page listing what you think you own, what you contribute to, and what you don't touch, then open your second-week 1:1 with: "I've written down how I understand my remit — can you tell me what's wrong on this page?"
  1. Block two protected work windows a week from day one. Being instantly reachable all day means you never produce anything long enough to be judged on. Put two 90-minute blocks in your calendar labelled with the actual task, and set a status message that tells people how to break through: "Heads down on the Q3 report until 11 — call me if it's urgent."
  1. Ask for the unwritten version of any documented process. Written procedures describe the official route; colleagues know which steps the team actually skips and which ones trigger a rejection. When someone sends you a wiki page, reply: "Got it, thanks. Is there anything on here that's out of date, or a step people usually do differently?"
  1. Run two 20-minute intro conversations a week for your first six weeks. Knowing who owns what saves days of routing work to the wrong person, and the people you've met are the ones who answer you fastest later. Send the same three-line invite each time: "I'm new on the X team and I'll be sending you Y. Could I get 20 minutes to ask what you need from me and what usually goes wrong?"
  1. Flag slippage at the halfway point, never at the deadline. A manager can reassign, trim scope or buy you two days when there's time left; at 5pm on the due date they can only absorb the damage. Put a reminder at the midpoint of every task in your first 90 days, and if you're behind, say: "I'm about half done and I don't think I'll finish by Thursday. I can either cut the competitor section or get it to you Monday — which do you prefer?"
  1. Keep a personal fixes file from your first login. The password resets, VPN quirks, file paths and approval chains you solve once will all come back, and writing them down turns you into the person who can onboard the next hire. Use whatever note app you already have, one line per fix, dated — and at day 60, offer the cleaned-up version to your manager as a starter guide.
  1. Ask for feedback at day 30, not at your probation review. Talya Bauer, author of a SHRM Foundation guideline on onboarding, has said that research and conventional wisdom both suggest employees get about 90 days to prove themselves in a new job, and SHRM advises leaders to check in with new employees in 30-day increments — if yours doesn't, start it yourself. Ask one narrow question rather than "how am I doing?": "In the first month, what's one thing I should do differently in the next month?"

Habits That Backfire vs. Habits That Work

Most new-starter mistakes are good instincts pointed the wrong way. The behaviours in the left column look identical to the ones in the right from a distance — the difference is in the mechanism.

Both look likeWhat backfiresWhat works instead
Asking lots of questionsYou message a senior colleague eight times on day three — "where's the brand folder?", "who approves this?", "what's the file naming?" Each one takes them out of their own work, and by the fourth they're answering in one word.You collect the same eight questions in your running list and bring them to the Tuesday buddy slot. You get the folder, the approver, the naming rule and the reason behind the naming rule in twelve minutes.
Being keenIn week two you volunteer for a cross-team project, a conference write-up and the social committee. In week five you deliver your first real task late, and that's the only thing anyone remembers.You deliver your assigned work on time through weeks one to four, then at your day-30 check-in say: "My core tasks are landing on schedule now — I'd like to take the conference write-up if it's still open."
Showing initiativeYou rebuild the team's tracking spreadsheet on day four because the old one is clunky. It turns out finance pulls a report off it on the 1st, and your version breaks it.You note the clunky bits as you use them for three weeks, then bring one slide to your 1:1: "This takes me about 40 minutes a week. Here's a version that takes ten — who would I need to check with before changing it?"
Being responsiveYou reply to every message within two minutes, all day, every day. Six weeks in you have a reputation for being helpful and nothing finished with your name on it.You keep two 90-minute blocks and answer everything else in batches at 11am and 4pm, with a status line saying when you're back. People learn your rhythm within a fortnight.
Taking feedback wellYour manager says your updates are too long. You say "sorry, I'll fix that" — and three weeks later you send another 600-word update, because you never agreed what shorter means.You say: "So five bullets rather than paragraphs, and only decisions and blockers? I'll do that for the next three and we can check at the end of the month whether it's working." Then you diarise the check.
Admitting a problemYou realise on Monday you can't hit Thursday's deadline, hope it resolves itself, and tell your manager Thursday afternoon. The client call is Friday and nothing can be moved.You flag it Monday with two options — cut a section or move to Monday — and the manager picks one. Half the stress, and you've shown you track your own work.
Learning the cultureYou accept every invitation and spend four weeks in meetings where you have no role, then discover you've missed the one recurring review where your work gets approved.In week one you ask your buddy: "Which of these meetings do I actually need, and which one would hurt most if I missed it?" You attend those and decline the rest with a line asking for the notes.

The pattern across all seven pairs: the version that works has a time attached to it — a weekly slot, a halfway-point check, a day-30 question — and the version that backfires happens whenever the impulse strikes.

Frequently asked questions

What if my employer doesn't assign me an onboarding buddy?+

Appoint one informally. SHRM's 2022 figures showed the benefit rises sharply with contact — 56 percent of new hires who met a buddy once in 90 days said it helped them become productive, against 86 percent of those who met four to eight times — so the recurring slot matters more than the official title. Pick a colleague who has been there at least a year, ideally two, and ask in week one for a standing 20 minutes: "I'd rather save my questions up for you than interrupt the whole team." That is habit one, run by you instead of by HR.

How do I ask for feedback without sounding anxious about my probation?+

Use the narrow day-30 question from habit ten rather than "how am I doing?" Asking "what's one thing I should do differently in the next month?" gives your manager something small and specific to answer, and it reads as planning rather than reassurance-seeking. SHRM advises managers to check in with new employees in 30-day increments anyway, so you are usually just starting a conversation they already intended to have — and Talya Bauer's point that employees get roughly 90 days to prove themselves is a good reason not to wait until month three to find out what's missing.

I'm remote. Do these habits still work?+

They matter more, because nobody can see you struggling. The three that carry the most weight remotely are the recap message after every briefing (habit three), since you lose the corridor correction; the twice-weekly 20-minute intro calls (habit seven), since you won't meet anyone by accident; and the status line on your protected work blocks (habit five), which replaces the visible signal of someone sitting with headphones on. Keep your question list in whatever note tool you already use and paste it straight into the 1:1 invite so your buddy can prepare.

Sources

  2. Gallup — 8 Practical Tips for Leaders for a Better Onboarding Process (2021-08-12)
  3. Gallup — Employee Expectations: Building a Foundation for Engagement
  4. Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) — Take 90 Days to Create the Proper Career Mindset for New Hires
  5. Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) — Don't Underestimate the Importance of Good Onboarding

title: 7 Habits That Help You Build Trust Fast with a New Team
dek: Trust on a new team comes from small, repeatable behaviors your colleagues can predict, and from a handful of habits you can start on day one.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
People decide whether you are reliable long before they decide whether you are talented. On a new team, that judgment is built from small, observable things: whether you remember what you were told, whether your deadlines hold, whether you check before changing something that already works.

Below are seven habits with the specific mechanism behind each one — what to say, when to say it, and where. How directly you can speak up varies by employer, by industry and by country, so treat the scripts as starting points and adjust them to how your team actually talks.

Key takeaways

  • Send your manager a "here's what I think I understood" summary at the end of week one — it catches wrong assumptions while they are still cheap to fix.
  • Give status updates before anyone asks, including bad news, so people stop checking on you by day 30.
  • Ask "what's been tried before?" for your first 60 days instead of proposing fixes — you find out which problems are already known and which are political.

The Habits

  1. Keep a week-one glossary and read it back out loud. People quietly downgrade you when they have to explain the same acronym twice, and a written record stops that happening. Open one note on your first morning, log every acronym, system name, recurring meeting and who owns what, then at the end of day five message your manager: "Here's what I think I understood this week — tell me where I've got it wrong: [your list]."
  1. Ship one small, visible thing by day ten. A finished small task proves more than a well-argued plan, because it shows you can get something through your team's actual process — the approvals, the review, the place things get posted. Pick something nobody is defending: fix the broken links in the onboarding doc, take and post notes for the weekly team meeting, or clear the oldest low-priority ticket in the queue.
  1. Book 20-minute intro calls with everyone your work touches, inside the first 30 days. Trust forms faster with people who have met you once on purpose than with people who only see your name in a thread. Send a one-line invite — "I'm new on [team] and our work overlaps; can I get 20 minutes to ask you three questions?" — and ask the same three every time: what are you working on that my work could slow down or speed up, what does a good handoff from someone in my role look like, and what do new people here usually get wrong?
  1. Give the status update before anyone asks for it. The moment a manager has to chase you, they start building a mental habit of checking on you, and that habit is hard to undo. Set a recurring reminder for Friday at 3pm to send a three-line update (done / in progress / blocked), and if a deadline is going to slip, say so on the morning it becomes obvious, not the afternoon it is due: "The report's at about 80% — I'll have it to you Thursday at 4 instead of Wednesday because the data pull failed twice. Does that break anything downstream for you?"
  1. Batch your questions, but escalate real blockers within 30 minutes. Constant one-off pings make you feel busy and make other people feel interrupted, while silence on a genuine blocker costs the team a day. Keep a running question list in the same note as your glossary and bring it to your next 1:1, but apply a 30-minute rule: if you are stuck with no next step after half an hour, post it once in the team channel where others can see the answer rather than DMing three people separately.
  1. Ask "what's been tried before?" for your first 60 days. Most obvious problems on an established team are known problems with a history, and walking into that history uninvited is the fastest way to look careless. When you spot something, phrase it as research rather than a proposal: "I noticed we do the weekly report by hand — has anyone tried automating it? I'd like to know what went wrong before I suggest anything."
  1. Credit people by name, in the channel where the work happened, within a day. Public, specific credit costs you nothing and makes people willing to help you again, which is most of what you need in month one. Not "thanks everyone" in a DM, but in the team channel: "Thanks to Priya for walking me through the billing flow yesterday — saved me a day of guessing."

One thing to check rather than assume: how new people are expected to speak in meetings. In some workplaces you are expected to push back in week one; in others, and in some countries, that reads as disrespectful. Ask your manager in your first week: "When someone new here disagrees in a meeting, do they say it in the room or bring it to you first?"

Habits That Backfire vs. Habits That Work

Most trust-damaging behavior in a first month is a good instinct applied without a mechanism. These pairs look similar from the outside and land very differently.

Asking questions constantly vs. batching with a 30-minute rule

  • Backfires: You DM a teammate seven times on Tuesday — where's the template, what's the password policy, who approves this. Each one takes them 30 seconds and breaks their concentration for five minutes. By Thursday they answer slower.
  • Works: You park six of those in your questions list for Thursday's 1:1, and the seventh — a locked system you cannot get past — you post in the team channel after 30 minutes stuck, where two people see the answer and one says "I had that too."

Promising fast turnarounds vs. promising a date you've checked

  • Backfires: Asked in week one if you can have the analysis by Friday, you say "Absolutely, no problem," then discover on Thursday you need access you don't have. Your first delivery is late.
  • Works: You say what you actually know out loud:

Agreeing to a deadline you haven't verified

"Friday looks doable, but I haven't run this pull before. Let me confirm by end of day tomorrow — if I can't get access today, I'll tell you Friday is Monday."

Suggesting improvements early vs. asking what's been tried

  • Backfires: In your second week you say in a team meeting that the approval process should be cut from three steps to one. Two of those steps exist because of an audit finding, and the person who built it is sitting opposite you.
  • Works: You ask the person who owns it, privately, "what's the history of the three-step approval?" — learn about the audit, and in week eight propose removing only the step nobody can justify.

Being available for everything vs. being reliable on a few things

  • Backfires: You say yes to four side requests in your first month, run out of hours, and deliver your actual assignment late. People remember the late assignment.
  • Works: You take one side request, finish it early, and tell the next person: "I can't get to that this week without my main project slipping — can it wait until the 14th, or should I check with [manager] about priorities?"

Over-documenting your work vs. one scheduled update

  • Backfires: You send your manager long daily recaps of everything you touched. They stop reading them by week two, so when you bury "blocked on vendor access" in paragraph four, nobody acts on it.
  • Works: One Friday 3pm message with three labeled lines — done, in progress, blocked — where "blocked" is never more than one sentence and always names who can unblock it.

Socializing broadly vs. 20-minute calls with the people your work touches

  • Backfires: You go to every coffee and happy hour, know everyone's weekend plans, and still have no idea who signs off on your deliverables or what the person downstream needs from you.
  • Works: You run the 20-minute intro calls from habit 3, so in week five, when a handoff goes wrong, you already know who to call and they already know your name.

Taking credit carefully vs. giving credit specifically

  • Backfires: You write "I pulled together the migration plan" in your month-one summary. Two people who spent an hour each explaining the system to you read it.
  • Works: "Migration plan is drafted — Dan and Alex walked me through the legacy setup, which is why the rollback section exists." You still get credit for writing it, and both of them answer your next question.

Frequently asked questions

What changes if the team is fully remote?+

The habits that rely on being seen have to be deliberate instead. The 20-minute intro calls in habit 3 matter more, because there is no hallway version of them — book them as video calls in your first 30 days rather than waiting to bump into people. Habit 7 also carries more weight remotely: if you thank someone in a DM, no one else sees it, so post the specific thank-you in the team channel where the work happened.

My manager keeps canceling our 1:1. Where do my batched questions go?+

Move habit 5 into writing. Keep the same running question list, and send it as a short numbered message before the slot that got canceled: "Three things I'd have asked today — answer whichever are quick, I'll hold the rest." Pair it with habit 4's Friday update so your manager still sees your status weekly even when the meeting does not happen, and after two cancellations ask directly who else can answer day-to-day questions.

I was hired specifically to change things. Do I still wait 60 days?+

No, but you still run habit 6's question first. In your first week, ask your manager what the mandate actually covers: "What am I expected to change, and what should I leave alone for now?" Then before each proposal, ask the person who owns the current process what's been tried before — it takes one conversation and it stops you from relitigating a decision that was made for a reason you can't see yet.

title: 7 Ways to Get More Interviews Without Applying to More Jobs
dek: Most of these take under three hours a week, and several of them work on applications you have already sent rather than new ones.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
If you are sending out applications and hearing nothing, sending more of the same is rarely the fix. The higher-leverage moves are changing what happens to each application after you submit it, and building a handful of conversations with people who already do the work you want.

The seven strategies below are things you can start this week with no budget. None of them guarantees an interview — nothing does — but each one has a signal you can count, so you can tell within a fortnight whether you are actually doing it.

Key takeaways

  • Start with **Build a 25-company target list before you open another job board** — every other tactic gets easier once you have names.
  • **Pull exact keywords from each posting and use each one about twice** fixes applications you are already sending.
  • **Send three informational interview requests a week, asking for 20 minutes** is research, not a job ask — and it produces leads.

The Strategies

  • Build a 25-company target list before you open another job board. Decide the type of role and the type of employer you want, then write down actual organizations that match — CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated, advises identifying the job or company type first and then looking for network contacts in that field, using tools such as its Business Finder. Keep the list in one sheet with a column for a contact name and a column for whether you have a job alert set up for that employer. Signal: 25 named employers written down by the end of week one, each with either a contact or an alert attached.
  • Send three informational interview requests a week, asking for 20 minutes. An informational interview is an informal conversation with someone in a career or company you are targeting, and it is research rather than a request for a job offer (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Ask for something small and specific — a sample outreach message from the same source suggests requesting a 20-minute meeting scheduled a couple of weeks out. These conversations are described as helping you learn the work environment, judge whether a career or company fits, get advice on breaking in, and meet people who can pass on future contacts or leads. Signal: three requests sent every week, and one or two conversations actually on the calendar.
  • Pull exact keywords from each posting and use each one about twice. An applicant tracking system scores incoming applications and ranks them by how well each matches the employer's stated criteria (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated), and the same guidance notes that qualified people get filtered out when they miss the employer's chosen keywords, use fonts or formatting the system cannot read, or look as though they lack preferred experience. The recommended approach is to analyze the posting for its exact terms and use each identified keyword roughly twice — more repetition is not helpful — and to change those keywords for each different opening rather than sending one static resume everywhere. Tailor three things specifically: the job title line at the top, the tools and methods named in the posting, and the two or three bullets where you can attach a number. Signal: zero applications submitted without a keyword pass, logged in your tracker.
  • Ask someone who already holds the job to red-line your wording. The terminology that reads well to you may not be what the field actually uses; CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated, suggests asking someone in a similar job to check your wording, including finding such people on LinkedIn, and checking professional association sites or an Occupation Profile for additional keywords. Send one page, not a full packet, and ask a narrow question: which phrases here would a hiring manager in your team not recognize? Signal: two people in your target job title have marked up your resume within three weeks.
  • Switch on Open to Work with specific titles, locations, and start date. LinkedIn's Open to Work feature lets you signal that you are job searching either publicly, with a green #OpenToWork photo frame visible to all members, or privately so it is visible only to recruiters using LinkedIn Recruiter (contentin.io, undated). When you enable it you specify job titles, locations, start date and job types, and that information feeds recruiter search and job matching — so vague titles waste the feature. Signal: the titles you entered match the titles on your target list, and you review inbound messages weekly.
  • Audit what an employer finds when they search your name. Social and career networking sites such as LinkedIn, X and Facebook are described as essential job search tools for learning about industries and companies and meeting contacts, and employers also use them to find and check out candidates before deciding whether to interview or hire (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Search your own name in a logged-out browser, look at the first page of results, and fix the obvious gaps: a headline that names the work rather than your last job title, a profile photo, and privacy settings on anything you would not want a stranger reading. Signal: first-page results for your name are either professional or neutral, checked once a month.
  • Follow up once, seven business days after applying, to a named person. Pick one real person — the hiring manager, the team lead, or the recruiter named in the posting — and send a short note referencing something concrete from the job description rather than asking for a status update. Do it once per application, log the date, and let it go after that. Signal: a follow-up date recorded against every application in your tracker, and a running count of replies you can compare month to month (your own numbers only — reply rates vary enormously by field and employer).

Two of these need words. Rewrite both before sending: the bracketed parts are the minimum you have to change, and the sentence about why you are contacting that person is what makes it worth reading.

Informational interview request

Subject: 20 minutes about [job title] work at [company]?

Hi [first name] — I'm researching a move into [field or role type] and came across your profile while reading about [specific project, team, or topic you actually saw]. I'm not asking about openings; I'd like to understand what the work is really like day to day and what you'd tell someone trying to move in from [your current field]. Would you have 20 minutes in the next couple of weeks? I'm happy to work around your calendar. — [your name]

One-time follow-up after applying

Subject: [job title] application — [your name]

Hi [first name], I applied for the [exact job title, requisition number if there is one] role on [date]. The part of the posting about [specific responsibility or tool named in the ad] lines up closely with [one specific thing you have done, with a number if you have one]. If it's useful, I can send a short note on how I'd approach it. Either way, thanks for reading. — [your name]

Putting It Together

Do not try all seven in one week. Spend the first week almost entirely on Build a 25-company target list before you open another job board, because it decides who you contact and which keywords matter. Give it two sittings of about an hour. While the list is fresh, do Switch on Open to Work with specific titles, locations, and start date in the same sitting — you are copying the job titles off your own list into the field that feeds recruiter search, which takes ten minutes once you know what to type.

From week two, run two things in parallel on a fixed rhythm. On Monday, send your three messages for Send three informational interview requests a week, asking for 20 minutes, drawn from the target list rather than from whoever appears in your feed. On whichever days you apply, run Pull exact keywords from each posting and use each one about twice before you hit submit, and set a reminder seven business days out so Follow up once, seven business days after applying, to a named person happens without you having to remember it. That combination means every application leaves with the employer's own vocabulary on it and has one scheduled nudge behind it, while two or three conversations a month build up in the background.

Use the slower weeks for the two maintenance tasks. Ask someone who already holds the job to red-line your wording fits naturally at the end of an informational conversation — if the call went well, ask whether they would glance at one page. Audit what an employer finds when they search your name is a monthly half-hour, best done just before you start sending outreach, since the people you message will look you up. If you can only sustain three of the seven, keep the target list, the keyword pass, and the weekly outreach; the rest are multipliers on those.

Frequently asked questions

How much time does this take each week?+

Once the target list exists, a realistic week is about two to three hours: thirty minutes writing outreach messages, an hour or so on keyword passes for the applications you are actually sending, and whatever time the conversations themselves take. The front-loaded cost is the company list, which is a one-off few hours. If you have less time than that, drop the number of applications rather than the keyword pass.

Does informational outreach work if I'm changing careers?+

It is arguably more useful for career changers than for anyone else, because the stated purpose is learning rather than asking for a job — CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated, describes these conversations as a way to gain clarity on whether a career or company fits and to get advice on breaking into a field. Be upfront in the message that you are coming from another field; it gives the person a clearer question to answer. Expect some messages to go unanswered, which is normal and not a verdict on you.

Will my current employer see that I've turned on Open to Work?+

LinkedIn offers a recruiters-only setting that hides the public green badge, but it states that even then it cannot guarantee recruiters at your current company won't see the signal (contentin.io, undated). If being discovered would cause you a real problem, treat the private setting as lower risk rather than no risk, and lean harder on direct outreach instead.

Is there anything here I have to pay for?+

No. Every strategy above runs on a free account, a spreadsheet and your own time. Paid resume services and premium job board tiers may be worth it to you for other reasons, but none of the seven depends on one.

Sources

  1. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Take Your Network Online
  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Informational interview
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Applicant tracking systems
  4. contentin.io — What Does Open to Work Mean on LinkedIn?

title: 8 Best Job Boards for Remote Jobs
dek: A comparison of eight places to search for remote work: what each one costs, what each actually filters well, and where each one falls short.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
Remote job boards fall into three groups: paid screened boards, free remote-only boards, and the big general boards with a remote filter bolted on. Each group fails in a different way, so most people searching seriously end up using two or three at once rather than picking a winner.

This guide compares eight of them on cost, what they are genuinely good at, and the limitation you will hit after a week of use. Pricing and availability change, and some boards restrict listings by country or by US state, so check the current pages before you pay for anything.

Key takeaways

  • Use FlexJobs when you want pre-screened listings and will actually use the subscription — its annual plan is billed at $5.95/month, paid as $71.40 up front (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12).
  • Use We Work Remotely's free Basic membership to browse, save listings and follow companies at startups and small remote-first teams (We Work Remotely, undated).
  • Use LinkedIn's Remote workplace-type filter with a saved job alert to catch roles from companies that never post on remote-only boards.

At-a-Glance Comparison

Costs below are what each platform charges the job seeker, not the employer. Prices are listed in US dollars and change often — treat the figures as a snapshot of the cited date, not a current quote.

Tool/PlatformBest ForCostStandout FeatureLimitation
FlexJobsScreened remote and flexible listings outside techPaid; plans start at $9.95/month and the annual plan is $5.95/month, paid as $71.40 up front (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12)Markets 100% verified remote listings plus job search tools (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12)Nothing is browsable at depth without paying, and plans auto-renew unless you cancel
We Work RemotelyFully remote roles at startups and small distributed teamsFree Basic membership; Pro is $14.95/month on a 12-month commitment (We Work Remotely, undated)Free tier lets you browse, save listings, upload a resume and follow companies (We Work Remotely, undated)You must create an account to browse and apply, and application volume is capped below the Pro tier
Remote.coBrowsing by function rather than keywordFree to searchCategory pages for areas like accounting, customer service, entry-level and freelance work (Remote.co, 2024-09-26)Smaller listing volume than the big boards, and many entries route you to an external application page
LinkedInRoles at companies that never post on remote-only boardsFree to search; a paid Premium tier existsThe Remote option under the on-site/hybrid/remote workplace filter, plus saved job alertsEmployers mislabel hybrid roles as remote, and popular postings draw very large applicant pools
IndeedRaw volume and non-technical remote rolesFree to searchSaved searches with email alerts, plus company review pages attached to listingsDuplicate and stale postings are common, and staffing agencies repost the same role repeatedly
Remote OKFast scanning of new tech-leaning remote postingsFree to searchTag-based feeds (by role, stack and region) and an RSS feed you can pipe elsewhereHeavily weighted to engineering, marketing and crypto; listed pay ranges are estimates, not offers
WellfoundEarly-stage startup roles with direct founder contactFree to searchCompany profiles that state compensation and equity ranges on the listing itselfStartup-only, and many roles are early-stage with hiring timelines that stall
Working NomadsPassive, low-effort monitoring by categoryFree to searchCurated email digests split by job categoryIt aggregates from other boards, so you see duplicates and thin native filters

Detailed Breakdown

FlexJobs. This is a subscription board built around screening. FlexJobs markets full access to 100% verified remote jobs plus job search tools, with plans starting at $9.95/month (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12). Entry options include a 14-day full access trial for $2.95 that auto-renews at $23.95 every 4 weeks if you do not cancel, a 3-month plan at $9.95/month billed as $29.85 up front, and an annual plan at $5.95/month billed as $71.40 up front (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12). The screening claim is the platform's own description of its process, not an independently audited one — treat it as a reason to expect fewer scam listings, not a guarantee of none. FlexJobs is most useful if your field is administrative, healthcare-adjacent, education, bookkeeping or project management, where remote-only free boards are thin. Set a calendar reminder for the day before any trial renews.

We Work Remotely. The site reports 6M+ monthly visitors and a 90% fill rate on job posts, and its counter showed 42,261 jobs posted at time of access (We Work Remotely, undated) — all platform-reported figures, so read them as marketing to employers rather than your odds of hearing back. Employers pay $299 to post a job (We Work Remotely, undated), which filters out casual listers. For job seekers, a free Basic membership covers browsing, saving listings, uploading a resume and following companies, but an account is required to browse and apply at all (We Work Remotely, undated). Paid tiers add volume: Pro at $14.95/month on a 12-month commitment, with a $2.95 first month, unlocks unlimited applications, up to 5 custom job alerts and subscriber-only events, while TopAccess at $29.95/month on a 12-month commitment with no free trial adds partner marketplace access to Toptal, Arc and PeoplePerHour, unlimited Toptal resume tailoring and eligibility for a performance reward of up to $500 (We Work Remotely, undated).

Remote.co. A smaller, cleanly organised board that lists openings in categories such as remote accounting, customer service, entry-level and freelance jobs (Remote.co, 2024-09-26). Its value is browsing by function when you do not yet know the right job title to search for — useful if you are switching fields and the keyword you would type is the wrong one. Volume is the trade-off; check it weekly rather than daily.

LinkedIn. The reason to use it is not the board but the companies on it. Filter job search results by workplace type and select Remote, then save the search as a job alert so new postings arrive by email. Add a second alert with a tighter title so you are not reading the same generic feed twice. Two cautions: employers choose the workplace-type tag themselves, so hybrid and in-office roles leak into remote results, and claims that applying within the first hours improves your odds are anecdotal or drawn from platform-published posts, not settled evidence. Apply when your application is tailored, not when a timer says so.

Indeed. Best for raw coverage, especially in customer support, claims, scheduling, billing and sales roles that rarely appear on remote-only boards. Type Remote in the location field or use the Remote filter, then save the search and turn on email alerts from your account. Expect duplicates, agency reposts and listings that stayed up after the role closed. Scan the posting date before you spend time on a long application form.

Remote OK. A fast, dense feed organised by tags, with an RSS option if you prefer to read listings in a reader rather than a browser. Good for engineers, designers and growth marketers who want to see what posted today in under five minutes. Pay ranges shown on listings are estimates generated by the site, so do not quote them back to an employer as if they came from the company.

Wellfound. Startup-focused, and the useful part is that company profiles often publish compensation and equity ranges on the listing, which saves you a screening call to find out the band. Applications frequently reach a founder or a small hiring team directly. The limitation is structural: early-stage companies pause hiring, and job seeker profiles are the primary application route, so a thin profile is a real handicap here.

Working Nomads. A curation layer rather than a source. You pick categories and receive email digests, which makes it the lowest-effort way to keep a passive search alive while you are employed. Because it aggregates, many links lead back to boards you already check.

One constraint that cuts across all eight: a listing marked remote may still be restricted to specific countries, or to particular US states where the employer is registered to run payroll. That rule varies by employer and by state, and it is an employment and tax question rather than something a job board can resolve — read the posting's location line before applying and ask the recruiter directly if it is ambiguous.

Where to Access Each Tool

  • FlexJobs — the official pricing and plans page for current plan costs and renewal terms, then your account's subscription settings page to set or cancel renewals.
  • We Work Remotely — the remote jobs category index page to browse, plus the membership comparison page for Basic, Pro and TopAccess tier details.
  • Remote.co — the remote jobs board category index pages (accounting, customer service, entry-level, freelance and the rest) rather than the homepage.
  • LinkedIn — the Jobs tab search results page, with the on-site/hybrid/remote workplace filter set to Remote; then the saved jobs and job alerts management page to manage alert cadence.
  • Indeed — the job search results page with Remote in the location field or the Remote filter applied; then the My Jobs and saved search pages in your account to enable email alerts.
  • Remote OK — the per-tag listing pages for your role or stack, plus the RSS feed URL if you read listings in a feed reader.
  • Wellfound — the job seeker signup and profile editor first, since applications run through the profile, then the jobs search page.
  • Working Nomads — the email digest signup page, choosing categories individually rather than subscribing to everything.

Frequently asked questions

Is a paid remote job board worth it if free boards exist?+

It depends on whether your field is well served by free boards. If you work in engineering, design or growth marketing, the free remote-only boards carry most of what a paid board would show you. If you work in administration, bookkeeping, education or healthcare support, a subscription like FlexJobs — $9.95/month on the 3-month plan or $5.95/month on the annual plan, billed as $71.40 up front (FlexJobs, 2026-05-12) — buys you screened listings in categories the free boards barely cover. Decide after a month of free searching, not before.

Should I pay for an upgraded tier on a free board?+

Only if you have hit the specific cap the upgrade removes. On We Work Remotely, Pro at $14.95/month on a 12-month commitment lifts the application limit and adds up to 5 custom job alerts, while TopAccess at $29.95/month on a 12-month commitment adds partner marketplace access and resume tailoring (We Work Remotely, undated). A 12-month commitment is a long bet on a search you hope will be short, so check the cancellation terms on the membership page first.

How many boards should I actually use at once?+

Two or three, chosen for different coverage: one remote-only board for roles at distributed companies, one general board with a remote filter for employers who post nowhere else, and optionally one digest for passive monitoring. More than that and you spend your search time reading duplicates. Give each one a fixed slot in your week rather than checking all of them daily.

Do boards that advertise a high fill rate mean I'm more likely to get hired?+

No. We Work Remotely's reported 90% fill rate and 6M+ monthly visitors describe employer outcomes and site traffic (We Work Remotely, undated), and they are figures the platform publishes about itself. A high fill rate tells you listings are real and roles get closed; it says nothing about your individual chances against the other applicants in the same pool.

What should I tailor before applying through any of these boards?+

Match the job title in the posting to the title line on your resume where it is honest to do so, mirror the three or four skill terms the posting repeats, and put a number on your two most relevant bullet points — volume handled, cycle time, budget, headcount. On boards like Wellfound where a profile is the application, make those edits in the profile itself, since that is what the hiring team reads.

Sources

  1. FlexJobs — FlexJobs Subscription Pricing (2026-05-12)
  2. We Work Remotely — We Work Remotely (Employers landing page)
  3. We Work Remotely — Frequently Asked Questions | Remote Jobs & Hiring - We Work Remotely
  4. Remote.co — Remote Jobs in Today's Popular Categories - Remote.co (2024-09-26)
