title: 9 Communication Habits Top Performers Use in Their First Year
dek: The specific phrases, timings and check-ins that make a new hire easy to work with — plus the near-identical habits that quietly annoy a team.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
Most of what gets you a reputation as a strong new hire in your first year is not talent. It is a short set of communication habits — reading a brief back before you start, batching your questions, flagging bad news early — repeated on a predictable schedule until people stop having to wonder what you are doing.

The stakes are real early on. Nearly one-third of new hires quit within their first six months, according to research cited by SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management, 10 August 2017), and the same body has been cited as finding that up to 20% of turnover happens in the first 45 days (HiringThing blog, citing SHRM, 2024). Onboarding researcher Talya Bauer notes that employees get roughly 90 days to prove themselves (SHRM, 10 August 2017). The habits below are the ones you can start on day one and still be running at month twelve.

Key takeaways

  • A Friday five-line update sent before 3pm means your manager never has to ask what you worked on — and you have a written record when review season arrives.
  • Reading the brief back in your own words before you start ("so you want a one-page draft by Thursday, Priya reviews it") catches the misunderstanding while it still costs ten seconds instead of three days.
  • Asking for feedback on one named thing — not "any feedback for me?" — gets you a usable answer, because the other person does not have to invent a topic on the spot.

The Habits

  1. The Friday five-line update. A short written summary stops your manager from having to reconstruct what you did, and it gives you a paper trail for your first review. Every Friday before 3pm, send five bullets by email or direct message: finished this week, in progress, blocked on, learned, planned for next week.
  1. The batched question list. Interrupting a busy colleague eleven times a day costs them their concentration; one list costs them twenty minutes. From your first week, keep a running note titled "Ask [manager's name]" in whatever your team already uses — a plain doc or notes app is fine — and bring it to your 1:1 instead of sending each item as it occurs to you.
  1. The read-back. Repeating an assignment in your own words surfaces the mismatch before you spend three days building the wrong thing. Do it at the end of every briefing conversation for your first 90 days: "So what I'm hearing is you want a one-page draft by Thursday, Priya reviews it before it goes to the client — have I got that right?"
  1. The 30-minute stuck rule. This protects you from both failure modes — the new hire who asks before trying, and the one who disappears for two days. Set a timer when you hit a wall; at 30 minutes, ask, and open with what you already tried: "I've been trying to get the export to run for half an hour. I checked the permissions and the date range. Where would you look next?"
  1. Naming your own deadline. Volunteering a date makes you easy to plan around and removes the need for anyone to chase you. When you take a task, say the date out loud: "I'll have a draft to you Wednesday at noon. If it's going to slip, you'll hear from me Tuesday morning."
  1. Asking for feedback on one named thing. Feedback-seeking behaviour — the deliberate effort to find out whether what you are doing is adequate — is a well-studied habit in organisational research (Ashford, 1986, as cited in academic work on the topic), and positive supervisor feedback has been found to improve employee performance in a three-wave study of 368 employees and their direct supervisors (research study hosted on ResearchGate, undated). Pick one artefact per week for your first 90 days: "On Monday's deck — was the level of detail right for that audience, or too much?"
  1. Early bad news. Managers can usually fix a late deliverable; they cannot fix one they learn about on the due date. The moment you know a date is at risk, send one message with three parts: what slipped, the new date, what you need. "The data pull is two days behind because the source file changed. New date is Friday the 14th. If you want it Wednesday, I'd need to drop the regional breakdown."
  1. The connection map. Bauer describes four levels of onboarding effectiveness — compliance, clarification, culture and connection (SHRM, 10 August 2017) — and connection is the one nobody schedules for you. In your first 30 days, book three 15-minute intro calls a week and ask one question in each: "What does a good week look like for you, and where does your work touch mine?"
  1. The written close-out. Verbal agreements in meetings evaporate; a three-line recap makes ownership visible without anyone having to be the enforcer. Within an hour of any meeting where work was assigned, post a short recap in the shared channel or thread the team already uses, with a name and a date on each item.

Two of these are worth hearing in full, because the wording does most of the work.

Raising a slipping deadline on day 40

"Quick heads-up before you hear it elsewhere: the vendor hasn't sent the figures, so the Thursday report will be Monday instead. I've emailed them and copied you. If Thursday is firm, I can send it with last month's numbers flagged as provisional — your call."

Asking for feedback in a 1:1 in month two

"One thing I'd like your read on. In the client call yesterday I jumped in to answer the pricing question — was that the right call here, or should I have handed it to Dan? I genuinely can't tell yet how this team handles that."

Habits That Backfire vs. Habits That Work

The habits that damage a new hire's reputation rarely look lazy. They usually look like effort pointed in the wrong direction. Each row below is the same instinct, played two ways.

SituationWhat backfiresWhat works
You have questions in week twoYou send your manager nine separate messages between 9am and 4pm. Each one is reasonable; together they teach her that answering you is a full-time job, and she starts replying slowly.You keep the "Ask [manager]" note, send only the one item that is blocking you right now, and bring the other eight to Thursday's 1:1. She answers all eight in fifteen minutes and feels helpful rather than interrupted.
You want to show you are workingYou message "just checking in — making good progress!" three times a week. There is nothing in it she can act on, so it reads as needing reassurance.You send the Friday five-line update at 2:45pm with one line under "blocked on." She reads it in forty seconds and unblocks you on Monday.
You are briefed on a taskYou nod, say "got it," and go away. Three days later you hand in a twelve-page analysis when what was wanted was a one-page summary for a board pack.You read the brief back — "one page, Thursday, Priya reviews it" — and she says "actually make it two pages and skip the methodology." Ten seconds, three days saved.
You want to improveYou end every 1:1 with "any feedback for me?" Your manager says "no, you're doing great," because she has not prepared and cannot think of anything on the spot.You ask about one named thing: "Was Monday's deck too detailed for that audience?" She has an actual opinion about that deck and gives it to you.
A deadline is slipping in month threeYou stay quiet and work weekends to rescue it. You miss it anyway by a day, and your manager finds out from the person who was waiting on it.You send the three-part message on the Tuesday — what slipped, new date, what you need — and she reshuffles the review slot. The work is late; your reliability is not in question.
You are building relationshipsYou send a blanket "would love to connect!" message to twenty people in your first week. Most ignore it, because there is no reason attached.You book three 15-minute calls a week with people whose work touches yours and ask what a good week looks like for them. By day 30 you know who to ask about what.
Something gets decided in a meetingYou rely on everyone remembering. Two weeks later, two people each thought the other owned the follow-up, and nobody wants to be the one who raises it.You post the three-line recap within the hour, with a name and a date beside each item. Nobody has to chase anyone, and corrections arrive the same day while the meeting is fresh.

How much of this is formalised for you depends heavily on the employer. Organisations with a standard onboarding process have been reported to see 50% greater new-hire productivity, and 69% of employees are said to be more likely to stay three years after a strong onboarding experience (Click Boarding statistics cited by SHRM, 10 August 2017). If your employer has none of that — common in small firms and startups — these habits are the structure you build yourself. Norms also vary by workplace and country: how direct you can be about a slipping deadline, and whether written recaps read as diligent or distrustful, differ between teams. Watch what your most-respected colleague does for two weeks and copy the format, not the personality.

Frequently asked questions

My manager keeps cancelling our 1:1s. What then?+

Fall back on the two habits that do not need a meeting. Keep sending the Friday five-line update before 3pm — it is the one thing that keeps your work visible when calendar time disappears — and convert the batched question list into a single message sent at a fixed time each week, with the questions numbered so they can be answered in order. If three 1:1s in a row are cancelled, raise it once with a specific ask rather than a complaint: "Can we move our 1:1 to a slot that protects it better, or would you rather I send questions in writing on Thursdays?"

How long do I need to keep this up before I can relax?+

Treat the full set as a 90-day protocol, since conventional wisdom and research both suggest employees get about 90 days to prove themselves (Talya Bauer, cited by SHRM, 10 August 2017). After that, the read-back can become occasional — you will know the house style by then — but keep the Friday update, the early bad news message and the written close-out running through month twelve. Worker productivity has been reported to peak after a year of employment (Gallup, cited in a HiringThing blog post, 2024), so your first year is still a ramp, not a plateau.

I work fully remote. Does any of this change?+

Three habits carry more weight. The written close-out after meetings matters more because there are no corridor corrections; the connection map needs deliberate scheduling because nobody will bump into you; and naming your own deadline substitutes for the visible signal of being seen at your desk. Keep the 30-minute stuck rule tighter too — say 20 minutes — because remote teams cannot see you struggling.

Sources

  1. SHRM (Society for Human Resource Management) — Don't Underestimate the Importance of Good Onboarding (2017-08-10)
  2. HiringThing (blog), citing Gallup — 2024 Employee Onboarding Statistics You Need (2024)
  3. ScholarWorks IUPUI (academic thesis citing Ashford, 1986) — Effects of Feedback Seeking Behavior on Supervisor
  4. ResearchGate (hosting academic study) — Positive feedback, feedback seeking and performance: Feedback orientation as a moderator

title: 9 Job Search Tactics for Career Changers
dek: Nine concrete moves — target-company lists, informational interviews, ATS-aware rewrites — each with a weekly cadence and a signal that tells you it's working.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
Changing careers makes a job search slower, because you are arguing a case as well as applying. The fix is not more applications — it is a small set of repeatable weekly actions that build evidence you can do the new work, plus a way to see which ones are producing replies.

For context on pacing: among all unemployed people in 2024, the average duration of unemployment was 21.6 weeks and the median was 9.6 weeks (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). Career changers often sit on the longer side of that, so plan a search you can sustain for months rather than sprint for three weeks.

Key takeaways

  • Build a list of 8-10 target companies and contact 1-2 each week — a steady pipeline beats a burst of applications.
  • Book two informational interviews a week with people doing the job now — the fastest way to learn the new field's vocabulary.
  • Scan 10-15 postings for your target title before you touch your resume — tailor to what actually repeats, not to guesswork.

The Strategies

Pick three to start. Running all nine badly is worse than running three on a schedule.

1. Scan 10-15 postings for your target title before you touch your resume

CareerOneStop, the U.S. Department of Labor's job-search site, recommends scanning 10-15 job postings with your targeted job title and noting the requirements that come up most often, then formatting your resume with applicant tracking systems in mind, since those systems have become common in U.S. hiring (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). Tailoring means three specific things: matching the posted job title in your headline, carrying over the exact phrasing of recurring skills, and putting a number on results you can actually verify. Signal of success: you can list the five requirements that appeared in most of those postings, and each one appears somewhere in your resume in the employer's words.

2. Build a list of 8-10 target companies and contact 1-2 each week

CareerOneStop's sample job search plan suggests building a list of 8-10 companies to approach with job inquiries, using its Business Finder tool, and aiming to contact 1-2 businesses every week (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). Keep the list in one spreadsheet with columns for company, the person you contacted, the date, and the next action date — that spreadsheet is your tracking system. Signal of success: two logged outreach contacts per week, every week, with no row sitting past its next-action date.

3. Book two informational interviews a week with people doing the job now

An informational interview is an informal conversation with someone working in a career or company that interests you, used to learn about the work environment, gain clarity, get advice, and meet further contacts (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). The same guidance says to make contact by phone or email, introduce yourself and your situation — such as exploring a career change — and explain the purpose of the call. Personalize the message below before sending; the bracketed parts are not optional.

Outreach email — edit every bracket before sending

Subject: [Your current field] person moving into [target field] — 20 minutes?

Hi [Name] — I'm [your name], currently [current role] and working toward a move into [target role]. I found your profile through [specific source: alumni directory, a post you wrote, a mutual contact]. I'm not asking you to pass my resume on; I'd like 20 minutes to ask how [specific part of their work] actually operates day to day. [Two options for times]. Happy to work around your calendar.

Signal of success: two conversations booked per week. Reply rates to cold outreach vary widely by field and by how specific your message is, so treat any ratio you read as approximate.

*4. Run the ONET Interest Profiler before you lock in a target title**

My Next Move, from the U.S. Department of Labor's Employment and Training Administration, helps new job seekers, students, and career explorers investigate over 900 occupations and includes the ONET Interest Profiler, a standardized assessment that aligns your interests with potential career paths through a series of questions (U.S. Department of Labor; National Center for ONET Development). Do this before you rewrite anything — a pivot aimed at a title you half-chose wastes months. Signal of success: a shortlist of three occupation titles you can spell out, not a vague field.

5. Feed your old job titles into mySkillsmyFuture for adjacent roles

mySkillsmyFuture identifies career options based on your current or past jobs (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). Career changers routinely overlook the adjacent role that reuses 70% of what they already do — the tool surfaces those by starting from where you've been rather than where you'd like to be. Signal of success: at least two roles on your list that you had not previously considered.

6. Write a two-minute elevator speech that names the pivot up front

CareerOneStop's networking guidance tells job seekers to write an elevator speech — roughly a two-minute description of who you are and what you're looking for — before reaching out to contacts (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). As a changer, your first sentence should name the move explicitly, then give one piece of proof: a project, a certificate, a volunteer stint. Signal of success: you can say it out loud in under two minutes without reading, and three people repeat your target role back to you correctly.

7. Filter Job Finder for "Remote Jobs Only" to widen your map

CareerOneStop's Job Finder lets you enter a job title keyword and a location, and includes a filter to select "Remote Jobs Only" (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). Run the same target title twice each week — once local, once remote-only — and note which version returns more postings; that difference tells you whether geography is your constraint. Signal of success: a saved weekly list of postings for each of your three shortlisted titles.

8. Draft in your own voice, then run one AI pass for clarity

CareerOneStop suggests drafting your resume in your own voice first, then using free AI tools such as ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot to suggest alternatives or improvements (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). Order matters — drafting with the tool first produces generic text that buries the transferable experience a changer needs to foreground. Signal of success: every suggestion you accept is still something you'd say in an interview without flinching.

9. Book a session at your nearest American Job Center

American Job Centers are physical and virtual centers across the United States; CareerOneStop maintains their contact details and surveys the centers twice a year (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor). What each center offers varies by state and by local workforce board — some run resume clinics and employer events, others focus on training referrals — so ask what is available in your area rather than assuming. Signal of success: one booked appointment and a written note of which local services you qualify for.

No single tactic here produces an interview on its own. They work by compounding.

Putting It Together

A realistic first week is three strategies, not nine. Start with *Run the ONET Interest Profiler before you lock in a target title on day one, because everything downstream depends on knowing which title you're aiming at. Give it an evening, come out with three shortlisted occupations, then move straight into Scan 10-15 postings for your target title before you touch your resume** for the strongest of the three. Reading those postings is also research for your conversations — you'll pick up the words the field uses for things you already do under a different name.

Week two is where outreach starts carrying the load. Pair Build a list of 8-10 target companies and contact 1-2 each week with Book two informational interviews a week with people doing the job now. They feed each other: the target-company list tells you who to ask for a conversation, and each conversation usually produces one or two more names to add to the list. Keep both in the same tracker so you can see at a glance which companies you've touched, when, and what you promised to send next.

From there, hold the cadence rather than adding more. Two company contacts and two conversations a week is roughly eight of each a month, which is enough volume to tell whether your framing is landing. If four weeks pass with almost no replies, the problem is usually the message or the target title, not the effort — go back to Scan 10-15 postings for your target title before you touch your resume and check whether you are describing yourself in the language those postings actually use.

Frequently asked questions

How many hours a week does this take?+

Two company contacts and two informational conversations, plus one resume revision, fits into roughly five to eight hours if you are working full time. The research-heavy steps are front-loaded in the first week or two; after that the weekly load drops to outreach and follow-through on what you promised people.

Do these government tools cost anything?+

CareerOneStop, My Next Move, mySkillsmyFuture and the American Job Center network are public services from the U.S. Department of Labor and its state partners, so they are free to use. What individual American Job Centers provide beyond the basics varies by state and local workforce board, and training funding in particular has eligibility rules you'd need to ask about directly.

Will informational interviews actually lead to a job, or am I just chatting?+

They are for learning the field's language, testing whether the work suits you, and meeting people — not for asking for a job, and asking directly tends to end the conversation. CareerOneStop notes that many openings are never posted publicly and that employers often find candidates through networking, referrals and direct contact from job seekers, which is why the conversations matter even when nothing is open that week.

How long should I expect a career-change search to take?+

There is no reliable figure for changers specifically, but general unemployment duration gives you a floor: among all unemployed people in 2024, the median was 9.6 weeks and the average 21.6 weeks (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024). Build a plan you can run for several months at a steady pace rather than one that burns out in a fortnight.

title: Behavioral vs. Case Interviews: A Prep Guide
dek: One format asks what you already did; the other asks what you would do in the next twenty minutes — and almost none of the prep overlaps.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
Behavioral interviews ask you to describe how you handled real past situations so the interviewer can judge your behavior and personality (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Case interviews hand you a business problem and watch you structure it, question it, and do arithmetic on the spot — BCG calls this a case study or problem-solving interview (BCG, undated), and McKinsey formally names its version the Problem-Solving Interview (McKinsey & Company, undated).

The two formats differ in pacing, in what silence signals, in what sits on your desk, and in what a sensible follow-up note says. This guide compares them dimension by dimension, gives you a separate prep checklist for each, and ends with a task-by-task reference table. Expect specifics to vary by employer, country office and role level — consulting, finance and tech all run these formats slightly differently.

Key takeaways

  • Behavioral interviews reward prepared, self-contained stories; the STAR structure — Situation, Task, Action, Result — is the standard framework (MIT CAPD, undated).
  • Case interviews reward audible reasoning: BCG's published 'Don't' list for case interviews names Stay Silent, Rush Your Response and Panic Under Pressure (BCG, undated).
  • Your desk differs: a case needs pen and paper in reach (Bain & Company, undated); a behavioral interview needs a one-page story grid you can glance at, not read from.

How the Formats Differ

Pacing and who drives the clock

  • Behavioral: the interviewer asks, you answer in a contained block, then they probe. CareerOneStop notes behavioral questions are more probing and more specific than traditional interview questions (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated), so budget for two or three follow-ups on a single story.
  • Case: one prompt opens a back-and-forth that runs most of the slot. BCG describes candidates structuring an approach, asking thoughtful questions, analyzing data and performing quick calculations (BCG, undated) — you set the pace between data drops.

Body language and what silence signals

  • Behavioral: steady eye contact and settled posture support a story you already know. Bain's in-person tips cover eye contact, posture and minimizing fidgeting (Bain & Company, undated).
  • Case: the same posture rules apply, but silence is read as being stuck rather than being thoughtful. Announce a pause before you take one.

Desk, materials and tech setup

  • Behavioral: a clear surface, your resume, and a short prompt card. If it is a video round, CareerOneStop advises checking computer, camera and microphone and practicing on the employer's platform, such as Zoom or Teams (CareerOneStop, undated).
  • Case: Bain advises bringing pen and paper to in-person case interviews (Bain & Company, undated) and, for virtual cases, a quiet well-lit space with a neutral or blurred background, tested internet, camera and microphone, notifications off, and verbally signaling when you are taking notes (Bain & Company, undated).

What the interviewer is recording

  • Behavioral: evidence of past behavior. McKinsey recommends preparing two personal examples demonstrating impact in each of four designated theme areas for its Personal Experience Interview (McKinsey & Company, undated) — a useful shape for any employer's version.
  • Case: how you got there. BCG's 'Do' list names Listen Actively, Think Structurally, Communicate Clearly, Clarify Assumptions and Show Your Thinking (BCG, undated).

Follow-up etiquette

  • Behavioral: CareerOneStop says a thank-you note should include appreciation, continued interest, a brief restatement of your qualifications, and the date and time you will follow up (CareerOneStop, undated), sent soon after — the same day is best, and email is best if a decision will be made quickly (same source).
  • Case: same four elements, but reference the problem rather than relitigating your answer. Sending corrected math after the fact rarely changes a score and can read as second-guessing; if you genuinely misread an exhibit, one sentence is the limit.

Format-Specific Prep Checklist

Behavioral interview

  1. Build a story grid: four themes down the side, two examples each across — the shape McKinsey recommends for its Personal Experience Interview (McKinsey & Company, undated). Eight stories, one line each.
  2. Write each one in STAR — Situation, Task, Action, Result (MIT CAPD, undated) — and end every Result with a number you can defend, e.g. "onboarding time at Harlow Freight dropped from 11 days to 6."
  3. Record a mock interview with a friend, as CareerOneStop's virtual-interview guidance suggests, watching for natural gestures and visible engagement (CareerOneStop, undated). Cut any answer running past 2 minutes.
  4. If it is a panel — two or more interviewers, possibly HR, the hiring manager, the supervisor and a team lead (CareerOneStop, undated) — ask the recruiter for names, titles and seating or screen order, and write them on a card beside your keyboard.

Case interview

  1. In person: two working pens, a blank unlined pad in landscape, business professional dress, and arrival early enough to settle (Bain & Company, undated).
  2. Virtual: neutral or blurred background, light in front of you, camera at eye level, notifications off, and a tested mic and connection (Bain & Company, undated).
  3. Drill arithmetic on paper, not mentally: ten percentage-change sums, five break-evens and five market-size estimates, timed at 60 seconds each.
  4. Rehearse clarifying out loud — restate the question, state two assumptions, ask one scoping question — since BCG lists Clarify Assumptions and Show Your Thinking among its 'Do's (BCG, undated).
  5. Practice signaling your pauses, because on video the interviewer cannot see your pad:

Signaling a pause on a virtual case

You: "I'd like 60 seconds to structure this. I'll be writing, not reading." Interviewer: "Fine — but while you write, tell me what you think the client's actual decision is." You: "Whether to keep the Dunmore plant open past next year. I'll come back with the two or three figures that settle it."

Quick Reference

Prep taskBehavioral interviewCase interview
Test audio and videoCheck computer, camera and mic and practice on the employer's platform, e.g. Zoom or Teams (CareerOneStop, undated)Same checks, plus screen-share of a PDF exhibit and confirm your mic picks you up while you look down at paper (Bain & Company, undated)
Set the roomQuiet space, notifications off, face lit from the frontAdd a neutral or blurred background and clear desk space wide enough for a landscape pad (Bain & Company, undated)
Items within reachResume, job ad, story grid card, waterTwo pens, blank unlined paper, calculator only if the interviewer permits it (Bain & Company, undated)
Content prepTwo examples per theme across four themes, each written in STAR (McKinsey & Company, undated; MIT CAPD, undated)Three reusable structures plus timed arithmetic drills; practice asking one scoping question before structuring (BCG, undated)
Mock runFriend asks five probing follow-ups; record and cut answers over 2 minutes (CareerOneStop, undated)Partner reads a prompt, withholds data until you ask, and interrupts once to test that you don't rush or go silent (BCG, undated)
During the interviewAnswer, pause, let the follow-up comeNarrate; announce every pause aloud and say when you are writing (Bain & Company, undated)
Follow-up noteAppreciation, continued interest, brief restatement of qualifications, date and time you'll follow up — same day is best (CareerOneStop, undated)Same four elements; name the problem you worked on, and limit any correction to one sentence

Frequently asked questions

What changes when a case interview is also a panel, held over video?+

Ask the recruiter in advance who will be on the call and who runs the case, since a panel may include HR, the hiring manager, the supervisor and a team lead (CareerOneStop, undated). Address your structure to the case-giver, but look at the camera when summarizing. Say names aloud before answering, because gallery view scrambles seating order across devices.

How do I switch gears when both formats run back to back in one day?+

Treat them as separate rounds with a reset in between. Clear your case paper off the desk before a behavioral slot so you are not glancing at calculations, and put your story grid away before a case. Two minutes between rounds is usually enough to swap materials, re-read the interviewer's name, and drink water.

Should I send one thank-you note or one per interviewer?+

Send one per interviewer where you have their email, each referencing something specific from that conversation. Keep the four standard elements: appreciation, continued interest, a brief restatement of your qualifications, and the date and time you will follow up (CareerOneStop, undated). Send soon after — the same day is best, and email is best if a decision will be made quickly.

  6. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Master Virtual Job Interviews with These 4 Tips video
  7. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Thank-you Notes
  8. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Follow-up after interview

title: Best Job Boards for Tech and Engineering Careers
dek: A side-by-side look at six platforms tech job seekers actually use, what each one costs, and the specific gap in each that forces you to combine them.
author: Ingrid Castellanos
body:
No single job board covers the tech market. Dice leans toward contract and enterprise engineering roles, Wellfound toward startups, Built In toward city-specific tech scenes, Hired toward a curated matching model, LinkedIn toward everything plus the recruiters behind it, and Teal isn't a board at all — it's where you keep track of what you found elsewhere.

This guide compares what each platform is genuinely good at, what it costs you as a job seeker versus what it costs the employers posting there, and where each one falls short. Most people end up using two boards and one tracker.

Key takeaways

  • Use Dice for contract, defense and enterprise engineering roles — it's free for tech professionals to use as job seekers (Dice, undated).
  • Use Wellfound when you want early-stage startup roles, since its free employer tier means small teams post there that never reach bigger boards (Recooty, undated).
  • Use Teal's Chrome extension to bookmark roles from more than 50 job boards in one click and keep every application in one tracker (ToolRadar, 2026-06).

At-a-Glance Comparison

Tool/PlatformBest ForCostStandout FeatureLimitation
DiceContract, enterprise and cleared engineering rolesFree for tech professionals as job seekers (Dice, undated); premium job-seeker features start at a monthly subscription (Scale Jobs, undated)Deep tech-only taxonomy and a candidate profile recruiters search directlyHeavy staffing-agency presence, so the same role can appear from several agencies at once
WellfoundEarly-stage and venture-backed startup rolesFree for job seekers; employers can post on a free Access tier (Recooty, undated)Startup profiles with funding stage and team size alongside the listingThin coverage of large enterprises, government and non-startup employers
Built InTech roles at startups and mid-size companies, by cityFree for job seekersEmployer profiles that highlight tech stacks and benefits, plus personalized job alerts (Built In, undated)Coverage is concentrated in specific metro tech hubs, so remote-only or smaller-market searches thin out fast
HiredExperienced engineers who want employers to approach themDescribed as completely free to use for job seekers with no hidden charges (Underdog.io, undated)Reverse model — companies send interview requests to your profileYou may not be accepted into the marketplace, and roles skew toward funded companies hiring at mid-to-senior level
LinkedInFinding the hiring manager and recruiter behind a postingFree tier plus Premium Career at a stated monthly rate (Salesbread, undated)Recruiter and employee visibility on almost every company you'd apply toHuge applicant volume per posting and a large share of reposted or aggregated listings
TealTracking and tailoring applications across every other boardFree Forever plan with unlimited resumes and unlimited job tracking; Teal+ at $13 every 7 days, $29 every 30 days, or $79 every 90 days (Teal, undated)Chrome extension for one-click job bookmarking from more than 50 job boards (ToolRadar, 2026-06)It sources no jobs of its own — it only organizes what you find elsewhere

Detailed Breakdown

Dice

Dice is a tech-only board, which is its whole argument. Searching "engineer" there returns engineering roles rather than sales engineers and engineering managers at insurance firms. It is free for tech professionals to use as job seekers (Dice, undated), and the company reports 44,000 new job seekers per month against 7.8 million registered tech professionals (Dice, undated) — platform-reported figures, so treat them as marketing numbers rather than audited ones.

Employers pay per job slot: a single slot runs $399 for 30 days, and the Starter plan includes 3 job slots per month with 250 candidate views per month (Dice, undated). That matters to you for one reason — candidate views are a metered resource, so recruiters there are searching profiles deliberately rather than browsing. Fill out your Dice profile with specific stack keywords (languages, cloud platforms, frameworks, clearance status if you hold one) because that profile is the searchable object.

Dice also offers premium job-seeker features such as increased profile visibility and advanced search filters starting at a monthly subscription price (Scale Jobs, undated). Any claim that paying lifts you in recruiter search results is platform-reported; there is no independent measure of how much difference it makes. Try the free tier for a month first and see whether recruiters contact you at all.

The real limitation: staffing agencies post heavily on Dice. You will see one client role advertised by four intermediaries with different titles. Cross-check the job description text against the others before applying twice.

Wellfound

Wellfound is where startups hire. Its free Access plan lets employers post jobs, review applicants, create branded company profiles, and use built-in ATS tracking (Recooty, undated), and that free tier includes unlimited job posts with no credit card required (Pin, 2026-07). The consequence for you: two-person companies that would never pay $399 for a slot still post there. Pricing spans five tiers up to a Recruit Pro plan according to the official pricing page (Pin, 2026-07), with an Essentials plan adding custom screening questions, applicant filters and response templates (Recooty, undated).

There's also a Promoted Jobs add-on that prioritizes listings for greater visibility starting at a set price (Recooty, undated). So listing order on Wellfound is partly paid. A role near the top isn't necessarily newer or better — it may just be promoted.

The real limitation: if you want a bank, a hospital system, a federal contractor or a Fortune 500 platform team, Wellfound is the wrong board. Use it for seed-to-Series-C companies and little else.

Built In

Built In describes its platform as including personalized job alerts, employer profiles that highlight tech stacks and benefits, and career development resources (Built In, undated). A comparison site describes it as best for tech roles at startups and mid-size companies and for understanding company culture before applying (Skillora, undated).

The tech stack detail on employer profiles is the practical win. Before you apply, you can see whether a company runs the stack you want to keep working in — and you can pull their listed technologies into your resume's skills section where they genuinely match your experience.

The real limitation: Built In organizes around metro tech markets. If you're searching outside those hubs, or filtering to fully remote only, the volume drops sharply compared with a national board.

Hired

Hired inverts the usual flow: you build a profile, and companies send interview requests. It is described as completely free to use for job seekers with no hidden charges (Underdog.io, undated), because employers carry the cost — Hired's Basic employer plan starts at a stated monthly price (SaaSworthy, undated) and it charges a placement fee typically set at a percentage of the hired candidate's base salary (Flexiple, undated).

Understand what that fee structure does to the role mix. When a company pays a percentage of base salary on a successful hire, it uses the channel for roles worth that fee — generally mid-level and above, at funded companies. Entry-level and support-adjacent roles are rarer.

The real limitation: it's a curated marketplace. Profiles are screened for acceptance, and acceptance isn't guaranteed. Treat it as a passive channel running in the background, not your primary search.

LinkedIn

LinkedIn's value for tech job seekers is less the job listings and more the people attached to them. Premium Career, the plan marketed to job seekers, is priced at a stated monthly rate (Salesbread, undated), costs a stated amount when billed annually (BotDog, undated), and includes 5 InMail credits per month along with LinkedIn Learning access and applicant insights (Salesbread, undated).

Five InMails a month is a constraint that forces discipline. Spend them on engineering managers and recruiters at companies where you've already applied — not on cold outreach at scale. Something like:

InMail to a hiring manager after applying — personalize before sending

Hi [Name] — I applied for the [exact job title] role on [date] and saw you lead the [team name] team. I spent the last [number] years on [specific system or problem that matches their stack], including [one concrete result with a number you can defend]. Happy to send more detail if it's useful.

Rewrite that in your own words and replace every bracket with specifics from the posting and from their engineering blog or team page. A visibly templated InMail reads worse than no InMail.

Claims that applying within a certain window of a posting improves your odds are widely repeated and usually anecdotal or platform-reported — not established fact. Applying promptly is sensible; treating a specific hour threshold as a rule isn't.

The real limitation: applicant volume per posting is high, and a large share of listings are aggregated or reposted from company sites. Use LinkedIn to identify the opening and the people, then apply on the employer's own careers page where that option exists.

Teal

Teal is a tracker and resume tool, not a board. Its Chrome extension was named one of the Web Store's Favorites of 2023 for one-click job bookmarking from more than 50 job boards (ToolRadar, 2026-06), which means you can save roles from Dice, Wellfound, Built In and LinkedIn into one list as you browse.

The official pricing page lists Teal+ at $13 every 7 days, $29 every 30 days, or $79 every 90 days, with a Free Forever plan offering unlimited resumes and unlimited job tracking (Teal, undated). Unlimited tracking on the free plan covers the core job most people need it for.

Use it to tailor concretely: match the job title on your resume to the posting's exact title where it's honest to do so, pull the stack and tooling keywords the description repeats, and make sure each bullet carries a number you can explain in an interview.

The real limitation: it surfaces no jobs. If your pipeline is empty, Teal does nothing for you until you've found roles on an actual board.

Where to Access Each Tool

  • Dice — the job seeker registration page for a free account, and the employer pricing page if you want to see current slot and plan costs.
  • Wellfound — the job seeker sign-up page; check the official pricing page for the current tier list, since the employer side determines who posts there.
  • Built In — the national homepage, then switch to your city's market page before setting up job alerts.
  • Hired — the job seeker profile creation flow, not the employer or "for companies" section.
  • LinkedIn — the Premium Career plan comparison page inside your account settings, where current rates and the free trial terms are shown for your region.
  • Teal — the official pricing page for current Teal+ and Free Forever terms, and the Chrome Web Store extension listing to install the job bookmarking tool.

Prices and plan contents change, and some tiers differ by country. Check the platform's own pricing page rather than a third-party summary before you pay for anything.

Frequently asked questions

Should I pay for LinkedIn Premium Career or Teal+ if I can only afford one?+

They solve different problems. Premium Career gives you 5 InMail credits a month plus applicant insights (Salesbread, undated), which helps if your bottleneck is reaching people inside companies. Teal+ sits on top of a Free Forever plan that already includes unlimited resumes and unlimited job tracking (Teal, undated), so if your bottleneck is organization, you may not need to pay at all. Diagnose which problem you actually have over two weeks of searching, then pay for that one.

Is it worth using Dice and Wellfound at the same time?+

Yes, if your target range spans both company types — their listings barely overlap. Dice skews to enterprise, contract and agency-represented roles, while Wellfound's free employer tier (Recooty, undated) pulls in small startups that wouldn't pay for a slot elsewhere. If you already know you want one or the other, running both just adds noise.

Do I need a paid Dice subscription to get noticed by recruiters?+

Dice is free for tech professionals as job seekers (Dice, undated), and premium features like increased profile visibility start at a monthly price (Scale Jobs, undated). The visibility benefit is platform-reported, not independently verified, so run the free profile for a month with full stack keywords filled in and count the inbound messages. If you get none and your profile is genuinely complete, then test the paid tier for a single month.

How many of these should I use at once?+

Two boards and one tracker is a workable ceiling for most people. Pick boards that match your target company size — one broad or enterprise-leaning, one startup-leaning — and route everything into a single tracker so you can see what stage each application is at. More boards mostly means seeing the same aggregated listings repeatedly.

Is Hired worth setting up if I'm already applying actively?+

It costs you nothing as a job seeker (Underdog.io, undated) and runs passively once your profile is live, so it's low-downside. But because employers pay a placement fee based on a percentage of base salary (Flexiple, undated), the roles skew mid-level and above at funded companies, and acceptance into the marketplace isn't automatic. Set it up and forget it — don't let it replace active applications.

faq.a: Dice is free for tech professionals as job seekers (Dice, undated), and premium features like increased profile visibility start at a monthly price (Scale Jobs, undated). The visibility benefit is platform-reported, not independently verified, so run the free profile for a month with full stack keywords filled in and count the inbound messages. If you get none and your profile is genuinely complete, then test the paid tier for a single month.

faq.q: How many of these should I use at once?
faq.a: Two boards and one tracker is a workable ceiling for most people. Pick boards that match your target company size — one broad or enterprise-leaning, one startup-leaning — and route everything into a single tracker so you can see what stage each application is at. More boards mostly means seeing the same aggregated listings repeatedly.

faq.q: Is Hired worth setting up if I'm already applying actively?
faq.a: It costs you nothing as a job seeker (Underdog.io, undated) and runs passively once your profile is live, so it's low-downside. But because employers pay a placement fee based on a percentage of base salary (Flexiple, undated), the roles skew mid-level and above at funded companies, and acceptance into the marketplace isn't automatic. Set it up and forget it — don't let it replace active applications.

title: Career Change Resume Examples
dek: Two annotated resume templates and a cover letter opening, each matched to a different kind of pivot, plus the edits to make before you send one.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
Changing fields means your job titles no longer explain what you can do, so the resume has to do that work instead. The examples below show two common pivots — a long-tenured worker moving to a new industry, and a shorter sideways step into an adjacent role — and how the layout changes between them.

Both are templates with bracketed placeholders. Fill in your real titles, dates and numbers; rewriting a responsibility for clarity is fine, inventing one is not.

Key takeaways

  • Example 1 fits you if you have 8+ years in one field and are moving to a different industry: skills group first, job titles sit underneath.
  • Example 2 fits you if you are stepping into an adjacent role (such as admin to project coordinator): dates lead, with skill-style headings inside each job.
  • The formatting choice that differs most is where your employment dates sit — top of the page in Example 2, below a skills block in Example 1.

Example Resumes & Cover Letters

Both resumes stay inside the same basic layout rules: 1–2 pages, left-aligned text, one-inch margins, a simple font such as Times New Roman, Cambria or Arial, at 10–12 point (CareerOneStop, undated). A person will typically scan your resume for 15–20 seconds, so your target-field evidence has to sit near the top (CareerOneStop, undated).

Example 1: 10+ years in one industry, moving to a different industry

TEMPLATE — replace every bracket before you send this

[YOUR NAME] [City, State] | [Phone] | [Email] | [Portfolio or professional profile URL]

Summary [X] years in [current field] moving into [target field]. Strongest in [target-field skill 1], [skill 2] and [skill 3], built by [specific responsibility you actually held]. Completed [certificate or course name, if you have one] in [year].

Relevant Skills

[Skill heading taken from the job ad, e.g. Operations Coordination] - Coordinated [type of work] across [X] teams, reducing [delay or error measure] by [X%] - Rebuilt [process name], cutting turnaround from [X] days to [Y] days

[Second skill heading, e.g. Data & Reporting] - Built [X] recurring reports in [software name], used by [X] managers each [week/month] - Tracked [budget or volume figure] and flagged [X] variances before period close

Professional Experience [Job Title], [Employer type or name], [City, State] — [Month Year]–[Month Year] [Job Title], [Employer type or name], [City, State] — [Month Year]–[Month Year]

Education & Certifications [Degree or credential], [Institution], [Year]

This is a combination format, which works well to highlight transferable skills, refocus experience for a career change, or minimize work gaps (CareerOneStop, undated). It puts the target-field evidence above job titles that would otherwise emphasize your lack of related experience — the main drawback of a straight chronological layout for career changers (CareerOneStop, undated). Crucially, the employer and date list is still there: a purely functional resume with no detailed work history can be misinterpreted by employers or rejected by an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), and is often viewed with suspicion because employers and dates are missing (CareerOneStop, undated).

Example 2: Adjacent move, 3–7 years' experience (e.g. administrative role to project coordinator)

TEMPLATE — replace every bracket before you send this

[YOUR NAME] [City, State] | [Phone] | [Email]

Objective [Current job title] seeking a [target job title] role, with [X] years supporting [type of projects] and [target-field skill].

Professional Experience

[Current Job Title], [Employer], [City, State] — [Month Year]–Present Project support: Scheduled and tracked [X] concurrent projects, improving on-time completion by [X%] Stakeholder communication: Wrote status updates for [X] departments, reducing follow-up requests by [X%] Process improvement: Documented [process name], cutting onboarding time for new staff by [X] hours

[Previous Job Title], [Employer], [City, State] — [Month Year]–[Month Year] Administration: Managed [calendar/records/vendor] workload for [X] staff with [X%] accuracy on [measure]

Skills [Software 1], [Software 2], [Method or tool], [Language if relevant]

Education & Training [Degree or credential], [Institution], [Year]

This is chronological with functional headings inside each job — the structure a worker used when moving from administrative assistant to project coordinator, because the move was a logical progression rather than a major career change, and the headings let her surface relevant project work (CareerOneStop, undated). Dates lead, which suits a steady work record (CareerOneStop, undated). The italic sub-labels do the sorting job that a separate skills block does in Example 1.

Example 3: Cover letter opening for a career change (any level)

TEMPLATE — replace every bracket before you send this

Dear [Hiring Manager Name or Hiring Team],

I am applying for the [job title] role at [organization]. I have spent [X] years in [current field], where [specific duty] was most of my week — the same [skill named in the job ad] your posting asks for. Last year I [action verb] [task], which [measurable result, e.g. raised X by X%].

I am making this move deliberately: I completed [course or certificate, if applicable] in [year] and have been doing [relevant volunteer, freelance or internal project work] since.

The letter is where you state the reason for the change in plain words, which the resume cannot do. Naming the skill from the posting and attaching one measured result to it keeps the opening concrete rather than aspirational. CareerOneStop's six-step career-change guide treats rebranding your resume as one step alongside researching the job market and exploring training (CareerOneStop, undated) — the letter is where that rebrand is explained.

How to Customize These Examples

  • Rewrite the Summary line in Example 1 so "[target field]" uses the exact words in the job ad, not your own label for the work. Indeed's career-change guidance recommends adding a summary or objective, a skills section and relevant projects when you pivot (Indeed, undated).
  • Rename the skill headings — "[Skill heading taken from the job ad]" in Example 1, and the italic sub-labels in Example 2 — to match the posting's terms. ONET OnLine's Skills Search lets you build a list of your soft skills and see which occupations use them, which helps you name transferable skills accurately (ONET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, undated).
  • Fill the Skills line in Example 2 with software you have actually used. ONET OnLine's Technology Skills Search finds occupations based on software used on the job, so you can check whether your tools carry into the target role (ONET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, undated).
  • Set real dates in the Professional Experience block of both examples. Use your actual months and years. If your history is long, include or emphasize only the jobs that add the most value, from the past 12–15 years (CareerOneStop, undated).
  • Replace every [X%] and [X] days with a figure you can defend in an interview. An estimate you can explain is fine; a precise number you cannot source is not.
  • Delete the Certifications line from Example 1 if you have none, rather than padding it. Indeed's guidance lists certifications and courses as an optional showcase for career changers (Indeed, undated).
  • Strip any table, text box, logo, column, image or graphic if you move these templates into a designed layout, and keep your name and contact details out of the page header or footer — an ATS may scramble that content (CareerOneStop, undated).
  • Swap the Example 3 greeting for a named person when the posting gives one, and replace "[organization]" everywhere it appears.

Frequently asked questions

What file type should I send?+

Send only the documents requested. If no format is specified, use Word, PDF or plain-text files, and avoid scanning a resume and sending it as an image, because it will not be recognized (CareerOneStop, undated). If the posting names a format, follow the posting.

How do I shorten Example 1 to fit one page?+

Resume length should be 1–2 pages, and you should only use two pages if your amount of experience makes it necessary (CareerOneStop, undated). To compress Example 1, cut the Relevant Skills block from three bullets per heading to two, and limit Professional Experience to jobs from the past 12–15 years (CareerOneStop, undated). Keep the dated employer list — removing it turns the resume functional, and a functional resume with no detailed work history can be misinterpreted by employers or rejected by an Applicant Tracking System (CareerOneStop, undated).

Can I put the skills block in a side column to save space?+

Avoid it. Tables, text boxes, logos, columns, images and graphics may be scrambled by an ATS (CareerOneStop, undated). Both examples are single-column and left-aligned with one-inch margins for that reason (CareerOneStop, undated). If you want the skills to stand out, use bold headings rather than a second column.

Which example should I use if I have a gap between jobs?+

Example 1. The combination format works well to highlight transferable skills from paid and unpaid work, refocus experience for a career change, or minimize work gaps (CareerOneStop, undated). Keep your real start and end dates in the Professional Experience block and let the skills section carry the first scan — a reader typically spends 15–20 seconds on it (CareerOneStop, undated).

Sources

  2. CareerOneStop — Resume styles
  3. CareerOneStop — Resumes
  4. CareerOneStop — Resume format
  5. CareerOneStop — Career Changers
  6. CareerOneStop — Work experience
  7. O*NET OnLine (U.S. Department of Labor) — O*NET OnLine
  8. O*NET OnLine (U.S. Department of Labor) — O*NET OnLine Help: Technology Skills Search
  9. Indeed — Updating Your Resume for a Career Change

title: Changing Careers Into Tech With No Experience: What It Actually Takes
dek: A clear-eyed look at the timelines, credentials and trade-offs behind a move into software, support or web work — and how to test the idea cheaply first.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
Moving into a technology job from an unrelated field is a documented route, but it is a project with a timeline, a cost and a failure rate — not a decision you make in a weekend. Most career changers who land a first technical role spend somewhere between 9 and 24 months on it, working around a current job, and the hardest part is almost never learning to code. It is getting an employer to take a first look at someone with no paid technical history.

This roadmap sets out what the federal data actually says about which tech occupations are growing, a step-by-step plan built on publicly available resources, a side-by-side look at which of your existing skills carry over, and a checklist to see whether you can afford to start now.

Key takeaways

  • Realistic timeline: 9-24 months from first study session to first paid technical role, assuming 8-15 hours of study a week alongside existing work.
  • Biggest obstacle: no verifiable paid technical history, which screens you out before skill is ever assessed — portfolio work, apprenticeships and internal moves exist to solve that specific problem.
  • First concrete action: open the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook and the O*NET OnLine profile for three target job titles and compare the stated entry-level education, projected growth and annual openings before you buy any course.

Why People Make This Switch

Three signals in the federal data explain most of the movement into tech, and one of them is a warning rather than an invitation.

Volume of openings in software roles. Employment of software developers, quality assurance analysts and testers is projected to grow 10 percent from 2025 to 2035, much faster than the average for all occupations, with about 106,100 openings projected each year (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). That sits on a base of 1,905,400 jobs in 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). A large occupation with steady replacement demand is a more forgiving target for a career changer than a small one, because hiring happens continuously rather than in rare bursts.

Entry requirements that are not uniform. The BLS lists a bachelor's degree in computer and information technology or a related field as the typical requirement for software developers, with some employers preferring a master's degree (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). But ONET OnLine places software developers in Job Zone Four, where "most of these occupations require a four-year bachelor's degree, but some do not" (ONET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, 2025). For web developers and digital designers, stated educational requirements range from a high school diploma to a bachelor's degree (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). That variation is the gap career changers work in — but note Job Zone Four also expects several years of work-related experience or training, so the degree is not the only hurdle.

A caution about the traditional on-ramp. Computer support roles have long been the common entry door. Employment of computer support specialists is now projected to decline 3 percent from 2025 to 2035, with about 48,700 openings a year, all expected to come from replacing workers who leave, as organizations implement automated tools such as chatbots for troubleshooting (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). The door is not closed — 903,100 people held these jobs in 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — but plan support work as a stepping stone with a next step attached, not a destination.

Step-by-Step Transition Plan

  1. Pick two target job titles and write down their entry requirements. (1-2 weeks.) Use the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook and O*NET OnLine, both free. Compare projected growth and annual openings: software developer, QA analyst and tester roles show about 106,100 openings a year, web developer and digital designer roles about 13,600 on a base of 220,100 jobs, and computer support specialists about 48,700 openings all from replacement need (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Smaller occupations are not worse, but they require a narrower, more geographically flexible search.
  2. Reality-test the work before you spend money. (2-4 weeks.) Complete a free introductory course or tutorial series in the specific skill — writing code, configuring a machine, building a page — and keep a log of hours. If you cannot hold 6-8 hours a week for a month without external pressure, the longer plan will not survive contact with month five.
  3. Choose one structured credential or curriculum and finish it. (8-16 weeks for an entry-level IT certification; 6-12 months for a full development curriculum.) For infrastructure and support tracks, CompTIA A+ is an internationally recognized entry-level IT qualification issued by CompTIA and accredited by ANSI since 2008 (Per Scholas, reporting on CompTIA A+). It requires passing two exams, Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102), each a computer-based test with a 90-minute limit combining multiple-choice, drag-and-drop and performance-based questions (New Horizons, reporting on CompTIA A+). Exam voucher and training prices change and differ by country, so check the current price on CompTIA's own site before committing; if you have military or veteran status, note that CompTIA A+ is listed in the Army COOL database as approved for the DoD 8140/Cyberspace Workforce Program and eligible for GI Bill and promotion points (Office of the Secretary of Defense, Army COOL).
  4. Build three or four finished projects that someone else can use. (3-6 months, overlapping step 3.) Finished and deployed beats ambitious and abandoned. Put the code or files in a public repository on a free platform such as GitHub, with a plain-English description of the problem each project solves.
  5. Search registered apprenticeships and earn-while-you-learn programs in parallel with your study. (2-6 weeks of searching, then program length as listed.) CareerOneStop, sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor, lists apprenticeships in industries including information technology and describes them as combining a full-time job with training — "an affordable entry point to a high-paying job without the typical student debt associated with college" (CareerOneStop). CareerOneStop also states that 94 percent of apprentices who complete an apprenticeship stay employed in their job (CareerOneStop). Program length and eligibility are set by each sponsor and stated in the listing.
  6. Try the internal move before the external one. (3-6 months.) If your current employer has any technical function, ask to take on a reporting, data, testing or systems task inside your existing role. An internal transfer converts "no experience" into "experience at a company that already trusts you," and it is usually the shortest path available.
  7. Apply at volume with tracking, and treat rejection as data. (3-9 months, often running past your study end date.) Record every application, the job title, the stated education requirement and the outcome. If you get no responses after 40-60 applications, change one variable — target title, location radius, or the top third of your résumé — rather than applying harder.
  8. Keep the credential alive once you have it. (Ongoing, 3-year cycle.) CompTIA A+ requires 20 Continuing Education Units over a three-year certification period, or re-passing the required exams, to stay current (Office of the Secretary of Defense, Army COOL).

Skills & Qualifications: Old vs New

The column that matters is the last one. Budget your months against the "learn from scratch" rows and stop re-learning what you already have.

Skill or credentialWhat a non-technical role asked of youWhat the tech role asksTransfer or learn from scratch
Explaining things to people who are not expertsCustomers, patients, clients, studentsStakeholders, product owners, end users filing ticketsTransfers directly — name specific situations on your résumé
Working to a deadline with incomplete informationShifts, cases, campaigns, closing periodsSprints, releases, incident responseTransfers directly
Structured troubleshootingDiagnosing why a process or order went wrongIsolating a fault across hardware, OS, network or codePartly transfers — the method carries over, the subject matter does not
Programming fundamentals (a language, data structures, testing)Rarely requiredCore to software developer and QA rolesLearn from scratch — expect 6-12 months of consistent study
Version control and collaborative code workflowNot applicableExpected from day one on most teamsLearn from scratch — weeks, not months
Hardware, operating systems and networking basicsNot applicableCore to support and infrastructure roles; covered by the CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 exams (New Horizons, reporting on CompTIA A+)Learn from scratch — 8-16 weeks of study is a common range
Formal education signalVaries by fieldTypically a bachelor's degree in computer and information technology or a related field for software developers, with some employers preferring a master's (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025); a high school diploma up to a bachelor's for web developers and digital designers (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Already held, or substituted with certifications and portfolio depending on the employer and the role
Entry route without a degreeVariesNetwork support specialists typically need an associate's degree and user support specialists some college courses, but candidates may qualify with a high school diploma plus relevant IT certifications (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025); moderate-term on-the-job training is listed for these roles (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Transfers if you already hold the diploma — add the certification

Readiness Checklist

Answer each one yes or no today. Four or more "no" answers in the money and time rows means your plan needs a different shape, not more willpower.

  • I have at least three months of essential living costs saved in an account I can access without penalty.
  • I know the dollar cost of my chosen study path, including exam vouchers, and I have that money set aside or scheduled.
  • I have blocked 8-15 hours a week in a written calendar for the next 12 weeks, and I have told the people affected.
  • I have completed at least 20 hours of free introductory material in the target skill and can describe what the work actually involves.
  • I have read the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook entry and the O*NET OnLine profile for my two target job titles, including the stated entry-level education.
  • I have checked the current wage data for those job titles on the BLS page for my state or metro area, not a salary figure quoted by a course provider.
  • I have one finished project, deployed or demonstrable, that someone other than me can open.
  • I have the names and contact details of at least three people currently working in the target role, and I have messaged at least one of them.
  • I have searched the CareerOneStop apprenticeship listings for information technology openings within my commuting radius or open to remote applicants.
  • I have asked my current manager, in writing, whether any technical or data task inside the business can be added to my role.
  • I have set a specific review date 6 months from now and written down the one measurable result I expect by then.
  • I have a stated fallback: the job, income or hours I return to if there is no offer by month 18.

Frequently asked questions

Will my pay go up or down when I switch?+

Expect a dip before any rise. First technical roles are paid at entry level regardless of how senior you were in your previous field, and the BLS lists software developer roles as requiring no prior work experience in a related occupation at entry (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — which is helpful for getting in and unhelpful for your starting offer. Pay is usually a base salary, sometimes with a bonus or equity at larger employers, and it varies sharply by state, metro area, employer size and whether the role is support, web or software engineering. Check the wage tab of the relevant BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook page and the state-level data for your own location before you accept or reject anything; do not plan around figures quoted in course marketing.

How long does this realistically take?+

For a support or infrastructure route built around an entry-level certification such as CompTIA A+ — two exams, each with a 90-minute limit (New Horizons, reporting on CompTIA A+) — 8-16 weeks of study plus 3-6 months of applying is a common span, so roughly 6-12 months. For a software developer or web developer route, 9-24 months is the realistic band: 6-12 months of study and portfolio work, then 3-9 months of applications. An apprenticeship compresses the earning timeline because you are working while training (CareerOneStop), but places are limited and program length is set by the sponsor.

What are the chances this does not work out?+

Real, and worth planning for. The honest framing is that most people who drop out do so in months 3-6, before any portfolio exists — not because they failed an interview. Protect against that with the fallback item on the readiness checklist and a fixed 6-month review date. One data point on the apprenticeship route is encouraging: CareerOneStop reports that 94 percent of apprentices who complete an apprenticeship stay employed in their job (CareerOneStop) — note that this measures people who completed, not everyone who started.

Do I need to go back to college for a degree?+

It depends on the role. The BLS lists a bachelor's degree in computer and information technology or a related field as typical for software developers, with some employers preferring a master's (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), and O*NET places the occupation in Job Zone Four, "Considerable Preparation Needed," with an SVP range of 7.0 to less than 8.0, while noting that most but not all occupations in that zone require a four-year degree (O*NET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, 2025). Requirements for web developers and digital designers range from a high school diploma to a bachelor's degree (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), and support specialist candidates may qualify with a high school diploma plus relevant IT certifications (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Read the posted requirements for the specific roles you want in your own area rather than generalising.

Is help desk still a sensible first job in tech?+

As a stepping stone with a planned next move, yes; as a ten-year plan, the data argues against it. Computer support specialist employment is projected to decline 3 percent from 2025 to 2035, with all of the roughly 48,700 annual openings coming from replacing workers who leave, partly because organizations are implementing automated tools such as chatbots for troubleshooting (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Compare that with software developer, QA analyst and tester roles at 10 percent projected growth and about 106,100 openings a year, and web developer and digital designer roles at 5 percent growth and about 13,600 openings a year, driven by continued expansion of e-commerce and retail online offerings (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). If you start in support, pick a second destination on day one and keep studying for it.

Can I do this while working full time?+

Most career changers do, and it is the main reason the timeline stretches to 12-24 months rather than 6. Eight to 15 hours a week is a sustainable range for an adult with a job; 25-plus hours a week is sustainable for a few weeks and then stops. The alternative is an earn-while-you-learn route: CareerOneStop describes apprenticeships as combining a full-time job with training and as an affordable entry point without the typical student debt associated with college (CareerOneStop), which removes the income problem but requires you to win a place first.

Does the certification expire?+

Entry-level IT certifications generally need maintaining. CompTIA A+ requires 20 Continuing Education Units over a three-year certification period, or re-passing the required exams, to keep the credential current (Office of the Secretary of Defense, Army COOL). Build that into your plan and your budget rather than treating the credential as a one-time purchase, and confirm current renewal rules and fees with the issuing body, since they change.
