title: How to Write a Cover Letter for a Career Change
dek: Switching fields means your resume alone won't connect the dots, so the letter has to do it — here's what belongs in each of its four short parts.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
A career change cover letter has one job: explain, in a page or less, why you are moving fields and why the skills you already have transfer to the role in front of you. It does the connecting work your resume can't, because your resume lists job titles from an industry the reader may not know.

This guide walks through what to collect first, the order to draft in, and two short template excerpts you can adapt. Everything here assumes you are applying to a posted opening in the US; norms differ by employer, by state and by country, so check the posting's own instructions before you follow any general rule.

Key takeaways

  • Name the career change in the first two paragraphs and frame it as a deliberate move, not an apology for missing experience.
  • Biggest mistake: restating your resume. Use the letter to connect past results to the new role's requirements.
  • Quick win: lift three exact phrases from the job posting and answer each with a specific result you produced.

What to Gather Before You Start

Open a blank document and paste all of this in before you write a sentence. Drafting is much faster when you are arranging material rather than hunting for it.

  • The full job posting, copied as plain text. You will mine it for the exact job title, the listed requirements, and the employer's own wording.
  • The exact target job title and any requisition or job ID number. Use the employer's wording, not your interpretation of it.
  • The company name, spelled and punctuated as the employer writes it, plus one specific, verifiable detail about the organization — a product line, a service area, a recently announced program mentioned on its own site.
  • The hiring manager's or recruiter's name and title, if the posting or the company site lists it. If it doesn't, note the team or department name instead.
  • Three to five achievements from your current or previous field, each with a number attached. Volume, time saved, error rate, budget size, headcount trained, percentage change. Write them as rough notes now; you will shape them later.
  • A written list of your transferable skills, matched to the posting's requirements. If you are not sure which of your skills carry over, the ONET Career Changers Matrix lists, for each occupation code, up to 10 related occupations that use similar skills and experience, so a worker may transfer with minimal additional preparation (ONET Resource Center (U.S. Department of Labor/Employment and Training Administration), undated). That gives you vocabulary for the new field.
  • Your education and training relevant to the new field, with completion dates — degrees, certificates, licenses, courses in progress. A career change letter should show the value of your education and training alongside transferable skills (Coursera, undated).
  • The number of years you spent in your previous field, expressed the way you want it read ("six years in", "a decade of").
  • Your finished resume. You need it open so you can deliberately avoid repeating it.
  • Your contact block: name, city and state, phone, professional email address, and the date you will send.

If any achievement on your list has no number, either find the number or replace the achievement. Never estimate a figure you cannot support, and never adjust a job title, date or credential to fit the new field better — rewording a responsibility for clarity is fine, inventing one is not.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Draft in this order. The opening and the closing are the easiest to write once the middle exists, but writing the opening first gives the letter a direction, so start there and revise it last.

  1. Set the page up before you type. Use a simple, professional font such as Arial or Helvetica at 10 to 12 points, left-aligned, single-spaced, with one-inch margins, aiming for one page (Indeed, undated). Cover letters should normally be only one page long (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Set this now so you can see the page filling up as you write.
  2. Write the heading and greeting. A good cover letter includes a heading and greeting, a brief introduction, your highlights, and a closing (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Put your name and contact details at the top, then the date, then the employer's details, then the greeting. Example: `Dear [Hiring Manager Name], ` — or, if no name is published, `Dear [Department Name] Hiring Team,`.
  3. Write the opening paragraph: role, source, hook. The first paragraph should state the job you are applying for, how you learned of the opening, and one line on what especially interests you about the job or employer (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Example sentence:

I'm applying for the [Job Title] role ([Req #]) posted on your careers page, and I was drawn to it because [Company Name] handles [specific detail you verified] in-house rather than outsourcing it.

  1. Name the career change in one sentence, immediately after. Don't make the reader work it out from your job titles. A career change letter should explain why you are changing careers and highlight transferable skills rather than dwelling on the experience you lack (Coursera, undated; Upwork, undated). Example sentence:

After [number] years in [previous field], I'm moving into [new field] because the part of my work I consistently did best — [transferable skill] — is the core of this role rather than a side task.

  1. Write the qualifications paragraphs. One paragraph is usually enough for the opening and the closing, while the qualifications step may run to two or more paragraphs, as long as the letter stays within a page (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Take two or three requirements from the posting and answer each with a result. If you use bullets, keep them in the action verb, task, measurable result shape:
  • Rebuilt the intake process for [type of request], cutting average turnaround by [X%] across [number] monthly cases.
  1. Write the employer paragraph, without repeating your resume. This paragraph explains your interest in the employer and should not repeat information already on your resume (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Tie your new training in here. Example sentence:

I finished [Certificate or Course Name] in [Month Year] specifically to work on [problem the employer works on], and your [team or product] is where that applies most directly.

  1. Close with a plan of action. Most cover letters explain why you're writing, refer to your qualifications, and close with a suggested plan of action such as a follow-up (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Example sentence:

I'd welcome the chance to walk through how [transferable skill] transfers to [Job Title]; I'll follow up by [date] if I haven't heard back, and I'm reachable at [phone] or [email].

  1. Cut to length and read it aloud. A good cover letter can be about 200 to 400 words in just three or four short paragraphs (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Delete any sentence that repeats a resume bullet word for word, and delete apologies for what you haven't done.
  2. Consider the T format if the posting is a strict checklist. An alternative style lists the requirements from the job posting side-by-side with your qualifications (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). This can suit a career change because it forces a direct match for every requirement. Be aware that two-column layouts and tables are a documented parsing problem for some Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software, so if you submit into an online form, paste a plain single-column version into any text box and keep the T format for email or a PDF attachment.
  3. Do a final accuracy pass. Check the company name, the job title, the hiring manager's name, your own dates and credentials, and every number you quoted. One wrong company name undoes the rest.

Example Snippet

Both excerpts below are templates to adapt, not copy. The bracketed placeholders are there so the text can't be mistaken for a finished letter — replace every one, and replace the wording around them too, or the reader will recognise the pattern.

Excerpt 1: opening and pivot (template to adapt, not copy)

Template to adapt, not copy — career change opening

Dear [Hiring Manager Name],

I'm excited to apply for the [Job Title] position at [Company Name], which I found on [where you saw it]. After [number of years] in [current or previous field], I'm transitioning into [new field] to apply my experience in [transferable skill #1], [transferable skill #2], and [transferable skill #3].

The move isn't a detour. In my last role I spent most of my week on [task that overlaps with the new role], and your posting lists it as the first responsibility. What decided me on [Company Name] specifically was [one verified detail about the organization].

That opening structure follows a published career change template that states the role and company, the length and nature of prior experience, the new field, and three transferable skills (Monster, undated), combined with the advice to state the position, make a connection to why the company interests you, and lead with relevant skills rather than missing experience (Upwork, undated).

Excerpt 2: qualifications paragraph with evidence (template to adapt, not copy)

Template to adapt, not copy — qualifications

Your posting asks for [requirement quoted from the posting]. In [previous field], I [action verb] [specific task], which reduced [metric] by [X%] over [time period] across [number] [cases, accounts, sites]. I also [action verb] [second task], supporting [number] [users, clients, projects] at a time.

To close the gap between that work and [new field], I completed [Certificate or Program Name] in [Month Year] and have since [concrete practice project, volunteer work or freelance engagement]. I'd rather show you the output than describe it: [one line pointing to a portfolio, sample or reference].

Two cautions. Keep the numbers true — if you can't source a figure, describe the scope instead ("a team of [number]", "a [X]-state territory"). And don't let this paragraph become a paraphrase of your resume; the second paragraph of a cover letter should add your interest and reasoning rather than repeat what the resume already says (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated).

Frequently asked questions

My draft is 600 words. How much do I need to cut?+

Aim for roughly 200 to 400 words in three or four short paragraphs, on one page (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). Unless the job description sets a length, there is generally no required word count, but the letter should focus on the details most relevant to the job (Indeed, undated). Cut the sentences that repeat your resume first, then any background on why you left your old field beyond one clear sentence.

Should I send a PDF or a Word file?+

Follow the posting's instructions if it names a format. If it doesn't, PDF preserves your layout for a human reader, while .docx is sometimes requested by recruiters who need to edit or re-save it. If you are pasting into an application form rather than attaching a file, strip out tables, columns, and any text sitting in page headers or footers — those are documented parsing problems for Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software. Name the file with your own name and the role, not "cover letter final v3".

Do I need an objective statement or a line about salary?+

No objective statement — the whole letter is already your statement of intent, and repeating it wastes your opening. On pay, say nothing unless the posting asks you to include expectations or a history. If it does ask, answer in one line in the closing paragraph and check current rates for the role in your state before you name anything. Pay rules and disclosure requirements vary by state and by employer, so read the posting carefully.

There's no name on the posting. Who do I address it to?+

Check the company's site and the posting itself for a recruiter or team lead. If nothing is published, address the department or team — "Dear [Department Name] Hiring Team" — rather than "To Whom It May Concern," which reads as a mass mailing. Don't guess a name you can't verify.

Is it acceptable to draft this with an AI tool?+

It's fine to use AI programs such as ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot to help write a cover letter, but the draft should then be edited to reflect your own voice, skills, experience, and interest (CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor), undated). For a career change that editing pass matters more than usual: a generated draft will not know which of your results actually transfer, and it will happily invent a credential you don't hold. Check every fact in the output against your resume.

Should I explain why I'm leaving my current field in detail?+

One sentence, forward-looking. Explain what you are moving toward, not what went wrong. A career change letter should explain why you are changing careers, show the value of your education and training, and highlight transferable skills (Coursera, undated) — none of that requires criticising a previous employer or industry. If there's a gap in your dates, state it plainly in a clause and move on.

  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Cover letters (Veterans)
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Write effective cover letters
  4. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Cover Letter Template
  5. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Cover letters sample
  6. O*NET Resource Center (U.S. Department of Labor/Employment and Training Administration) — Career Changers Matrix - O*NET 21.1 Data Dictionary
  7. Indeed — How to Write a Cover Letter (With Examples and Tips)
  8. Coursera — How to Write a Cover Letter When You're Changing Careers (Sample + Tips)
  9. Upwork — Career Change Cover Letter Guide With Examples
  10. Monster — How to Write a Career Change Cover Letter (Template & Examples)

title: How to Write a Cover Letter When One Isn't Required
dek: Optional cover letters are the part of an application most people skip — here is how to decide, what to gather, and how to draft one that earns its page.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
When a job posting leaves the cover letter field blank or marks it "optional," you have a choice most people resolve by doing nothing. Writing one is usually worth the thirty minutes: Indeed (June 2026) notes that a cover letter can only help your application unless the posting specifically asks you not to send one, and that including one signals you take the opportunity seriously. This guide covers what to collect first, how to draft each paragraph in order, and what a short, adaptable excerpt looks like.

The bar for an unrequested letter is higher, not lower. Nobody asked for it, so it has to say something your resume cannot — which means specifics about this employer and this role, not a restatement of your work history.

Key takeaways

  • Send one unless the posting tells you not to; Indeed (June 2026) says optional means write it.
  • Biggest mistake: summarising your resume. Use the letter for context, motive and one proof point.
  • Quick win: name the exact job title from the posting in your first sentence.

What to Gather Before You Start

Open a blank document and paste these in before you write a word. Drafting from a collected pile is far faster than drafting from memory.

  • The full job posting, copied as plain text. Postings get taken down. Save the wording, including the exact job title and any reference or requisition number, so you can quote it back accurately.
  • The exact target job title. Write it out separately: "Senior Logistics Coordinator," not "the coordinator job." It goes in your opening sentence and often in the filename.
  • Three to five quantifiable achievements from your own records. Pull them from performance reviews, project wrap-ups, dashboards, invoices or your current resume. Each one needs an action, a task and a measurable result — for example, "Rebuilt the weekly inventory report, cutting preparation time by [X] hours per week." Use real numbers you can defend in an interview; never invent them.
  • Your current resume file. The letter must not contradict it on dates, titles or employers, and matching the font keeps the pair looking like one application.
  • The hiring manager's name and title, if the posting, the company careers page or the job board lists it. If you cannot confirm a name, stop looking — Indeed's sample letter (June 2026) uses "Dear Hiring Manager," which is a safe default.
  • Two or three specific details about the employer, taken from its own website, product pages, annual report or recent announcements. Note where you found each one so you can reference it precisely.
  • The application instructions. Check whether there is an upload field, a text box with a character limit, or an email address only. This decides your format before you draft.
  • Your contact block: full name, phone number, professional email address, city and region, and a portfolio or professional profile link if relevant.
  • The date you intend to submit. Indeed's formatting guidance (July 2026) places the date and contact information at the top of the letter, so you need it as written content, not an afterthought.
  • Your formatting defaults. Indeed (July 2026) recommends a standard professional font such as Arial, Calibri, Georgia or Times New Roman at 10–12 point, 1-inch margins on all sides, and left-aligned text.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Draft in this order. Writing the opening last is a common trick, but when the letter is optional the opening is the whole argument for reading on, so build towards it deliberately.

1. Confirm a letter is welcome. Scan the posting for explicit instructions. Indeed (June 2026) advises that where a cover letter is listed as optional you should err on the side of submitting a good one, and that a letter can only help unless the posting specifically requests you not send one. It also notes that an employer may expect to see one attached even if nobody reads it in the first pass. - Example: if the field says "Cover letter (optional)," write one. If it says "Please do not attach a cover letter," don't — follow the instruction and put the effort into your resume. 2. Set up the page before you type sentences. Apply the formatting defaults you gathered: a standard font at 10–12 point, 1-inch margins, left-aligned text, single spacing with a blank line between paragraphs and after the salutation (Indeed, July 2026). 3. Write the header: date and contact information. Indeed's structure (July 2026) runs date and contact information, salutation, opening paragraph, middle paragraph or paragraphs, closing paragraph, then ending and signature. - Example: `Jordan Ellis | [City, Region] | [phone] | [email]` on one line, the date beneath it, then the employer's name and address if you have it. 4. Choose the salutation. Use the hiring manager's name if you confirmed it; otherwise use the generic form from Indeed's example (June 2026). - Example: `Dear Hiring Manager,` 5. Draft the opening paragraph: role, source, and the one-line reason you are writing. Name the exact job title so there is no ambiguity about which posting this is. - Example, adapted from Indeed's sample opening (July 2026): "I am excited to be applying for the [Job Title] position at [Company Name], which I saw advertised on [source]." - Add one sentence stating your angle: "I have spent [X] years running [function] in [industry], and your posting's emphasis on [specific requirement] is the part of the work I do best." 6. Draft the first middle paragraph: one proof point with a measurable result. Pick the achievement from your list that maps most closely to the top requirement in the posting. Indeed's sample letter (July 2026) illustrates the pattern with a line about improving a click-through rate and reducing a landing page bounce rate through AB testing — an action, the method, and two numbers. - Example: "At [Current or Former Employer], I redesigned the onboarding checklist used by [X] new hires per quarter, which cut time-to-first-task from [X] days to [Y] days." 7. Draft the second middle paragraph: why this employer, specifically. This is the paragraph a resume cannot do. Use one of the details you gathered from the company's own materials and connect it to something you can contribute. - Example: "Your careers page describes [specific programme or product] as the next focus area. I built something similar at [Employer], where I [action] and [measurable result]." 8. Draft the closing paragraph. State what you want to happen next, make any practical point the employer needs (notice period, location, availability), and thank them once. Indeed (June 2026) suggests closing with an attention-grabbing final thought rather than a limp sign-off. - Example: "I would welcome the chance to talk through how I would approach [specific challenge from the posting] in the first ninety days. I am available for a call on any weekday afternoon." 9. Add the ending and signature. A simple "Sincerely," followed by your typed full name is enough; add a scanned or typed signature only if you are sending a formal PDF letter. 10. Cut to length. Indeed (July 2026) recommends keeping the letter to one page, aiming for three to five concise paragraphs totalling 250–400 words; its June 2026 guidance sets the same 250–400 word range across three to four paragraphs, with half a page to a full page as the acceptable span. Delete any sentence that only repeats your resume. 11. Check every fact against your resume, then read the letter aloud to catch repetition. Confirm the company name, job title and hiring manager's name are spelled correctly — these are the errors that get noticed. 12. Save and submit in the right format. Indeed (July 2026) recommends saving as a PDF unless the posting specifies otherwise, to preserve formatting, with a clear filename such as FirstName_LastName_CoverLetter.pdf. If the application uses a plain text box instead of an upload, paste the text and re-check the paragraph breaks survived. Avoid putting your contact details only in a document header or footer, or laying the letter out in tables or columns — those are the elements an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is documented to parse poorly.

Example Snippet

Both excerpts below are templates to adapt, not copy. Every bracket is a decision you have to make with your own facts; a letter submitted with brackets still in it, or with generic filler left in place, reads worse than no letter at all.

Opening and proof paragraph

Template to adapt, not copy — do not submit with brackets intact

Dear [Hiring Manager Name or "Hiring Manager"],

I am excited to be applying for the [Exact Job Title] position at [Company Name], advertised on [job board or careers page]. I have spent [X] years in [function] within [industry], and the posting's focus on [specific requirement quoted from the ad] describes the work I have been doing since [year].

At [Current or Former Employer], I [action verb] the [specific process or project], which [measurable result — e.g. reduced processing time by [X%] across [X] accounts]. The same approach would transfer directly to [specific responsibility named in the posting].

Closing paragraph

Template to adapt, not copy — do not submit with brackets intact

[Company Name]'s work on [specific product, programme or initiative you found on their own site] is the reason I applied rather than waiting for a similar role elsewhere. I would like to talk through how I would handle [specific challenge from the posting] in the first [X] weeks.

Thank you for considering my application.

Sincerely, [Your Full Name] | [phone] | [email]

A quick test before you submit: if you could swap in a different company name and the letter would still make sense, you have written a summary of yourself rather than an application. Replace at least one sentence in each middle paragraph with something only true of this employer.

Frequently asked questions

The application has a text box instead of a file upload. Does that change what I write?+

The content stays the same, but strip the formatting. Remove the date and address block, keep the salutation and paragraphs, and check after pasting that your line breaks survived — some forms collapse them. If the box shows a character limit, write to the limit rather than trying to squeeze in a full page, and lead with the sentence naming the job title in case the reader only sees the first line in a preview pane.

Should I paste the letter into the email body or attach it?+

If you are applying by email with no form, do both in a sense: write a short note in the email body naming the role and saying your resume and letter are attached, then attach the letter as a PDF, which Indeed (July 2026) recommends unless the posting says otherwise. Use a clear filename such as FirstName_LastName_CoverLetter.pdf. Don't paste the full letter into the body and also attach an identical copy — pick the attachment and keep the email note to two or three lines.

Can I reuse one letter across several applications?+

You can reuse the structure and your proof paragraph, but not the employer-specific sentences. Keep a master file with your three to five quantified achievements written out, then rebuild the opening and the "why this employer" paragraph for each application. That is usually ten to fifteen minutes of work once the master exists, and it is the part a reader can tell you skipped.

Should I mention salary expectations or availability?+

Only if the posting asks. If it does, answer in the closing paragraph in one plain sentence and check current market rates for your role, level and location on a reputable salary source or national statistics body before you name anything. Norms differ sharply by country and sector — in some markets stating a figure unprompted is routine, in others it is not — so follow the employer's instruction rather than a general rule.

How do I know whether my draft is too long?+

Count the words rather than eyeballing the page. Indeed (July 2026) suggests three to five concise paragraphs totalling 250–400 words on a single page, and its June 2026 guidance puts acceptable length at half a page to a full page across three to four paragraphs. If you are over, cut whole sentences that restate your resume before you cut anything specific to the employer.

What if I genuinely have nothing to add beyond my resume?+

Then you are probably underselling your context. A letter can explain a career change, a relocation, a gap you are comfortable addressing, why you want this particular employer, or how one specific achievement maps to one specific requirement in the posting. If after gathering your materials you still have nothing beyond a restatement, a very short three-paragraph note naming the role, one proof point and your availability is better than a padded page.

  2. Indeed — How To Format Your Cover Letter for Maximum Impact (2026-07)
  3. Indeed — FAQ: Is a Cover Letter Necessary? (Plus What Optional Means) (2026-06)

title: How to Write a Resume After a Long Employment Gap
dek: A practical drafting order for a resume that has a break in it — what to collect, how to date the roles honestly, and where the gap itself goes.
author: Ingrid Castellanos
body:
A long break in your work history changes a few decisions on your resume: which format to use, how precisely to date your jobs, whether the gap gets its own line, and which recent activity goes at the top. It does not change the basic job of the document, which is to show an employer what you can do for them now.

This guide takes you through it in drafting order — what to gather, what to write first, and a template excerpt you can adapt. It assumes you are writing truthfully about real dates and real roles, because everything that follows depends on that.

Key takeaways

  • Keep reverse-chronological order where you can: CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) says most employers prefer it, gap and all.
  • Don't hide dates you cannot hide — some Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software reads months and days (CareerOneStop).
  • Quick win: give the break its own dated entry with one factual label, then list any training, freelance or volunteer work beneath it.

What to Gather Before You Start

Open a blank document and collect these first. Drafting goes faster when you are arranging facts rather than hunting for them.

  • The target job posting, copied into a plain text file. You will mine it for the exact job title, the named tools, and the repeated phrases.
  • The target job title, written out as the employer writes it. If the posting says "Accounts Payable Specialist," that is the title your summary should echo — not "finance professional."
  • An accurate date list for every paid role: employer name, your job title, start month and year, end month and year. Check payslips, tax records, contracts, pension statements or your own online profile rather than relying on memory.
  • The start and end dates of the break itself, to the month. ResumeLab treats a break shorter than nine months as not really an employment gap at all, so pin down the actual span before you decide how to handle it.
  • Three to five quantifiable achievements from past roles — anything you counted, cut, sped up, sold, trained or fixed. A rough number is fine at this stage; you will tidy it later.
  • A written list of what you did during the gap: caregiving, treatment and recovery, study, relocation, raising children, redundancy and job search, freelance jobs, volunteering, unpaid work for a family business.
  • Certificates, course completions and licences with their dates, including anything finished during the break and anything that has since expired.
  • A tools and systems list — software, machinery, platforms, languages — plus a note of which have changed version or been replaced since you last used them.
  • Your old resume and any performance reviews or reference letters you kept. These are the fastest source of forgotten detail.
  • Current contact details: phone, email you actually check, city and region, and your online professional profile link if you have one.
  • One or two plain sentences explaining the break, drafted for your cover letter rather than your resume. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) says it is not necessary to explain a gap on the resume itself — the cover letter or the interview is the place for it.
  • Current contact details for two or three referees, so you are not scrambling for them after the interview.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Draft in this order. Each step produces something you can see on the page before you move on.

  1. Pick the format. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) names three styles — chronological, functional and combination — and says most employers prefer a chronological resume listing jobs in reverse order, newest first. A functional resume groups skills and accomplishments into categories instead of under job entries; Indeed's career advice lists that as one way to reduce the visual weight of a gap, alongside dropping months or giving the gap its own entry. A combination keeps a reverse-chronological job list but leads with a skills block. Start with combination unless your break is very long and your skills are the stronger story.
  2. Write the header. Name, city and region, phone, professional email, profile link. Put it in the body of the document, not in the page header — SSA's Choose Work guidance (2024) says text in document headers can fail to parse, and to bold section names instead. Example: `Dana Whitfield — Leeds, UK — 07xxx xxx xxx — dana.whitfield@email.com`.
  3. Write the summary last-but-place-it-first. Three lines, present tense, aimed at the target title. Example: "Accounts Payable Specialist with [X] years in high-volume invoice processing, returning to full-time work after a planned career break for caregiving. Recently completed [Certification Name], [Year]."
  4. Build the experience section in reverse order. One line per role: title, employer, location, dates. Then two to four bullets each, in the form action verb plus task plus measurable result — for example, "Reconciled supplier accounts across [X] entities, cutting unmatched invoices by [X%] within two quarters."
  5. Decide how precise your dates will be. CareerOneStop says that if the gap was under a year you can list years only rather than months — but also warns that some applicant tracking systems look for month or even day of employment, so year-only dating is not foolproof. For a long break, date everything to the month and let the gap show.
  6. Give the break its own entry if it is long. Indeed's advice includes listing a long gap as an entry in the experience section. Example: "Career Break — Full-Time Caregiving, March [Year] – August [Year]. Maintained [Professional Body] membership; completed [Course Name], [Year]." LinkedIn added a Career Break option to profiles in March 2022, with categories including caregiving and health and well-being, so the label will read as familiar.
  7. Add anything that kept your hands in. Freelance pieces, volunteering, committee roles, a family business, a short contract. Format them exactly like paid jobs, with honest titles. Example: "Volunteer Bookkeeper, [Organisation Name], [Year]–[Year]: processed [X] monthly transactions and produced quarterly reports for a committee of [X]."
  8. Trim the far end. CareerOneStop says a long work history does not need every job, and that you can leave off a role held before an early-career gap. Cut anything that no longer supports the target title.
  9. Write the skills section from the posting. Use the employer's wording for tools you genuinely use: "SAP, Excel (pivot tables, VLOOKUP), Xero, invoice matching, month-end close." Add education and certifications underneath with their years.
  10. Do the formatting pass. SSA's Choose Work guidance (2024) recommends body text in an ATS-friendly font such as Calibri, Arial, Helvetica, Georgia or Times New Roman at 10–12 points, and no pictures, tables, columns or text boxes, since those are the elements that commonly break parsing. Indeed suggests line spacing between single and 1.5. That same SSA post cites LinkedIn's figure that almost 99% of Fortune 500 companies use computerised applicant tracking systems, so the plain layout is worth the dull appearance.
  11. Check the dates against your records one last time. Every month and year on the resume should match what an employer would see on a reference check or a tax record. Rewording a vague old job title for clarity is fine; changing a date is not.
  12. Draft the cover letter line about the break. One factual sentence and a pivot forward — a report on LinkedIn's 2022 career-break survey (FDM Group) states 51% of employers would likely call back a candidate if they knew the context of the break, and 46% see people returning from breaks as an untapped talent pool.

Example Snippet

Resume excerpt — template to adapt, not copy

Template to adapt, not copy — replace every bracketed placeholder with your own verified details.

SUMMARY [Target Job Title] with [X] years in [industry or function], returning to full-time work after a [length] career break for [caregiving / health / study / relocation]. Completed [Course or Certification Name] in [Year]; experienced with [Tool], [Tool] and [Process].

EXPERIENCE Career Break — [Caregiving / Health and Well-Being / Full-Time Study], [Month Year] – [Month Year] - Completed [Course Name] through [Training Provider], [Year]. - Managed [X] hours per week of scheduling, budgeting and liaison with [X] external services.

[Job Title], [Company Name], [City] — [Month Year] – [Month Year] - Processed [X] [invoices / orders / cases] per month, reducing average turnaround by [X%] over [X] months. - Trained [X] new team members on [System Name], cutting onboarding time from [X] weeks to [X].

Cover letter paragraph — template to adapt, not copy

Template to adapt, not copy — one factual sentence about the break, then forward to the role.

I took a [length] break from [Month Year] to [Month Year] to [reason, stated plainly and without apology]. During that time I kept my [Professional Body] membership current and completed [Course Name] in [Year]. I am now looking for a full-time [Target Job Title] role, and your posting's focus on [specific requirement from the posting] matches what I did at [Previous Company Name], where I [achievement with [X%] or [X] result].

Keep both excerpts short in your own version. The resume states the break as a fact; the letter supplies the context.

Frequently asked questions

How long should my resume be now that I have added a career break entry?+

Indeed's career advice says a resume should be one page in most cases, with some exceptions where two pages are appropriate — typically long technical, academic or senior histories. A break entry is only two or three lines, so it rarely pushes you over. If you are over length, cut the oldest roles before you cut recent achievements.

Should I send a PDF or a Word file?+

Follow the application instructions first. Where they are silent, the two sources disagree on the same criterion of machine readability: SSA's Choose Work guidance (2024) says to save as PDF or DOCX and avoid GIF, PNG, JPG or TXT, while Betterteam advises using .doc or .docx unless the posting specifically asks for a PDF, on the grounds that PDFs are not compatible with every applicant tracking system. DOCX satisfies both pieces of advice, so it is the safer default.

Do I need an objective statement to explain that I am returning to work?+

No. A short summary aimed at the target job title does the same work and says more about what you offer. If you want one line about returning to full-time work, fold it into the summary rather than adding a separate objective block.

What if the break has not ended — I have no current job to list?+

That is the normal situation when you are applying. Date the break entry from its start month to "Present" and list what you are doing now: study, volunteering, a course in progress, job-search-related training. Do not invent a current role or stretch an old end date to cover the period.

Should my online profile match the dates on my resume?+

Yes — mismatched dates are the detail that gets noticed. LinkedIn added a Career Break option to the Experience section in March 2022, with categories such as caregiving and health and well-being, so you can record the period there in the same way you have on the resume.

How do I handle references after several years out?+

Contact former managers and colleagues before you submit anything, confirm they are willing, and check their current job title and contact details. Do not list references on the resume itself unless the posting asks for them; keep a separate one-page list ready to send.

Sources

  2. CareerOneStop (sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor) — Resume styles
  3. Social Security Administration – Choose Work! (Ticket to Work) — How to Make Your Resume Applicant Tracking System Friendly (2024-08-08)
  4. Betterteam — How to Prepare an ATS Resume
  5. Indeed Career Guide — Q&A: When Can a Resume Be Two Pages?
  6. Indeed Career Guide — Q&A: Is a Two-Page Resume Okay?
  7. ResumeLab — How to Explain Employment Gaps on Resumes [25 Tips]
  8. Indeed Career Guide — How To Explain Employment Gaps on Your Resume
  9. LinkedIn — LinkedIn Members Can Now Spotlight Career Breaks on Their Profiles (2022-03)
  10. FDM Group — Why You Should be Using LinkedIn's Career Break Feature…Today!

title: How to Write a Resume for a Job You're Overqualified For
dek: A focused approach to trimming scope without hiding facts, so a hiring manager sees a fit for the role in front of them instead of a flight risk.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
Being overqualified is a framing problem, not a skills problem. The reader of your resume has to believe you want this job, will stay in it, and can take direction from someone less experienced than you — and they decide that from the top third of page one. Your job when drafting is to narrow the focus to what the role actually needs, keep every title, date and qualification truthful, and let numbers do the persuading.

This guide walks through what to collect first, the order to draft each section, and two short template excerpts you can adapt. It does not ask you to hide anything: employers may assume an overqualified hire wants more money, is treating the job as a stopgap, will get bored or will struggle taking direction (TopResume, undated), and the fix is a focused resume plus a cover letter that answers those doubts head-on.

Key takeaways

  • Target the posting, not your career: cut unrelated detail, but never alter a job title, date, degree or responsibility.
  • Biggest mistake is a resume that reads like a promotion request — seniority language instead of results the role needs.
  • Quick win: drop graduation dates and unrelated advanced credentials (Indeed, undated), and keep history to the last 10–15 years.

What to Gather Before You Start

Open a scratch file and collect these before you write a single line of the resume. Each one is a document or a data point, not a mood.

  • The target job posting, copied into a plain document so you can highlight repeated words. You will mirror its exact job title and its named tools.
  • Ten to fifteen postings for the same job title from different employers. Scanning that many is the recommended way to spot the requirements that come up most often, which become your core qualifications list (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated).
  • Your master career history: every employer name, exact job title as it appeared on your contract or payslip, and start and end month and year. You will cut from this, never edit it.
  • Three to five quantifiable achievements that match the target role's level of responsibility — each one with a number attached: volume handled, time saved, error rate, retention, budget, headcount trained.
  • The exact target job title, written down character for character as the employer words it.
  • A list of your degrees, licences, certificates and memberships, with award dates noted separately so you can decide which dates to show.
  • The tools, systems and software named in the posting — ticketing systems, spreadsheets, scheduling tools, machinery, languages — and an honest note of your level with each.
  • The posting's stated file format and application route: whether it asks for .docx, PDF, a web form, or plain text.
  • Your contact block: full name, city and region, one phone number, one professional email address, and a professional profile link if you keep one current.
  • Two or three sentences on why you want this specific job — relocation, a deliberate step back from management, a change of field, hours that fit your life. That raw material belongs in the cover letter, not the resume, but drafting it now keeps your summary honest.

Step-by-Step Instructions

Draft in this order. Writing the summary last is tempting, but writing it third forces you to decide what the resume is arguing before you fill in history.

1. Set the page up before you write. Use a single-column layout with one-inch margins, a simple font such as Times New Roman, Cambria or Arial, at 10–12 point (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Because an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) scans left to right, avoid tables, text boxes, columns, logos, images and graphics, and keep your contact details out of the page header or footer where parsing can miss them (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). - Example file name to use: `[Firstname]-[Lastname]-Resume-[Job Title].docx` 2. Write the header. Name on its own line, then a single line of contact details. No photo, no full street address. - Example: `[First Name] [Last Name] | [City, State/Region] | [phone] | [professional email]` 3. Add a headline that names the job you are applying for. This is the fastest way to stop a reader filing you under "former director, will leave in six months." A headline states your current target, so it is not a claim about a past title. - Example: `Customer Support Specialist — [Industry] | [CRM Tool] | Bilingual [Language A]/[Language B]` 4. Write the summary. Keep it to 3–4 sentences or 3–5 bullet points, placed under the headline (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Skip it only if you have three years of experience or less, or your history already shows a clear consistent progression (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated) — if you are overqualified, keep it, because the summary is where you frame intent (TopResume, undated). - Example sentence: `Hands-on [target role] with [X] years in [field], now focused on front-line [function] work after leading a team of [X]; looking to apply [skill] and [tool] daily rather than manage from a distance.` 5. Build a core qualifications list from the postings you collected. Six to ten short items, each one a phrase the employer actually used. Plain bullets in one column, no skills bars or ratings graphics. - Example line: `[CRM Tool] · [Scheduling System] · Complaint resolution · [Language] fluency · Shift handover reporting` 6. Draft the experience section. Cover the last 10–15 years and leave off roles unrelated to your current goal (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated); trimming early-career entries is a standard approach when you are overqualified (AutoTailor, undated). Write about 5–8 bullets per relevant job, each one or two lines (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Rephrase scope so it reads at the level of the target job, but keep titles, dates and real responsibilities exactly as they were — submit a focused, truthful resume rather than one that hides experience (GotResumeBuilder, undated). Lead with the measurable result, not the seniority of the title (LinkedIn collaborative article, undated). - Example bullet: `Resolved an average of [X] customer cases per week across phone and email, cutting average first-response time by [X%] over [X] months.` 7. Finish education and credentials. List qualifications truthfully. You can leave off graduation dates and advanced credentials unrelated to the job, both of which can flag age or overqualification (Indeed, undated; TopResume, undated). Removing an irrelevant certificate is editing; removing a degree the job requires is not. - Example line: `[Degree], [Subject] — [Institution], [City]` 8. Do the final pass and choose the file format. Employers typically scan a resume in under 10 seconds (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated), so read only the top third and ask whether it names the target job. Keep the document to 1–2 pages, using the second page only when the volume of experience needs it (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). If the posting names no format, Word, PDF or plain text are all acceptable and you should avoid sending a scan (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). - Example check: `Does the headline, summary and first bullet contain the exact phrase [target job title]?`

Example Snippet

Both excerpts below are skeletons. Every bracket must be replaced with something you can evidence in an interview.

Summary for a deliberate step down

Template to adapt, not copy

[Target Job Title] with [X] years in [industry], including [X] years doing [core task of the target role] directly. Chose to move from [previous scope, e.g. managing a team of X] back to hands-on [function] work and have kept current with [tool or system named in the posting]. Known for [specific strength the posting asks for] and for training colleagues on [process], reducing [error or rework measure] by [X%]. Committed to a [shift pattern / site / team] role for the long term in [City].

Experience bullets that lead with results

Template to adapt, not copy

[Job Title as it appeared officially] — [Employer Type or Name], [City] — [Month Year]–[Month Year]

- Processed [X] [orders/claims/cases] per month in [system], maintaining accuracy above [X%] across [X] consecutive quarters. - Rewrote [X] standard procedures for [process], cutting average handling time by [X%] and reducing repeat queries by [X%]. - Trained [X] new starters on [tool], shortening time-to-independent-work from [X] weeks to [X] weeks. - Coordinated with [department] on [recurring task], clearing a backlog of [X] items within [X] weeks.

Notice what the bullets do not say: nothing about strategy ownership, board reporting or restructuring. The underlying facts are unchanged; the emphasis sits on the work the target job involves every day.

Frequently asked questions

How long should my resume be if I have twenty years of experience?+

One to two pages, with the second page used only when the amount of experience requires it (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). The same source notes that two pages are quite acceptable for experienced professionals when squeezing onto one makes it crowded and hard to read. Conventions differ by country and by field — academic and medical CVs run longer — so check what is normal where you are applying.

Should I include an objective statement instead of a summary?+

A summary that highlights your top skills and accomplishments is the more common choice and sits directly under your headline (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). An objective only earns its space if it answers a question the reader would otherwise ask, such as a move to a new region or a shift to shift-based work. If you write one, keep it to a single line and make it about the employer's need, not your own career plan.

Which file format should I send?+

Follow the posting. If it names nothing, Word, PDF or plain text are all workable and you should not send a scanned image of a printed page (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Jobscan recommends converting a Word resume to PDF when you apply unless the posting specifically asks for a .docx file (Jobscan, May 2025). Keep a plain-text (ASCII) version on hand, since some job sites and Applicant Tracking Systems cannot read a Word-formatted file (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated).

Do I need to explain on the resume why I'm applying for a more junior job?+

No — the resume shows fit, the cover letter explains motive. Leaning on the cover letter is one of the standard moves when you are overqualified (TopResume, undated). Use two or three sentences there: what draws you to this specific role, what you are deliberately stepping away from, and how long you intend to stay. Keep it matter-of-fact and avoid apologising for your own experience.

Should I put my salary expectations on the resume?+

Leave pay off the resume unless the application explicitly asks for it, and then answer in the field or cover letter provided. Employers may assume an overqualified hire expects a high salary (TopResume, undated), so it helps to be ready with a range you can defend. Check current rates for the exact job title in your area using your national labour market statistics body or several live postings for the same role before you name anything.

Do I need to rewrite the resume for every application?+

Rewrite the headline, summary and core qualifications list each time, since those are the parts that mirror the posting's wording. The experience section usually only needs reordering and a few swapped bullets once you have built the full version. Keep one master file with everything in it, then save each tailored copy under the job title you are applying for.

title: How to Write a Resume With No Experience
dek: Coursework, volunteer shifts, part-time work and personal projects all count as evidence — here is how to turn them into bullets an employer can scan.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
Writing a resume with no formal experience is mostly a sorting problem, not a writing problem. You almost certainly have material — classes, volunteering, a part-time job in an unrelated field, a project you finished on your own — and the task is to pick the parts that match the job you want, then describe them in the employer's words.

This guide takes you from gathering the raw material through to a saved, named file, with a template you can adapt at the end. Nothing here asks you to invent a job, a date or a duty you didn't do.

Key takeaways

  • Mirror the posting: scan several ads for your target title and reuse the requirements that keep repeating (CareerOneStop, U.S. Dept. of Labor).
  • Avoid a skills-only functional layout — CareerOneStop warns an Applicant Tracking System (ATS) is likely to reject it.
  • Quick win: name the file with your full name plus the job title before you attach it.

What to Gather Before You Start

Open a blank document and paste all of this in before you write a single line of the resume. Drafting goes faster when you are editing material rather than hunting for it.

  • The job posting you are applying to, copied as plain text so you can highlight the words it uses.
  • Five to ten other postings for the same target job title. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) recommends scanning a number of postings for your targeted title to find the requirements and keywords that come up most often.
  • The exact job title you are aiming for, written at the top of your notes — "warehouse associate", "junior data analyst" — so every later choice is measured against it.
  • A list of the transferable skills named in those postings, such as collaboration, people skills, precision and follow-through — the examples CareerOneStop gives — with a note beside each one you can actually evidence.
  • Every role you have held, paid or unpaid: part-time shifts, internships, placements, casual work, a family business, a club committee. For each, write the organisation, the city, your title and the start and end dates by month and year.
  • Your education record: school or college name, programme, graduation date (or expected date), plus a list of modules, labs or assignments that relate to the target job.
  • Three to five things you finished, each with a number attached. CareerOneStop advises highlighting achievements with figures, offering phrasings like "Saved 125 hours per project", "Increased sales by 15%" or "Trained 32 new staff". Yours might be items processed per shift, people served, a group size you coordinated or a deadline you beat.
  • Certificates, licences and training, with the issuing body and the date awarded.
  • A tools list: software, equipment, languages, platforms you can use without supervision.
  • Your contact details: phone, an email address that is just your name, your city and region, and a link to a portfolio or professional profile if you have one.

If an item has no number yet, leave it in anyway and estimate honestly later. If you cannot stand behind the figure, describe the work without one rather than inventing it.

Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Choose the layout before you type. CareerOneStop describes three basic styles — chronological, functional and combination — and warns that a functional format, although it highlights transferable skills well, is likely to be rejected by an Applicant Tracking System (ATS). With little experience, a combination layout usually works best: a short skills-led top section, then dated education and experience underneath. Keep it to a single column of plain text, because tables, side columns, graphics and text placed in headers or footers are the elements parsers commonly mangle. Set your document up with one simple font and clear section headings, like this: `EDUCATION`. 2. Write the header. Name on the first line, then one line of contact details. For example: > Template line — adapt, do not copy > [Your Full Name] | [City, Region] | [phone] | [firstname.lastname@email.com] | [portfolio or profile URL] 3. Write a short summary aimed at the employer. CareerOneStop says a summary should state your top accomplishments or skills, and notes that experts differ on whether to include an objective — if you use one, make it specific and directed at the employer rather than general or self-serving. Two or three lines is plenty. Example: "Recent [qualification] graduate with [X] months of customer-facing retail experience and coursework in [subject], seeking the [Job Title] role at [Company Name]." 4. Put education near the top while it is your strongest evidence. Name the institution, the qualification, the date, then two or three relevant details. Example line: "Completed a [length] group project analysing [topic], presenting findings to a panel of [X] staff." 5. Write the experience section, whatever the work was. CareerOneStop advises that if you have little experience in the job you are applying for, you should emphasise the transferable skills you built in past jobs that relate to your new goal. Use the same structure in every bullet: action verb, the task, the measurable result. Example: "Served an average of [X] customers per shift, resolving [X] billing queries per week without escalation." 6. Add project, volunteer and activity sections to fill the gap. Format these exactly like jobs — title, organisation or project name, dates, bullets. Example: "Built a [tool or report] using [software], cutting the time to produce weekly figures by [X%] for a team of [X]." 7. Consider the optional sections that fit you. CareerOneStop lists professional memberships or associations, publications or other work products, and community involvement as sections to add depending on your circumstances. Add one only if it supports the target title. Example: "Member, [Association Name], since [Month Year]; attend monthly [topic] workshops." 8. Build the skills section from your keyword notes. Group the tools and skills that appeared most often across the postings you scanned, and only ones you would be comfortable demonstrating. Example: "Skills: [software], [software], inventory counting, scheduling, written reporting, [language] (conversational)." 9. Edit for the first pass. CareerOneStop notes that employers spend only a short time scanning a resume before deciding whether it meets the minimum qualifications, so the top third has to carry your strongest match. Cut anything that does not tie back to the target title, make verb tenses consistent, and read every bullet aloud to catch padding. 10. Save and name the file. CareerOneStop advises saving and sending as a PDF to preserve formatting unless another format is specified, and using a file name with your full name, or full name plus job title — the example given is Sarah-Smith-Marketing-Coordinator.docx. Keep a plain-text (ASCII) version too: CareerOneStop notes this may be required when a job site or applicant tracking system cannot read a Word-formatted resume.

Example Snippet

Both excerpts below are templates to adapt, not copy. The brackets are deliberate — replace every one with your own detail, and delete any line you cannot evidence.

Top section: header, summary, education

Template to adapt, not copy

[Your Full Name] [City, Region] | [phone] | [firstname.lastname@email.com] | [profile or portfolio URL]

SUMMARY [Qualification] graduate with [X] months of [type of work] experience and coursework in [subject]. Comfortable with [software] and [software]. Applying for the [Job Title] role at [Company Name].

EDUCATION [Qualification], [Institution Name], [City] — [Month Year] (expected [Month Year]) - Completed a [length] project on [topic], presenting results to [X] classmates and [X] staff. - Relevant modules: [module], [module], [module].

Experience and projects bullets

Template to adapt, not copy

EXPERIENCE [Job Title], [Organisation Name], [City] — [Month Year] to [Month Year] - Processed [X] orders per shift and logged stock counts, reducing recount requests by [X%] over [X] months. - Trained [X] new seasonal staff on [system], shortening their first-week supervision time by [X] hours each.

VOLUNTEER AND PROJECTS [Project or Role Name], [Organisation Name] — [Month Year] to [Month Year] - Coordinated a team of [X] volunteers across [X] events, meeting every set-up deadline. - Rebuilt the [spreadsheet or record system] in [software], cutting weekly reporting time by [X%].

Notice the pattern in each bullet: an action verb, the task, then the result as a number. CareerOneStop suggests exactly this kind of quantified phrasing — "Saved 125 hours per project", "Increased sales by 15%", "Trained 32 new staff" — so use your own true figures in the same shape.

Frequently asked questions

How long should my resume be if I have no experience?+

One page is normally enough when your history is short — entry-level, student or career-start. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) notes that two pages are acceptable for experienced professionals, and that cramming content onto one crowded page can get a resume passed over. So the page count follows the material, not a rule.

Which file format should I send?+

Unless the posting specifies otherwise, CareerOneStop advises saving and sending a PDF to preserve your formatting. Keep a plain-text (ASCII) version in reserve, which the same source notes may be required when a resume site or applicant tracking system cannot read a Word-formatted file. If the employer asks for .doc or .docx, send that instead.

Should I include an objective statement?+

CareerOneStop reports that career experts differ on this, and says that if you do use one it should be directed to the employer and specific rather than general or self-serving. A one-line statement naming the role and the company is fine; a sentence about what you hope to gain personally adds nothing an employer can act on.

How far back should my history go, and does unrelated work count?+

CareerOneStop's general rule is to include your previous years of work history. With a short record, include all of it — unrelated jobs included — and use the bullets to pull out the transferable skills that match the posting. A supermarket shift can evidence accuracy, scheduling and dealing with people.

Should I put references on the resume?+

Usually not. Keep the space for evidence and prepare a separate list of names, titles, organisations and contact details to supply when asked. Ask each person first, and tell them which role you applied for so they are not caught cold.

Do I need to change it for every application?+

Change the target job title, the summary and the skills order at minimum. That is the point of scanning several postings for your target title before you draft: the repeated requirements tell you which of your existing bullets to move up and which to cut for each employer.

  6. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Does your resume speak to employers
  7. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Work experience
  8. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Optional sections

title: Internal Promotion Resume Examples
dek: Two annotated resume templates and one cover letter template for moving up inside the company you already work for, plus the edits to make first.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
Applying for a job where you already work is a different writing problem from applying cold. The people reading you may know your work, but they still have to compare you on paper against external applicants, and the file usually travels through the same system and the same screens as everyone else's. The examples below show two ways to structure that document: one for a straight step up on your current team, one for a move into a different department where your titles don't match the posting.

Everything in quotes is a template with bracketed placeholders. Replace every bracket with your own facts — never invent a title, a date or a number you can't support.

Key takeaways

  • Example 1 fits you if you're going up a level on the team you already work on and your recent work is the main evidence — it leads with a dated, chronological history under one employer heading.
  • Example 2 fits you if you're crossing into a different department and your job titles don't match the posting — it leads with a skills block before the work history.
  • The formatting choice that differs most is what sits directly under your name: a summary plus dated roles in Example 1, a 3–4 skill block in Example 2.

Example Resumes & Cover Letters

Both resumes assume one employer with more than one role inside it. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) suggests a reader scans a resume for roughly 15–20 seconds, so whatever matters most for the internal role belongs near the top, not on page two.

Example 1 — Vertical promotion on your current team (3–6 years with the employer, one prior internal move)

TEMPLATE — adapt every bracketed field before sending; this is not a ready-to-submit document

[Your Full Name] [City, State/Region] | [Phone] | [Work or personal email] | [Employee ID, if the internal form asks for it]

Summary [Current job title] with [X] years at [Current Employer], now responsible for [core area named in the posting]. Delivered [named project or process] across [X] teams. Trained [X] new team members since [Year].

Experience [Current Employer] — [City, State/Region] [Current Title], [Month Year]–Present (promoted from [Previous Title], [Month Year]) - Rebuilt [process or workflow] for [team/function], reducing [cycle time or error rate] by [X%] over [X] months. - Led [number] person working group on [initiative], delivering [outcome] [X] weeks ahead of the planned date. - Took on [responsibility named in the job posting] in [Month Year], covering [X] accounts/sites/cases per [week or month].

[Previous Title], [Month Year]–[Month Year] - Handled [main task], raising [named metric] from [X] to [X] across [time period]. - Documented [process], cutting onboarding time for new starters by [X%].

[Earlier Employer] — [City, State/Region] [Title], [Year]–[Year] - Managed [task], improving [metric] by [X%].

Skills [Skill from posting] · [System or tool used in the target role] · [Certification or licence, with issuing body and year]

Education [Qualification], [Institution], [Year]

This structure works here because your strongest argument is continuity: the same employer heading with two stacked titles shows the promotion visually, which CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) lists as something to note in the work experience section alongside employer, location, dates and accomplishments. The summary is four lines, inside the 2–4 sentence or 3–5 bullet range that same guidance suggests, so the reader hits your current responsibilities before the fold. Older roles are compressed to one bullet because the decision rests on recent work.

Example 2 — Lateral or cross-department internal move, where your titles don't match the posting (10+ years, mixed roles)

TEMPLATE — adapt every bracketed field before sending; this is not a ready-to-submit document

[Your Full Name] [City, State/Region] | [Phone] | [Email]

Key Skills for [Exact Job Title from the Internal Posting] - [Skill 1 from the posting]: [where you do it now], covering [X] [units] per [period]. - [Skill 2 from the posting]: [system or method], used daily since [Year]. - [Skill 3 from the posting]: [example], supporting [X] stakeholders across [X] departments. - [Credential or licence]: [issuing body], [Year].

Work History [Current Employer] — [City, State/Region] [Current Title], [Month Year]–Present - Coordinated [cross-functional task touching the target department], cutting [handoff delay or rework] by [X%]. - Volunteered for [secondment, committee or cover arrangement] in [Year], producing [deliverable] used by [X] teams.

[Earlier Internal Title], [Month Year]–[Month Year] - Ran [task], handling [X] [items] per [period] at [X%] accuracy.

[Prior Employer] — [City, State/Region] [Title], [Year]–[Year] - Delivered [project], increasing [metric] by [X%].

Education and Training [Qualification], [Institution], [Year] · [Internal or external course relevant to the target function], [Year]

The skills block goes first because your chronology doesn't make the case on its own — CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) suggests opening with 3–4 major skills for the targeted job title when the work history isn't the strongest selling point, and notes that most employers still prefer a chronological format otherwise. The history stays underneath in reverse order, so nothing is hidden. That same guidance suggests covering relevant jobs from the previous 10–15 years, which is why the pre-[Year] roles are cut rather than listed.

Example 3 — Short cover letter to send with either resume

TEMPLATE — adapt every bracketed field before sending; this is not a ready-to-submit document

Dear [Hiring Manager's Name],

I'm applying for the [Exact Job Title], [requisition number], posted internally on [Date]. I've been with [Employer] since [Month Year], currently as [Current Title] in [Department].

The posting asks for [requirement 1] and [requirement 2]. In my current role I [specific example tied to requirement 1], which [result, e.g. reduced [X%] of [metric]]. I also [example tied to requirement 2], working alongside [target department] on [named project].

I've spoken with [manager's name] about applying, and I'm happy to discuss handover of [current responsibility]. I'm available for interview [general availability].

Regards, [Your Name] | [Phone] | [Email] | [Employee ID]

Keeping it to four short paragraphs leaves the detail in the resume and uses the letter for the two things an external applicant can't say: that you already know the department, and that you've handled the internal courtesy of telling your manager. Naming the requisition number matters because internal postings are often tracked by number inside an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), which CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) describes as software employers use to receive applications and track your status.

How to Customize These Examples

Work through these in order before you reuse anything above.

  • Replace the header line of Example 2 — "Key Skills for [Exact Job Title from the Internal Posting]" — with the title exactly as written on the requisition, not your shorthand for it. Internal job families often have formal titles that differ from what the team calls the role day to day.
  • Rewrite the three skill bullets in Example 2 using words pulled from the posting itself. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) suggests scanning 10–15 postings to find the requirements, skills and credentials that come up most, and notes that the specific words you use carry the keyword matching. If only one internal posting exists, scan external postings for the same job family.
  • Fix the stacked title lines in Example 1 — "[Current Title], [Month Year]–Present (promoted from [Previous Title], [Month Year])". Use the titles and effective dates on your HR record, not approximations. An internal reader can check these, and you must never adjust a date or title to look better.
  • Replace every [X%] and [X] with a figure you can defend in the interview. If you don't have a number, rewrite the bullet around a volume, a frequency or a scope — "[X] sites", "[X] reports per month" — rather than leaving a vague claim.
  • Trim the Summary in Example 1 to 2–4 sentences or 3–5 bullets after you've added your own content, per the CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) range. Internal summaries tend to swell because you know too much context.
  • Rename the "Skills" heading at the bottom of Example 1 if the target department uses a different label — "Technical Skills", "Systems", "Licences" — so the section matches the vocabulary of the team reading it.
  • Cut the "[Earlier Employer]" block from Example 1 or Example 2 if it falls outside the previous 10–15 years, which is the window that same guidance suggests for relevant work history.
  • Delete the "[Employee ID, if the internal form asks for it]" field unless your internal application form actually requests it; otherwise it clutters the contact line.
  • In Example 3, change "[requisition number]" and "[Date]" to the real reference, and remove the sentence about speaking with your manager if that conversation hasn't happened yet. Don't write it as fact in advance.
  • Have two people read the final version, as CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) recommends, ideally one person inside the target department who can tell you whether your wording lands there.

Frequently asked questions

Should I send a PDF, a Word file, or plain text?+

Send whatever the internal application form specifies. If it gives you a choice, judge all three on the same two criteria — does the system accept it, and does the layout survive upload. PDF usually preserves the stacked title lines in Example 1; Word usually uploads cleanly and stays editable; plain text (ASCII) loses the bold and bullets but is sometimes required, as CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) notes, when a site or Applicant Tracking System can't read a Word-formatted file. Keep one copy of each version of your template so you're not reformatting under time pressure.

How do I get Example 2 down to one page?+

Decide first whether you need to. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) says two pages are quite acceptable for experienced professionals and that a crowded one-page resume may get passed over. If you still want one page, cut the "[Prior Employer]" block, reduce each older internal role to a single bullet, and move the training line onto the same row as the qualification. Don't shrink margins or type size to the point where the skills block stops being scannable.

Can I use years only instead of months in the date lines?+

You can, and CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) notes that years-only is an option if a gap was under a year — but it also warns that some applicant tracking systems look for month or day dates. For an internal move your dates are already on file, so months are usually the safer choice in both templates. Whichever you pick, use the same format in every date line on the document.

Should I add a quote from my current manager to the resume?+

Only with permission. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor, undated guidance) says a testimonial can work in a resume because it's a sales document, but that you should ask first. If you use one, put it as a single indented line under the Summary in Example 1 with the person's name and job title, and tell them you've done it — internally, they're likely to be asked about it.

  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Resumes (GetMyFuture)
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Resume FAQs
  4. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Does your resume speak to employers
  5. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Special tips
  6. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Spruce up your resume with the Resume Guide
  7. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — How-to Find a job now: Target your resume
