title: Product Manager vs Marketing Manager: Which Path Fits You?
dek: Both titles sit inside the same federal occupation code, so the real difference shows up in who you answer to, what you ship, and how pay is set.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
Product management and marketing management look similar from outside — both sit between customers, engineering and the commercial side, and both are usually filled by people with a few years of experience rather than straight out of school. The split is in what you own: a product manager owns what gets built and in what order; a marketing manager owns how it reaches a market and at what price position.

US federal data does not separate them cleanly. ONET lists both "Product Manager" and "Product Marketing Manager" as reported job titles under the Marketing Managers occupation, SOC 11-2021.00 (ONET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor), which means published pay and outlook figures cover the two paths together. This guide works through what that means for your decision, and where the paths genuinely diverge.

Key takeaways

  • Published pay data is shared: the 2025 median wage for Marketing Managers — the occupation that also carries the Product Manager title in O*NET — was $166,790 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so neither path has a documented federal pay advantage over the other.
  • Marketing has the wider published entry funnel: BLS lists sales representatives, market research analysts and public relations specialists as feeder roles (BLS, 2025), while product management is most often entered sideways from engineering, support, analytics or operations inside an existing employer.
  • Neither path is a 40-hour job: 84% of Marketing Managers respondents reported working more than 40 hours a week (O*NET OnLine), so choose on the work itself — roadmap trade-offs and build decisions versus pricing, positioning and demand — not on expected hours.

Setting the Context

Product manager. You decide what a product team builds next and why. That means talking to customers, writing requirements, ranking competing requests, agreeing scope with engineering and design, and reporting on whether the thing you shipped moved the number it was supposed to move. You rarely manage people early on; you influence a team you do not control.

Entry is usually sideways rather than straight in. Common starting titles are associate product manager, product owner, product analyst or technical program manager. Most people arrive from an adjacent seat — support, QA, data analysis, operations, engineering, or client-facing consulting — because employers want someone who already understands the product and the customer. There is no licence and no single qualifying exam. Job Zone Four applies to this occupation group, which ONET describes as "Considerable Preparation Needed," with most roles requiring a four-year bachelor's degree (ONET OnLine).

Marketing manager. You direct how a product or brand is positioned, priced and promoted. ONET's task list for Marketing Managers includes formulating and directing marketing policies, using sales forecasting and strategic planning, evaluating the financial side of product development — budgets, R&D appropriations, return-on-investment and profit-and-loss projections — and developing pricing strategies (ONET OnLine). Starting titles include marketing coordinator, marketing specialist, demand generation associate, brand associate and product marketing manager.

BLS states that advertising, promotions and marketing managers typically need a bachelor's degree plus work experience in a related occupation, with no on-the-job training expected, and names sales representative, market research analyst and public relations specialist as typical prior roles (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Some employers prefer candidates with a master's degree (BLS, 2025).

Within five years. From an associate product manager seat, the usual progression is product manager, then senior product manager, then group product manager or director of product — a shift from owning one feature area to owning a portfolio and other PMs. From a marketing specialist seat, progression runs to marketing manager, then senior or group manager, then director of marketing, brand or growth. Both ladders depend on employer size: a 60-person company may have one director and no layer in between, while a large firm may have four grades before you manage anyone. Plan on 3-6 years from an entry title to a manager-of-managers title in either path, and longer where headcount is flat.

If you want a professional home while you decide, the American Marketing Association is the national association ONET associates with this occupation (ONET OnLine).

Side-by-Side Comparison

DimensionProduct managerMarketing manager
Published median payNot tracked as a separate federal occupation; ONET lists Product Manager as a reported title under Marketing Managers, SOC 11-2021.00, with a 2025 median of $166,790 a year, or $80.19 an hour (ONET OnLine; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Median annual wage of $166,790 in May 2025 for marketing managers (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Pay spreadShares the same occupation code, so no separate published range exists; for the neighbouring advertising and promotions managers group the lowest 10 percent earned under $63,300 and the highest 10 percent over $286,240 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Sits in the same group as advertising and promotions managers, whose published 2025 median was $133,660 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — a reminder that "marketing manager" covers very different pay bands by specialism
Education employers reportONET's education survey for this occupation: 80% said a bachelor's degree is required for a new hire, 12% a high school diploma or equivalent, 6% a master's (ONET OnLine)BLS states a bachelor's degree is typically needed, and that some employers prefer a master's (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Prior experience expectedSame occupation group, so the same rule applies: work experience in a related occupation is typical, with no on-the-job training provided (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)BLS names the feeder roles explicitly: sales representatives, market research analysts, public relations specialists (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Typical work week84% of Marketing Managers respondents reported working more than 40 hours a week (O*NET OnLine)BLS: most work full time, some more than 40 hours a week; typically an office setting with travel to meet clients (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Daily tasksBuild-side tasks from the shared ONET list: evaluating the financial aspects of product development, including budgets, R&D appropriations, and ROI and profit-and-loss projections (ONET OnLine)Market-side tasks from the same list: formulating and directing marketing activities and policies, sales forecasting and strategic planning, and developing pricing strategies (O*NET OnLine)
Job security and outlookCovered by the same projection: 6 percent growth from 2025 to 2035, faster than the average for all occupations (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Marketing managers held about 421,600 of the group's roughly 454,800 jobs in 2025, with about 36,300 openings projected per year across the group (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)
Where the jobs areConcentrated in the same industries, led by professional, scientific and technical services at 23% and information at 10% (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)Also management of companies and enterprises 12%, finance and insurance 10%, wholesale trade 10% (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025)

Two things the table cannot tell you. First, pay structure differs by employer rather than by title: many roles in both paths are base salary plus an annual bonus tied to company or product targets, and at venture-backed technology firms equity is often part of the offer. Second, these are US figures. Pay, titles and expected qualifications vary by state and metro area within the US, and vary again in other countries. Check the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics pages for your state and metro, and read 15-20 live postings in your target city, before you anchor on any number.

Signs Each Path Is Right for You

Product management is likely the better fit if:

  • You already work next to a product team — support, QA, data, operations or implementation — and can name three decisions you would have made differently and why. That internal move is the most common entry route, and typically takes 6-18 months of deliberate positioning inside your current employer.
  • You are comfortable saying no in writing, to a named stakeholder, with a reason attached. Prioritisation is the job, and a PM who cannot decline requests becomes a ticket queue.
  • You can read a funnel or usage chart and form a hypothesis without an analyst translating it. BLS lists analytical and decision-making skills among the qualities these managers need (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • You enjoy working with engineers on constraints — what is technically cheap this quarter versus expensive — rather than finding that conversation frustrating.
  • You are fine with slow feedback. A roadmap bet can take two to three quarters to prove right or wrong, and you will be asked about it the whole time.

Marketing management is likely the better fit if:

  • You have held a sales, market research or public relations role, or want to — BLS names exactly those as the typical prior occupations (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so your experience maps onto the published entry route.
  • You like owning a number you can move inside a quarter: pipeline, qualified leads, trial starts, retention of a segment.
  • Pricing interests you as a problem. Developing pricing strategies is a core listed task for this occupation (O*NET OnLine), and it is one of the few places where positioning and finance meet.
  • You can write for a non-expert audience and judge creative work without producing it yourself. BLS lists creativity and communication skills alongside analytical skills for these managers (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • You want industry breadth rather than one sector. Marketing manager jobs spread across professional and technical services (23%), management of companies (12%), finance and insurance (10%), information (10%) and wholesale trade (10%) (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so the skill travels.
  • Client-facing travel suits you. BLS notes these managers may travel to meet clients (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), which is less common in product roles at the same level.

Frequently asked questions

Which one pays more after five years?+

Federal data cannot answer that, because both titles sit in the same occupation. O*NET lists Product Manager and Product Marketing Manager as reported job titles under Marketing Managers, SOC 11-2021.00, and the 2025 median wage for that occupation was $166,790 a year (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025; O*NET OnLine). What moves your number is industry, metro area and employer size rather than which of the two titles you hold. For a realistic five-year picture, compare the BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics figures for your state against senior-level postings in your target industry.

Which is easier to break into without a degree?+

Marketing, marginally, based on what employers report. In O*NET's education survey for this occupation, 12% of respondents said a high school diploma or equivalent is what a new hire needs, against 80% saying a bachelor's degree and 6% a master's (O*NET OnLine). BLS states a bachelor's degree is typical and that work experience in a related occupation is expected (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Without a degree, the workable route in either path is to enter through a feeder role — BLS names sales representative, market research analyst and public relations specialist — and move across internally over 12-24 months.

Is either path more secure than the other?+

They share one outlook. Employment of advertising, promotions and marketing managers is projected to grow 6 percent from 2025 to 2035, faster than the average for all occupations, with about 36,300 openings projected each year (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). The group held about 454,800 jobs in 2025, of which marketing managers accounted for roughly 421,600 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Security in practice tracks your industry: 23% of these jobs are in professional, scientific and technical services, which hires and cuts on project cycles, while finance and insurance at 10% tends to move more slowly.

How long does a switch from marketing to product management usually take?+

Plan on 6-18 months if you move internally at your current employer, where you already know the product and can take on a small feature area before changing title, and 12-24 months if you are changing employer at the same time. The shorter route works because BLS says this occupation expects prior experience in a related role with no on-the-job training provided (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — so the evidence has to come from work you have already done, not from a course.

title: Real Estate Agent vs Corporate Job: Pay, Growth, and Lifestyle Compared
dek: Commission income on a state licence you can earn in weeks, or a salaried desk role built on a degree — the numbers behind each choice, side by side.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
Real estate sales is one of the few occupations you can enter with a high school diploma and a state licence, but the median annual wage for real estate sales agents was $52,830 in May 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), and 54% of agents are self-employed, so that income is commission-based rather than salaried. Salaried corporate work generally asks for a bachelor's degree first: the median for business and financial occupations was $82,660 in May 2025, against $50,980 for all occupations (BLS, 2025).

This guide compares the two on pay, entry requirements, hours, outlook and ceiling, then lists the signals that point to each. Figures are United States federal data; pay, licensing and employment rules differ by country and by state, so check your local licensing body and current wage data before you commit.

Key takeaways

  • Pay: agents earned a median of $52,830 and brokers $73,220 in May 2025 (BLS, 2025); corporate management analysts earned a median of $101,860 and computer and information systems managers $175,140 (BLS, 2025) — but those corporate roles require a bachelor's degree, and the manager role also 5+ years of experience.
  • Entry cost: a real estate licence needs 40-180 hours of prelicensing education and $75-$485 in fees depending on the state (Homes.com News, undated); the corporate path usually starts with a multi-year degree.
  • Fit: choose agent work if you can absorb irregular commission income and want to set your own schedule including evenings and weekends; choose corporate if you want payroll pay and an occupation projected to grow 10-16% over 2025-35 rather than 2% (BLS, 2025).

Setting the Context

The real estate agent path. A sales agent is licensed to sell property but must work under a broker, and usually earns a portion of the commission on each property sold (BLS, 2025). Typical entry-level education is a high school diploma or equivalent (BLS, 2025). Every U.S. state requires a licence, and the usual conditions are being at least 18, holding a high school diploma or equivalent, completing prelicensing courses and passing an exam (BLS, 2025). The coursework load varies sharply: 40 hours in Alaska and Vermont up to 180 hours in Texas, with total fees from $75 in South Carolina and Wisconsin to $485 in Colorado (Homes.com News, undated). Licences then renew every 2 to 4 years, and most states require continuing education to renew (BLS, 2025).

Your starting title is sales agent or salesperson, affiliated with a brokerage. Within five years the standard step up is a broker's licence, which most states gate behind at least 2 years of experience as a licensed sales agent (BLS, 2025). Brokers can run their own business or work as an associate broker managing an independent office inside a larger company (BLS, 2025). That self-employment is the norm, not the exception: 55% of brokers and 54% of sales agents are self-employed (BLS, 2025). Median pay reflects the step: $52,830 for sales agents and $73,220 for brokers in May 2025 (BLS, 2025), with the two groups combined at $57,400 (BLS, 2025).

The corporate path. "Corporate job" covers salaried, payroll roles inside a company — analyst, coordinator, specialist, associate — usually entered with a bachelor's degree and sometimes an internship. Two BLS occupations show where it leads. Management analysts, which requires a bachelor's degree, had a 2025 median pay of $101,860 per year and 1,077,100 jobs in 2025 (BLS, 2025). Computer and information systems managers, which requires a bachelor's degree plus 5+ years of related work experience, had a 2025 median of $175,140 and 685,800 jobs (BLS, 2025). The group median for business and financial occupations was $82,660 in May 2025, above the $50,980 median for all occupations (BLS, 2025).

The practical five-year shape differs. In real estate, progression is a licence you qualify for after 2+ years and then a business you own. In corporate work, progression is internal promotion to a role like the manager position above, where the stated requirement is a degree plus five or more years of related experience (BLS, 2025). Titles, hiring norms and credential rules vary by employer and country.

Side-by-Side Comparison

DimensionReal estate agentCorporate (office/professional) job
Median paySales agents $52,830; brokers $73,220 (BLS, May 2025); combined $57,400, or $27.59/hour (BLS, 2025)Business and financial occupations group $82,660 (BLS, May 2025); management analysts $101,860 (BLS, 2025); computer and information systems managers $175,140 (BLS, 2025)
How pay arrivesCommission share paid per closed sale; 54% of agents and 55% of brokers are self-employed (BLS, 2025)Payroll salary; management analyst roles numbered 1,077,100 in 2025 and computer and information systems manager roles 685,800 (BLS, 2025)
Entry educationHigh school diploma or equivalent (BLS, 2025)Bachelor's degree for management analysts; bachelor's plus 5+ years of related experience for computer and information systems managers (BLS, 2025)
Up-front cost and study time40-180 prelicensing hours depending on state, total fees $75-$485 (Homes.com News, undated)A multi-year degree; tuition varies widely by country and institution — check the institution directly
Ongoing credential upkeepLicence renewal every 2 to 4 years, with continuing education required in most states (BLS, 2025)No universal licence for most corporate roles; employer- and function-specific training instead
10-year outlook2% growth 2025-35, slower than average, an employment change of 8,300 on a base of 530,600 jobs (BLS, 2025)Management analysts 10% and computer and information systems managers 16% growth 2025-35, both much faster than average (BLS, 2025)
Annual openingsAbout 40,400 per year, mostly from workers transferring occupations or leaving the labor force (BLS, 2025)Driven by growth as well as replacement — the two occupations above add 10% and 16% to large existing bases (BLS, 2025)
Hours and scheduleMost work full time, some more than 40 hours a week; schedules often include evenings and weekends, and many set their own schedule; some work part time (BLS, 2025)Schedule is typically set by the employer; hours, remote policy and overtime rules vary by employer and country
Daily tasksPresenting purchase offers to sellers, acting as intermediary in buyer-seller negotiations, and conferring with escrow companies, lenders, home inspectors and pest control operators so purchase terms are met before closing (O*NET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, 2025)Analysis, documentation, meetings and project delivery within a defined function; exact mix varies by role and employer
Ceiling and how you reach itBroker's licence after at least 2 years as a licensed sales agent in most states, then owning a business or managing an independent office as an associate broker (BLS, 2025)Promotion into management: the computer and information systems manager benchmark is a bachelor's degree plus 5+ years of related experience, at a $175,140 median (BLS, 2025)

Signs Each Path Is Right for You

Signs the real estate agent path fits

  • You can cover living costs through a stretch with no closings, because pay is commission-based and 54% of sales agents are self-employed rather than salaried (BLS, 2025).
  • You want to start earning without a degree: the typical entry education is a high school diploma or equivalent plus 40-180 hours of prelicensing coursework costing $75-$485 in fees, depending on the state (BLS, 2025; Homes.com News, undated).
  • Evening and weekend availability is an advantage to you, not a sacrifice — those hours are standard in the role, and many agents set their own schedules (BLS, 2025).
  • You would rather run a business than be promoted inside one: after at least 2 years as a licensed agent in most states you can qualify for a broker's licence and open your own firm (BLS, 2025).
  • You are comfortable chasing third parties — escrow companies, lenders, home inspectors, pest control operators — to keep a deal on track before closing (O*NET OnLine, 2025).
  • You can treat a 2-to-4-year licence renewal cycle with continuing education as routine admin rather than a burden (BLS, 2025).

Signs the corporate path fits

  • A fixed monthly figure matters more to you than upside: the business and financial occupations median was $82,660 against $50,980 for all occupations in May 2025 (BLS, 2025).
  • You already hold, or are willing to complete, a bachelor's degree — the stated entry requirement for management analysts (BLS, 2025).
  • You want to work in an occupation that is expanding rather than flat: 10% for management analysts and 16% for computer and information systems managers over 2025-35, versus 2% for brokers and agents (BLS, 2025).
  • You are willing to spend 5+ years building related experience in one field, the benchmark attached to a $175,140 median management role (BLS, 2025).
  • You prefer scheduled, employer-set hours to a calendar driven by client availability on evenings and weekends (BLS, 2025).
  • Your household budget, visa status or mortgage application depends on documented payroll income rather than variable commission.

Frequently asked questions

Which pays more after five years?+

On medians, the corporate path. A real estate sales agent who earns a broker's licence — possible after at least 2 years of licensed experience in most states — moves from a $52,830 median to a $73,220 median (BLS, May 2025). A corporate management analyst role, entered with a bachelor's degree, had a 2025 median of $101,860, and a computer and information systems manager role requiring 5+ years of experience had a median of $175,140 (BLS, 2025). Medians hide the spread, though: agent pay is commission-based, so individual earnings depend on market, brokerage split and deal volume. Check current BLS wage data and local brokerage commission splits for your area.

Which is easier to break into without a degree?+

Real estate, clearly. Typical entry-level education for brokers and sales agents is a high school diploma or equivalent (BLS, 2025), and the licence requires being at least 18, completing prelicensing courses and passing an exam (BLS, 2025). That coursework is 40 hours in Alaska and Vermont up to 180 hours in Texas, with fees from $75 in South Carolina and Wisconsin to $485 in Colorado (Homes.com News, undated). Management analyst and computer and information systems manager roles both list a bachelor's degree as the entry requirement (BLS, 2025).

Is the real estate job market still growing?+

Barely, on federal projections. Employment of real estate brokers and sales agents is projected to grow 2% from 2025 to 2035 — slower than average — an increase of 8,300 on a base of 530,600 jobs (BLS, 2025). O*NET lists 420,900 sales agent jobs in 2024 with 3-4% projected growth to 2034 (O*NET OnLine, U.S. Department of Labor, 2025). The access point is turnover, not growth: about 40,400 openings a year are projected, mostly from people transferring occupations or leaving the labor force (BLS, 2025).

Can I test real estate while keeping my corporate job?+

Partly. Most brokers and agents work full time, but some work part time and many set their own schedules, with evenings and weekends common (BLS, 2025) — which is when a salaried employee is free. You still need the licence first: 40-180 hours of prelicensing study and the state exam, at $75-$485 in fees (Homes.com News, undated). Before you start, check your employer's outside-work policy and your state licensing body's rules on holding a licence while employed elsewhere, as both vary.

Sources

  1. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Real Estate Brokers and Sales Agents : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025)
  2. Homes.com News — Real estate license requirements: A 50-state comparison
  3. O*NET OnLine (U.S. Department of Labor) — 41-9022.00 - Real Estate Sales Agents (2025)
  4. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Management Analysts : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025)
  5. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Business and Financial Occupations : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025)
  6. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Computer and Information Systems Managers : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025)

title: Resume Examples for Employment Gaps
dek: See a skills-first layout, a trimmed chronological layout, and a cover letter opening, each marked as a template with the edits you still have to make.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
A gap in your work history changes how you lay out a resume more than it changes what goes in it. The two resume templates below show the same material arranged two ways — one that leads with grouped skills, one that keeps dates in front but limits how far back they go — plus a short cover letter opening for when you want to name the gap yourself.

Every sample is a template with bracketed placeholders. Nothing here is ready to submit, and the second section lists the specific lines you have to change before you reuse any of it.

Key takeaways

  • Example 1 (skills-first) fits you if your gap ran more than a year, or if you've strung together several short contracts and the dates look busier than the work was.
  • Example 2 (trimmed chronological) fits you if you have a long record, the gap sits early in your career or lasted under a year, and your recent roles are the strongest thing you have.
  • The biggest formatting difference is where the dates sit: Example 1 groups proof under skill headings and keeps a short dated history near the bottom, while Example 2 puts dates at the head of every role and simply stops going back after the most recent 12–15 years.

Example Resumes & Cover Letters

Both resumes below assume the same underlying facts — real job titles, real dates, real duties. The difference is the arrangement. Most employers understand that the common reasons for a gap are continuing education or gaining new skills, caregiving, or a significant health issue, and it isn't necessary to explain the reason on the resume itself, though you might address it in a cover letter or interview (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated).

Example 1: Skills-first resume — gap of a year or more, or several short contracts

TEMPLATE — replace every bracketed field before you use this

[YOUR NAME] [City, State] | [Phone] | [Email]

SUMMARY [Target job title] with [X] years in [industry]. Returning to full-time work and currently [studying / volunteering / holding a part-time role] in [field].

KEY SKILLS

[Skill 1 — use the wording from the job posting, e.g. Patient Care] - Supported [X] clients per shift with [task], maintaining a [X%] on-time documentation rate - Trained [X] new team members in [procedure], cutting onboarding questions by about [X%]

[Skill 2 — e.g. Scheduling & Coordination] - Coordinated [X] appointments per week across [X] sites, reducing missed visits by [X%]

[Skill 3 — e.g. Records & Compliance] - Audited [X] files per month against [standard], resolving [X%] of errors before review

WORK HISTORY [Job title], [Employer name], [City, State] — [Month Year] to [Month Year] [Job title], [Employer name], [City, State] — [Month Year] to [Month Year] [Course, certificate, or volunteer role], [Provider name] — [Month Year] to [Month Year]

EDUCATION [Credential], [Institution], [Year]

If you've had frequent job changes, significant employment gaps, or several contract jobs, CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated, suggests starting with a skills section listing three to four major skills for your targeted job title, with related experience under each — which is what the Key Skills block does here. The dated history still appears, because leaving it out reads as evasive, but it sits below the proof rather than above it. CareerOneStop also publishes a sample in which a Certified Nursing Assistant uses a functional format to highlight strong caregiving skills, while a Supply Chain Manager uses a chronological format for consistent manufacturing experience (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated).

Example 2: Trimmed chronological resume — long career, gap early on or under a year

TEMPLATE — replace every bracketed field before you use this

[YOUR NAME] [City, State] | [Phone] | [Email]

SUMMARY [Target job title] with [X] years in [industry], focused on [specialism] and [specialism].

EXPERIENCE

[Job title] — [Employer name], [City, State] [Month Year] – Present - Managed [X] accounts worth [$X] annually, lifting renewal rates by [X%] - Rebuilt [process], cutting turnaround time from [X] days to [X] days

[Job title] — [Employer name], [City, State] [Month Year] – [Month Year] - Led a team of [X] through [project], delivering [X%] under budget

[Job title] — [Employer name], [City, State] [Month Year] – [Month Year] - Processed [X] orders per week with a [X%] accuracy rate

EARLIER EXPERIENCE [Job title], [Employer name] and [Job title], [Employer name] — [industry], [Year]–[Year]

EDUCATION [Credential], [Institution], [Year]

A chronological format is best for a steady work record and has the disadvantage that it emphasizes gaps in employment (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated) — so this version limits the exposure. It includes or emphasizes only the jobs that add the most value from the past 12–15 years and gives older, unrelated jobs a brief description (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated); if you're an experienced professional whose gap occurred early in your career, you don't need to list every job, and you can leave off the job before the gap (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated). Dates are right-justified on the role line, which CareerOneStop recommends so they're easy to find.

Example 3: Cover letter opening and closing — when you'd rather name the gap than leave it

TEMPLATE — replace every bracketed field before you use this

Dear [Hiring manager name],

I am writing to apply for the [exact job title] position at [Employer name], which I saw advertised on [where you saw it]. I spent [Month Year] to [Month Year] away from paid work for [reason you're comfortable giving — e.g. full-time caregiving / a health matter now resolved / completing a certificate in [subject]], and I have since [refresher step you actually took].

[Middle paragraph: two or three sentences matching your experience to the posting's requirements.]

My resume is enclosed. I would welcome the chance to meet and discuss how my [skill] and [skill] would serve your [team or function]. You can reach me at [phone] or [email].

Sincerely, [Your name]

The structure follows the pattern in CareerOneStop's sample letter (U.S. Dept. of Labor, undated): the first paragraph states the reason for writing, names the specific position, and says how you learned of the opening, and the closing mentions the enclosed resume and a desire to meet. Putting the gap in one sentence of the opening lets you control the wording and keeps the resume itself uncluttered. Say only what is true — rephrasing for clarity is fine, inventing a role, a date, or a course is not.

How to Customize These Examples

Work down the list before you send anything.

  • Rewrite the three Key Skills headings in Example 1. Replace [Skill 1], [Skill 2] and [Skill 3] with wording lifted from the posting you're answering — three to four major skills for the targeted job title (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated) — not the generic placeholders shown.
  • Replace every bracketed number in the bullets. Lines like "maintaining a [X%] on-time documentation rate" exist to show the shape: action verb, task, result. Put in figures you can defend in an interview, and drop the measure entirely if you don't have one rather than guessing.
  • Decide on months versus years in the WORK HISTORY block of Example 1 and the role lines of Example 2. If your gap was less than a year, you can choose to include only the years, but some Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software looks for month or even day of employment dates (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated). Pick one convention and use it on every line.
  • Cut or keep the EARLIER EXPERIENCE line in Example 2. Keep it as a single condensed line if those roles are unrelated; delete it if the gap sits right before it and the jobs add nothing (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated).
  • Change the SUMMARY line in both resumes. "Returning to full-time work and currently [studying / volunteering / holding a part-time role]" only belongs there if it's accurate; otherwise delete that clause rather than softening it.
  • Rename the sections to match your field. "KEY SKILLS" may read better as "Areas of Expertise" or "Core Competencies" in some industries; "WORK HISTORY" may read better as "Experience." Keep the headings as plain text lines.
  • Replace the three bracketed fields in the cover letter's first paragraph — job title, where you saw the opening, and the gap dates — because that paragraph is the one most likely to be read closely.
  • Rebuild the right-justified dates with a right tab stop, not with spaces or a two-column table. Companies use ATS software to receive and sort applications, and because it's so common, resumes should be formatted to be machine-readable (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated); tables, columns, and text placed in headers or footers are the elements documented as parsing badly.
  • Delete the bold TEMPLATE line at the top of each sample. It's there so the file can't be mistaken for a finished document.

Frequently asked questions

Should I send these as .docx or PDF?+

Judge both on the same two things: whether the employer named a format, and how the software handles it. On instructions, both are equally governed — check the job posting for accepted resume file formats (Indeed, undated) and the employer's application instructions (EduAvenues, undated), and follow whatever they say. On software handling, .docx may be best for ATS compatibility, though some systems accept PDFs (Indeed, undated); most ATS handle both, but some older systems struggle with PDFs (EduAvenues, undated). With no instruction either way, .docx is the safer default for both templates here, since neither relies on layout effects a PDF would need to preserve.

How do I cut Example 2 down to one page?+

Length depends on your level and field, so there's no single rule to apply. If you're early in your career or applying in a field that expects a short document, take the page out of Example 2 by condensing the EARLIER EXPERIENCE line to a single sentence, dropping any role outside the most recent 12–15 years (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated), and keeping two bullets per recent role instead of three. If you're an experienced professional in a field where longer resumes are normal, don't cut real relevant roles just to hit a page count.

Can I use the skills-first layout if my gap was short?+

You can, but it isn't usually necessary. A chronological format emphasizes gaps in employment and suits a steady work record (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated), so a short break inside an otherwise continuous history is often better handled by Example 2 plus the date convention you chose. CareerOneStop also publishes a sample in which someone picks a combination style — chronological with functional headings — because she has a steady work history with no break between jobs and her transition is a logical progression (U.S. Dept. of Labor, undated); you can borrow that middle setting by keeping Example 2's dated roles and adding one grouped skills block above them.

Do I have to explain the gap anywhere in these documents?+

Not on the resume. It isn't necessary to explain the reason there, though you might address it in a cover letter or interview (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated). Example 3 gives you a one-sentence way to do it in the letter if you'd rather raise it yourself. If you leave it out, make sure your dates are still accurate and consistent — fill the space with a course or volunteer role only if you actually did it.

  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Resume styles
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Work experience
  4. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Special tips
  5. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Cover Letter Template
  6. CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor) — Sample resumes
  7. Indeed — How to Write an ATS Resume (With Template and Tips)
  8. EduAvenues — ATS resume format: getting past the robots

faq.q: Should I send these as .docx or PDF?
faq.a: Judge both on the same two things: whether the employer named a format, and how the software handles it. On instructions, both are equally governed — check the job posting for accepted resume file formats (Indeed, undated) and the employer's application instructions (EduAvenues, undated), and follow whatever they say. On software handling, .docx may be best for ATS compatibility, though some systems accept PDFs (Indeed, undated); most ATS handle both, but some older systems struggle with PDFs (EduAvenues, undated). With no instruction either way, .docx is the safer default for both templates here, since neither relies on layout effects a PDF would need to preserve.

faq.q: How do I cut Example 2 down to one page?
faq.a: Length depends on your level and field, so there's no single rule to apply. If you're early in your career or applying in a field that expects a short document, take the page out of Example 2 by condensing the EARLIER EXPERIENCE line to a single sentence, dropping any role outside the most recent 12–15 years (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated), and keeping two bullets per recent role instead of three. If you're an experienced professional in a field where longer resumes are normal, don't cut real relevant roles just to hit a page count.

faq.q: Can I use the skills-first layout if my gap was short?
faq.a: You can, but it isn't usually necessary. A chronological format emphasizes gaps in employment and suits a steady work record (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated), so a short break inside an otherwise continuous history is often better handled by Example 2 plus the date convention you chose. CareerOneStop also publishes a sample in which someone picks a combination style — chronological with functional headings — because she has a steady work history with no break between jobs and her transition is a logical progression (U.S. Dept. of Labor, undated); you can borrow that middle setting by keeping Example 2's dated roles and adding one grouped skills block above them.

faq.q: Do I have to explain the gap anywhere in these documents?
faq.a: Not on the resume. It isn't necessary to explain the reason there, though you might address it in a cover letter or interview (CareerOneStop (U.S. Dept. of Labor), undated). Example 3 gives you a one-sentence way to do it in the letter if you'd rather raise it yourself. If you leave it out, make sure your dates are still accurate and consistent — fill the space with a course or volunteer role only if you actually did it.

title: Resume Mistakes to Fix Before You Apply
dek: A ranked checklist of fixable resume faults, from the ones that get you discarded in seconds to the small details that quietly cost you credibility.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
Most resume problems are not mysterious. They are a handful of specific, checkable faults — a typo in the first line, a job title buried under three lines of prose, a file that software cannot read properly — and each one has a fix you can make in an afternoon.

Work through the checklist below in order. It runs from the mistakes most likely to end your application to the ones that merely weaken it, then gives you a set of yes/no questions to run against the document on your screen right now.

Mistakes Checklist

1. Anything that is not true. Adjusted dates, an inflated title, a degree you did not finish, a responsibility that was really someone else's. A 2018 CareerBuilder survey reported that 75% of HR managers said they had caught a lie on a resume. Fix: state what actually happened and reframe it honestly — "[Job title], covering [duty] during a staffing gap" is accurate; a promotion you never had is not.

2. Spelling and grammar errors, especially in the top third. A 2013 CareerBuilder/Harris Interactive survey of over 2,000 hiring managers found 58% named typos as a mistake that leads to rejection, and resume experts cited by CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) list spelling errors as their top frustration. Fix: read it aloud backwards line by line, then have at least one other person check grammar, spelling and punctuation, as CareerOneStop advises.

3. Your job titles, dates and employer names are hard to find in a few seconds. An eye-tracking study by TheLadders found recruiters spent an average of six seconds on an individual resume, and reporting on that study noted 80% of that time went to name, current and previous titles, start and stop dates, and education. CareerOneStop similarly says employers often spend under 30 seconds on a first pass, and a 2018 CareerBuilder/Harris Poll survey of more than 1,100 hiring managers and HR professionals found 23% spend less than 30 seconds. Fix: put title, employer and dates on one clean line each, in consistent order, with the title in bold.

4. Year-only employment dates or an unexplained gap. CareerOneStop notes some applicant tracking systems (ATS) look for month or day of employment, not just year, and the 2013 CareerBuilder survey found 27% cited resumes without exact dates of employment as a mistake. Fix: use Month Year – Month Year throughout, and be truthful about the dates even where there is a gap.

5. One generic resume sent everywhere. The 2013 CareerBuilder survey found 36% cited generic, non-personalised resumes as a rejection trigger. Fix: mirror the posting's own terms for the skills you genuinely have, high on the page — CareerOneStop advises that qualifications should be easy to find near the top and match the posting's wording, because a reader typically scans for 15–20 seconds.

6. Copying large blocks of wording straight from the job posting. The same survey found 32% cited this. Fix: match key terms, not sentences; describe what you did in your own words.

7. No skills section. That 2013 survey found 35% cited resumes with no list of skills. Fix: add a short, scannable skills block with tools, systems and languages you can actually demonstrate.

8. Content trapped in places parsing software handles badly. Text inside headers and footers, multi-column layouts, tables and graphics are documented sources of parsing problems — contact details in a footer can be dropped entirely. Fix: single column, text in the body of the document, contact details as ordinary lines at the top.

9. Invented or decorative section headings. CareerOneStop recommends standard headings such as 'Work Experience', 'Education' and 'Skills' so both people and applicant tracking systems find them quickly. Fix: rename 'My Journey' and 'What I Bring' to the standard labels.

10. Duty lists with no result. "Responsible for social media" tells a reader nothing. Fix: use action verb plus task plus measurable result, for example:

Template bullet — adapt with your own numbers

Rebuilt [process or report] for [team/department], cutting turnaround time by [X%] across [number] monthly cases.

11. Overused filler words. Indeed's career guide lists 'enthusiastic', 'experienced', 'go-getter', 'self-starter', 'hard worker', 'team player' and idioms like 'out-of-the-box' as phrases to replace with specifics. Fix: delete the adjective and keep the evidence.

12. An unprofessional email address. The 2013 CareerBuilder survey found 31% cited this. Fix: set up a plain address built from your name.

13. Inconsistent formatting — mixed fonts, punctuation and spacing. Resume experts cited by CareerOneStop list too many fonts, inconsistent punctuation and messy layout among their top frustrations. Fix: CareerOneStop recommends simple fonts such as Times New Roman, Cambria or Arial at 10–12 point, left-aligned text and roughly one-inch margins.

14. Length that does not fit your experience. CareerOneStop recommends 1–2 pages, with your name on each page if you use two; conventions differ by country and by field, so check what is normal where you are applying. Fix: cut to fit, starting with the oldest material.

15. Jobs from more than 10–15 years ago, listed in full. CareerOneStop advises including relevant jobs from only the previous 10–15 years. Fix: compress older roles into a single 'Earlier experience' line, or drop them.

16. 'References available upon request'. Indeed's career guide calls the phrase outdated and unnecessary, says it wastes space and removes your control over when references are contacted. Fix: delete it and keep a separate references document, with permission asked in advance, to send when an employer requests it.

17. A photo, where it is not expected. The 2013 CareerBuilder survey found 13% cited resumes that include a photo. Norms vary widely by country, so check local practice before adding or removing one.

Quick Self-Audit

Answer each question against the file you are about to send. Every 'no' points back to a numbered item above.

1. Is every date, title, degree and duty on this page something you could evidence if asked?

If no, go to item 1 and rewrite the claim as what actually happened.

2. Has someone other than you read it for spelling, grammar and punctuation?

Your own eyes skip errors you made. If no, item 2 — send it to one person today.

3. Can a stranger find your most recent job title, employer and dates in six seconds?

Time someone. If they hunt, item 3 applies: simplify the layout of your experience lines.

4. Does every role show a month and a year for start and end?

If you see bare years, fix item 4 — and check that any gap is shown truthfully rather than papered over.

5. Did you change anything in this version for this specific posting?

If the file is identical to the last ten you sent, that is item 5.

6. Is any sentence lifted word-for-word from the job ad?

If yes, item 6 — rewrite it in your own words while keeping the key term.

7. Is there a visible skills section a reader could point to?

If no, item 7.

8. Are your phone number and email in the body of the document, not in a header or footer, and is the page a single column with no tables or graphics?

If no, item 8 — rebuild the top of the page as plain lines.

9. Are your section headings the standard ones?

Look for 'Work Experience', 'Education' and 'Skills'. If you see something more creative, that is item 9.

10. Does at least one bullet under each recent role end in a result rather than a duty?

If no, item 10 — add a number, a volume, a timeframe or a percentage you can stand behind.

11. Can you find 'hard worker', 'team player', 'self-starter' or 'out-of-the-box' anywhere?

Use the search function. Each hit is item 11.

12. Would you be comfortable reading your email address aloud in an interview?

If no, item 12.

13. Is every bullet punctuated the same way, in the same font, at the same size?

If no, item 13 — standardise to one simple font at 10–12 point, left-aligned.

14. Does the length match your actual experience and local convention, with your name on page two if there is one?

If no, item 14.

15. Is anything on the page from more than 10–15 years ago, described in full detail?

If yes, item 15 — compress it.

16. Does the document end with 'references available upon request'?

If yes, item 16 — delete the line and prepare a separate references list instead.

17. Is there a photo, and have you checked whether that is expected where you are applying?

If you have not checked, item 17.

Sources

  2. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Resumes
  3. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Does your resume speak to employers
  4. TheLadders — TheLadders Eye-Tracking Study
  5. Recruiter.com (reporting TheLadders study) — TheLadders Reveals Research Reporting that Resumes Spend Six Seconds with a Recruiter
  6. CareerBuilder — Employers Share Their Most Outrageous Resume Mistakes and Instant Deal Breakers in a New CareerBuilder Study (2018)
  7. CareerBuilder — CareerBuilder Releases Study of Common and Not-So-Common Resume Mistakes That Can Cost You the Job (2013-09)
  8. Indeed Career Guide — “References Available Upon Request” and Other Phrases To Avoid on Your Resume (2026-05-04)
  9. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Special tips

title: Resume vs CV (Curriculum Vitae): What's the Difference
dek: In US hiring these are two different documents with different jobs to do, and the same word means something else again once you apply abroad.
author: Ingrid Castellanos
body:
A resume is a short, targeted summary of the experience that matters for one job. A CV (curriculum vitae) is a full record of your academic and research work, and in the US it is mostly used for faculty, postdoc, fellowship and grant applications. Picking the wrong one usually means sending too much detail to an employer who wanted two pages, or too little to a search committee that wanted your whole publication list.

There is a third complication: in the UK, Ireland, much of Europe, Australia and many other countries, "CV" is simply the everyday word for the document a US employer would call a resume. The same request can mean two different things depending on where the job sits.

Key takeaways

  • A resume condenses your skills, qualifications and experience for one specific role; a CV lays out your full academic and research history (UC Davis Career Center, undated).
  • A CV has no fixed page limit and leads with publications and funding; a resume is tailored and trimmed for each application (CASRAI, undated).
  • Rule of thumb: send a CV for faculty, postdoc, research, fellowship and grant applications, and a resume for almost everything else (Indeed, undated) — unless the employer is outside the US, where "CV" usually just means resume.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Three documents get called by these two names. The table compares all of them on the same criteria, so you can see where they actually differ rather than guessing from the label on the job posting.

CriterionResumeCV (US academic and research)"CV" as used outside the US
Best for which job seekerYou are applying to private-sector, non-profit, government or staff roles, including staff positions inside universities. For most jobs, including business roles and staff positions within academia, employers are likely seeking the shorter resume-style document (Indeed, undated).You are applying for tenure-track and non-tenure-track faculty jobs, postdocs, research positions at national laboratories or research institutions, fellowships, scholarships, awards, and research grants (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated).You are applying to an employer in the UK, Ireland, Europe, Australia or elsewhere that uses "CV" as the standard word for a job application document, in any sector.
What it containsSkills, qualifications and experience set out succinctly as required for a job role (University of Kentucky, Gatton College Pigman Career Education Center, 2025). Anything irrelevant to that role gets cut.A full history of academic accomplishments (UC Davis Career Center, undated), organized by category, with publications and funding front and center (CASRAI, undated).The same core content as a US resume: contact details, work history, education, skills. Local conventions on personal details and references vary by country.
Section orderUsually contact details, then a short summary or skills block, then experience, education and anything relevant such as certifications. Order shifts depending on whether your strongest asset is experience or a recent degree.Contact details, qualifications, teaching experience, research publications, grants and prizes, professional activities, then referees (jobs.ac.uk, 2019), with reverse chronological order within each section (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated).Contact details, a short profile, work history, education, skills. Check the posting or the country's norms, as some expect references listed and some do not.
Typical lengthVaries by experience level and field: one page is common for early-career US business and staff roles, and two pages is routine once you have several years of relevant experience or work in a technical field. Follow any length stated in the posting.No length limit; it is a living document (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated). Graduate student CVs are typically two or three pages, and an academic CV is usually three to five pages (jobs.ac.uk, 2019), growing as your record grows.Typically the same length as a US resume for the same experience level — one to two pages for most roles — unless the employer states otherwise.
Applicant Tracking System (ATS) compatibilityCompanies use Applicant Tracking System (ATS) software to receive applications, sort them in the order received and track status, and this has become common in US hiring (CareerOneStop, undated). A reverse-chronological resume in a plain layout parses most reliably; a functional resume organized by skill rather than chronology is likely to be rejected by an ATS (CareerOneStop, undated).Academic applications often run through institution-specific portals that ask you to upload the CV alongside separate documents such as a research statement and teaching statement. Parsing still matters: text in headers and footers, multi-column layouts, tables and graphics are known to cause problems for software reading your file.Handled the same way as a resume: the same parsing risks apply. Save as the file type the posting asks for, keep the layout single-column, and keep your contact details in the body of the document rather than a header.
Where to check the rulesThe job posting and the employer's careers page. If a length or file format is specified, that instruction outranks any general advice.The posting, the hiring department's website, and your discipline's norms — section order and emphasis differ between the sciences, humanities and professional fields.The posting, plus the hiring country's conventions, which differ on photographs, dates of birth and personal details. Never state anything you cannot support.

Two things vary more than any guide can pin down. First, the employer: a university may ask for a resume for an administrative role and a CV for a faculty role in the same week. Second, the country: a request for a "CV" from a London employer and from a US search committee are asking for different documents. When the posting is ambiguous, write to the contact listed and ask which they want.

When to Choose Each

  • Choose a resume if you are applying to a company, non-profit or government agency; you are applying for a staff or administrative post at a college or university rather than a faculty post; or you are moving out of academia into industry and need to translate research work into skills an employer can use. For most jobs, including business roles and staff positions within academia, employers are likely looking for this shorter document (Indeed, undated). Tailor it for each posting and cut anything that does not support the role.
  • Choose a CV if you are applying for a tenure-track or non-tenure-track faculty position; a postdoc or a research position at a national laboratory or research institution; or a fellowship, scholarship, award or research grant (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated). Also choose it when a graduate program or a professional licensing body asks for your complete record. Keep publications and funding prominent (CASRAI, undated) and update it as a living document rather than rebuilding it each time.
  • Choose a "CV" in the non-US sense if the employer is based outside the US and uses that word in the posting; you are applying through an international branch of a US organization that follows local hiring conventions; or a recruiter in the UK, Ireland, Europe or Australia asks for your CV. In practice, send a resume-style document of resume length, formatted to local norms — not your academic CV, unless the role is itself academic.

If you genuinely cannot tell which is wanted, default to the shorter document and offer the longer one: "I've attached a two-page summary and can send my full CV with publications if that's more useful."

Frequently asked questions

A job ad says "send your CV" but the role is a normal office job. What do I send?+

Look at where the employer is. A US employer advertising a non-academic office role almost always means a resume — for most jobs, including business roles and staff positions within academia, employers are likely seeking the shorter resume-style document (Indeed, undated). An employer in the UK, Ireland, Europe or Australia using "CV" also means a short, targeted document, not an academic record. Send a tailored one- or two-page resume. If the posting asks for anything extra, such as references or a personal statement, add it as a separate section or file.

How do I turn my academic CV into a resume?+

Start from the job posting and work backwards. Keep the roles, skills and projects that support that job; cut the conference list, the full publication list and anything the employer has no use for. Then rewrite entries so each one shows what you did and what changed, rather than what your title was. > **Template — adapt with your own facts, never invent numbers** > Designed and taught [N] lab sections for [X] undergraduates per term, cutting assignment turnaround time by [X%] through a revised grading workflow. Keep the layout single-column and plain, since a reverse-chronological resume parses most reliably through an Applicant Tracking System (CareerOneStop, undated).

Can I keep both documents going at once?+

Yes, and if you are applying to both academic and non-academic roles you should. Treat the CV as your master record — it is a living document with no length limit (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated) — and update it whenever something is published, funded or awarded. Then build each resume from it by selecting and rewriting, so you are never starting from a blank page. Everything in both documents must be accurate: condensing and rephrasing is fine, changing titles, dates or credentials is not.

Is a skills-based layout a safe middle ground when I'm switching between the two?+

Be careful. A functional resume organized by skill rather than chronology may highlight transferable skills well, but it is likely to be rejected by an Applicant Tracking System (CareerOneStop, undated), and ATS use has become common in US hiring (CareerOneStop, undated). A better compromise is a reverse-chronological resume with a short skills summary near the top. On the CV side, keep reverse chronological order within each section (Princeton University Center for Career Development, undated) so a reader can follow your record.

Sources

  1. UC Davis Career Center — Resume vs CV
  2. Princeton University Center for Career Development — CV Writing Guide for Graduate Students
  3. jobs.ac.uk — How to Layout an Academic CV (2019-09-06)
  4. CASRAI — Academic CV Example: Annotated Template
  5. CareerOneStop — Resumes
  6. CareerOneStop — Applicant tracking systems
  7. University of Kentucky, Gatton College Pigman Career Education Center — Understanding Resumes vs. CVs: The Key Differences for Job Seekers (2025-02-20)
  8. Indeed — Resume vs. CV (Curriculum Vitae): Key Differences

title: Should You Switch From Accountant to Financial Analyst? A Decision Guide
dek: A structured way to weigh licensing, hours, advancement routes and the real cost of starting over before you hand in your notice at the accounting desk.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
Moving from accounting to financial analysis is a lateral shift, not a fresh start. Both roles sit in the same finance function, read the same statements and answer to the same CFO, but they are measured differently: accountants are judged on whether last quarter was recorded correctly, analysts on whether next quarter's forecast holds. This guide sets out what each path requires to enter, where each one leads, and the concrete signals that one fits you better than the other.

Where pay, hours and outlook are concerned, the guide points you to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook rather than quoting numbers second-hand — those figures are updated and you should read the current ones for both occupations side by side.

Key takeaways

  • Accounting buys regulatory protection: anyone filing a report with the Securities and Exchange Commission must be a licensed CPA (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), which locks in demand that no analyst credential matches.
  • Analysis buys a different ceiling: experienced analysts can move toward portfolio or fund manager roles, and a master's in finance or business administration may improve those chances (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — but most analysts work full time and some work more than 40 hours per week (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • If you want a defined credential ladder with state-level rules, accounting's CPA route (150 semester hours, 30 more than a usual four-year bachelor's, plus a national exam) fits; if you want to be paid for forward-looking judgement, the CFA charter's three exams and 4,000 hours of qualifying experience over at least three years fits.

Setting the Context

The accountant path. Accountants and auditors prepare and examine financial records, make sure statements are accurate and that taxes are paid properly and on time. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a typical entry-level education requirement for the occupation (2025) — check the current Occupational Outlook Handbook entry, because employers in public accounting and in industry read that requirement differently.

Entry titles are usually staff accountant, audit associate, tax associate or accounts payable/receivable accountant. The licensing question arrives early: any accountant who files a report with the Securities and Exchange Commission is required to be a licensed Certified Public Accountant (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). CPA licensure requires 150 semester hours of college coursework — 30 hours more than a usual four-year bachelor's degree — plus passing a national exam and meeting the other requirements of your state Board of Accountancy (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Those other requirements, including experience hours and ethics exams, differ by state, so the rules in Texas are not the rules in New York; your state board publishes the current list and fees.

Within about five years, entry-level public accountants may advance to senior positions and then become supervisors, managers or partners, open their own firm, or transfer to executive positions in management accounting or internal auditing (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). The branch point is usually whether you stay in public practice or move in-house.

The financial analyst path. Financial analysts guide businesses and individuals on decisions about spending money to earn a profit: they build models, value assets, assess investments and forecast results. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics also publishes a typical entry-level education for this occupation (2025) — again, read it directly rather than assuming it matches accounting.

Entry titles include financial analyst, FP&A analyst, credit analyst, equity research associate and investment analyst. Licensing works differently: the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) is the main licensing organization for the securities industry for some financial analyst positions, and most of those licenses require employer sponsorship (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). You cannot obtain them in advance on your own — you need the job first. The widely recognised voluntary credential is the CFA charter, which requires passing all three CFA exams (Level I, II and III), completing 4,000 hours of relevant professional work experience over a minimum of three years, and becoming a CFA Institute member (CFA Institute). Exam registration and membership fees change each cycle; take them from the CFA Institute site rather than from any guide.

Within five years, analysts may advance to senior analyst, then toward portfolio or fund manager roles, and a master's degree in finance or business administration may improve the chances of advancing (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).

What the switch actually costs. You are not retraining from scratch — you already read statements fluently, which is the part most career changers lack. What you are adding is modelling, forecasting and the habit of defending an estimate. A realistic plan is 6–18 months if you move internally from accounting into an FP&A team at the same employer, and 12–24 months if you are changing employer and function at once.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Both occupations are large enough that national figures are meaningful, but both are also published and revised annually. Open the two Occupational Outlook Handbook pages together and read the same rows for each.

DimensionAccountant / auditorFinancial analyst
Median annual payPublished by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics for May 2025; read the current figure in the Occupational Outlook HandbookPublished by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics for May 2025; compare against the accounting figure before assuming analysis pays more
Pay spreadBLS reports a 10th-to-90th-percentile wage range for accountants and auditors (May 2025)BLS reports a 10th-to-90th-percentile wage range for financial and investment analysts (May 2025); the width of each range, not the midpoint, tells you how much the top of the ladder pays
Required education and credentialsCPA licensure needs 150 semester hours — 30 more than a usual four-year bachelor's — a national exam, and your state Board of Accountancy's other requirements (BLS, 2025)CFA charter needs three exams, 4,000 hours of relevant experience over at least three years, and CFA Institute membership (CFA Institute); some roles also need FINRA licenses, most of which require employer sponsorship (BLS, 2025)
HoursBLS publishes the typical work schedule for the occupation (2025); busy season timing varies by employer and by tax jurisdictionMost work full time and some work more than 40 hours per week (BLS, 2025)
Job security and market sizeBLS publishes total jobs held and projected annual openings for accountants and auditors (2025)BLS publishes total jobs held and projected annual openings for financial analysts (2025); the accounting occupation is the larger of the two by headcount
Ten-year outlookBLS projects employment change for accountants and auditors, 2025–35BLS projects employment change for financial analysts, 2025–35
Growth ceilingSenior, supervisor, manager or partner; opening your own firm; or executive roles in management accounting or internal auditing (BLS, 2025)Senior analyst, then portfolio or fund manager; a master's in finance or business administration may improve advancement chances (BLS, 2025)
Daily tasksExamining and preparing financial records, verifying accuracy, ensuring taxes are paid properly and on timeModelling and valuing investments, forecasting, advising on where money should be spent to earn a return
Regulatory lock-inOnly a licensed CPA may file a report with the SEC (BLS, 2025) — a legal requirement no other credential substitutes forNo equivalent exclusive filing right; FINRA licenses attach to the employer relationship, not to you permanently (BLS, 2025)

Signs Each Path Is Right for You

Stay in accounting if:

  • You already have, or can realistically complete, the 150 semester hours CPA licensure requires — 30 hours beyond a usual four-year bachelor's (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — and your state board's remaining requirements are within reach.
  • You want work whose demand is written into regulation: SEC filings legally require a licensed CPA (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • You prefer a question with a correct answer. Reconciling to the cent and closing the books satisfies you more than defending an assumption that may be wrong.
  • Running your own practice appeals: public accountants may open their own firm (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), an exit route the analyst path does not offer in the same form.
  • You want predictability in where the ladder goes next — senior, supervisor, manager, partner — rather than advancement that depends on investment performance.
  • Caring responsibilities or a mortgage make a 12–24 month function change, with the pay uncertainty that comes with it, a bad bet right now.

Move to financial analysis if:

  • You already spend part of your month building forecast models or variance commentary, and that is the part of the job you reread before you send it.
  • You are comfortable committing to a multi-year credential: the CFA charter requires three exams plus 4,000 hours of relevant experience over at least three years (CFA Institute).
  • You accept that some analyst roles need FINRA licenses you cannot get alone, because most require employer sponsorship (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) — so you must land the job before the license.
  • You want the portfolio or fund manager route specifically, and you are willing to consider a master's in finance or business administration, which may improve advancement chances (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • Longer weeks are acceptable: most analysts work full time and some work more than 40 hours per week (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025).
  • You would rather argue for a number in a meeting than prove one in a file.

If you fit both lists, the lowest-risk test is an internal move: ask to own one recurring forecast or budget pack for two quarters and see whether the forward-looking work holds your attention when the close is also due.

Frequently asked questions

Which one pays more after five years?+

There is no single answer, and the honest check takes ten minutes. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes median annual pay for accountants and auditors and for financial analysts as of May 2025, plus the 10th-to-90th-percentile wage range for accountants and auditors and for financial and investment analysts. Read all four numbers together: the percentile ranges tell you how much upside each path has, which matters more at the five-year mark than the medians do. Pay within both occupations also varies by state, industry and whether you are in public practice, industry or asset management.

Which is easier to break into without a bachelor's degree?+

Neither is designed for that route. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists a typical entry-level education for each occupation (2025) — check both entries directly. Accounting has the harder credential requirement at the licensed level: CPA licensure needs 150 semester hours of coursework, which is 30 more than a usual four-year bachelor's, plus a national exam and your state Board of Accountancy's other requirements (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025). Analyst roles do not require that, but some need FINRA licenses that most often require employer sponsorship (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025), so you need an employer willing to hire you first.

Which has more job security?+

Compare three published figures for each occupation in the Occupational Outlook Handbook: total jobs held (2025), projected annual openings (2025) and the projected 2025–35 employment change. Accounting is the larger occupation by headcount, and the CPA requirement for SEC filings (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025) creates demand no other credential can fill. Analyst demand is less rule-bound and tends to track employers' capital and investment activity.

Do I need the CFA charter to become a financial analyst?+

Not to start. The charter requires passing Level I, II and III, completing 4,000 hours of relevant professional work experience over a minimum of three years, and becoming a CFA Institute member (CFA Institute) — so by design it is earned alongside the job, not before it. Current exam registration and membership fees are published by the CFA Institute and change each cycle; check them there before committing.

How long does the switch usually take?+

Plan 6–18 months if you move internally into an FP&A or analysis team at your current employer, where your knowledge of the books is an advantage and the hiring manager already knows your work. Plan 12–24 months if you are changing employer and function simultaneously. Credentialing runs on its own clock: the CFA charter cannot be completed in under three years of qualifying experience (CFA Institute).

Sources

  1. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Accountants and Auditors : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025-05)
  2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Financial Analysts : Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025-05)
  3. CFA Institute — CFA Exam Information | CFA Institute
