title: The Complete Guide to Running a Confidential Job Search While Employed
dek: Privacy settings, reference timing and interview scheduling decide whether your search stays quiet — set each one up deliberately before you send a single application.
author: Priya Sehgal-Wren
body:
Looking for work while you still have a job is the strongest position to search from, and the most fragile. One public resume, one recruiter InMail seen by the wrong colleague, or one 2pm "dentist appointment" too many, and you lose the leverage that made your search safe in the first place.

This guide walks through how to configure the platforms you'll actually use, build a parallel identity for your search, handle references and interview scheduling, and keep records somewhere your employer can't read. It names the specific settings to change — not just the principle behind them.

Key takeaways

  • Set job-board resume visibility before uploading anything: Indeed's default is "Employers can't find you" (Indeed support, undated), and CareerBuilder offers a confidential resume that hides contact details.
  • Use LinkedIn's Open to Work "Recruiters only" option, which shows no green profile banner — but know LinkedIn says it cannot guarantee recruiters at your own company never see it (LinkedIn Help, as cited by Contentin).
  • Run the entire search from a personal email address, personal phone and personal device, with a tracker that lives outside any employer-owned account.

Why This Strategy Matters

The risk in an employed job search is rarely that someone finds out you're looking. It's that they find out at the worst possible moment — before you have an offer, before you've banked a bonus, before a project you were counting on for your resume is finished. Once your employer knows, you no longer control the timeline. You become the person who is leaving, and decisions about raises, promotions and new work start getting made around you.

The second problem is that job platforms are built for discovery, not discretion, and their defaults differ from each other. Indeed says its default profile setting is "Employers can't find you," meaning the profile is shown only to employers you apply to or send a resume to, and is not publicly searchable (Indeed support, undated). CareerBuilder takes a different approach: its "Hide contact details" option keeps your resume publicly searchable but hides your contact information, letting employers reach you through a confidential CareerBuilder email address that you can simply ignore (CareerBuilder, undated). Monster's "Privacy Plus" lets you block a set number of companies from finding your public resume, something Monster itself describes as useful if you don't want your current employer to see it (Monster, undated). None of that happens automatically. You have to go and set it.

Be sceptical of visibility statistics while you do. One career-advice site claims profiles with Open to Work enabled receive up to 40% more recruiter InMail messages (CareerBldr, undated) — treat that as an unverified vendor-side claim rather than a benchmark, and the same goes for any response-rate or time-to-hire number you see quoted without a named study behind it. No setting, tool or tactic guarantees an interview.

Confidentiality is a process, not a secret. The readers who get caught usually aren't careless about privacy settings; they're careless about the boring operational edges — the work laptop, the reference who mentions it over coffee, the recurring calendar hole at 11am every Thursday.

Step-by-Step Process

  1. Search for yourself the way a colleague would. Open a private browsing window, log out of everything, and run your own name against your employer and the word resume — for example, `"Priya Raman" resume "[Current Employer]"` and then `"Priya Raman" CV filetype:pdf`. Write down every old job-board profile, personal site or PDF that surfaces, because those are the things you need to take down or lock before you start applying.
  2. Set resume visibility on every board before you upload a file. Decide per platform: leave Indeed on "Employers can't find you" so your profile only reaches employers you actually apply to (Indeed support, undated); use CareerBuilder's "Hide contact details" confidential resume if you want to stay searchable without exposing your phone number (CareerBuilder, undated); use Monster's "Privacy Plus" to block named companies from finding your public resume (Monster, undated). Note one trap: Monster says that if you apply using a posted resume, information marked confidential — contact details, current company, references — is included in that application anyway, so the employer can reach you.
  3. Configure LinkedIn's Open to Work as "Recruiters only." Click the "Open to" button below your profile photo and headline, choose "Finding a new job," fill in target job titles, locations, job types and start date, then set visibility to "Recruiters only" rather than "All LinkedIn Members" (as documented by MagicPost and JobQuest, undated). That option shows no green profile banner and shares your status privately with people using LinkedIn Recruiter.
  4. Create a separate search identity. Register a personal email in the format `firstname.lastname.career@[your provider]`, add your personal mobile number to it, and use that pair on every application. Standardise your subject lines so nothing routes to a work inbox by accident — for example: `Application — [Job Title], Req [Number] — [Your Name]`.
  5. Build two versions of your resume. The applied version names your employer and carries metrics; the version you post publicly on any board describes it generically — "regional logistics operator, 400+ staff (name on request)" — and uses the posting's exact job title in your headline plus three keywords lifted from the requirements section, such as "demand planning," "S&OP" and "SQL." Keep both files in personal cloud storage, never on an employer-owned drive.
  6. Recruit two references who don't report to your current employer. Ask a former manager and a former peer, in writing, with an explicit confidentiality request. Personalise this before sending — do not paste it as written:

Reference request email

Subject: Quick confidential favour — reference for [Role Type] roles

Hi [Name], I'm running a quiet search for [role type] roles and would value your name as a reference for the [specific project you worked on together] work. My current employer doesn't know I'm looking, so I'd be grateful if you kept this between us. Happy to send the job description and a short reminder of what I did on [project] so you're not caught cold. — [Your Name]

  1. Pre-block your interview availability in your work calendar. Put a recurring private hold from 8:00–9:30am two mornings a week, labelled consistently ("personal appointment") so it reads as routine rather than as a pattern of sudden absences. Then ask employers for those slots first: "I have availability Tuesday or Thursday before 9:30am, or any time after 5:30pm."
  2. Read your own contract and handbook before you talk to a competitor. Look specifically for notice period, non-solicitation, moonlighting and non-compete clauses, and note which US state or country's law the contract names. The FTC's April 2024 final noncompete rule is not in effect — a district court order on 20 August 2024 stopped the FTC from enforcing it, and the FTC voted to formally vacate the rule on 5 September 2025, returning the question largely to state law and case-by-case enforcement (FTC, 2024–2025; AVMA, September 2025). This is not legal advice; if a clause looks like it bites, pay a qualified employment lawyer in your jurisdiction for an hour.
  3. Set up a tracker outside every employer system. A personal spreadsheet with columns: Company | Role | Source | Date applied | Contact | Last touch | Next action | Date of next action. Fill the "next action" column with something specific like "follow up with [hiring manager] on 14th if no reply," because an empty next-action cell is how applications die quietly.
  4. Lock in a weekly 60-minute cadence and one outreach message. For example, Sunday 7–8pm: three tailored applications, two outreach notes, tracker updated. Personalise the note below for each recipient — the bracketed detail is the whole point of it:

Outreach to someone doing the job you want

Subject: Question about [specific team] at [Company]

Hi [Name], I work in [your function] and I'm exploring [role type] moves quietly — I'd appreciate your discretion. I noticed [specific thing: a product launch, a team restructure, a talk they gave]. Would you be open to 15 minutes to tell me what the [team] actually measures success on? Happy to work around your calendar. — [Your Name]

Before You Start Checklist

  • Old job-board and personal-site profiles found in step 1 either deleted or set to a private visibility option.
  • Personal email and personal mobile added to every platform profile, with all work contact details removed.
  • Applications, drafts and your tracker stored on a personal device and personal cloud account — nothing on an employer laptop, VPN, work phone or work Google/Microsoft account.
  • Only reputable, free-to-use job banks on your list; CareerOneStop (sponsored by the U.S. Department of Labor) names CareerBuilder, Indeed and ZipRecruiter as examples and notes its own Job Finder combines these with state job banks (CareerOneStop, undated).
  • A note to yourself of the scam red flag CareerOneStop names: you should never have to pay to search job openings, and posting your resume should be free (CareerOneStop, undated).
  • Public-facing resume version scrubbed of your employer's name, client names and anything confidential.
  • Two references confirmed in writing, neither of them anyone who reports to or socialises with your current manager.
  • One-line answer rehearsed for "are you looking?", plus a decision made in advance about what you will say if an offer requires a reference from your current employer.
  • Contract clauses on notice period, non-solicitation and non-compete read and summarised in your own words, with a note of any clause you want a lawyer to look at.
  • Interview-window holds already in your work calendar for the next three weeks, so you never have to invent a reason at short notice.

Frequently asked questions

What if a recruiter at my own company sees my "Recruiters only" Open to Work signal?+

LinkedIn says it takes steps to avoid showing the "Recruiters only" signal to recruiters at your own company, but states it cannot guarantee they will never see it (LinkedIn Help, as cited by Contentin, undated). Treat it as low risk rather than no risk. If your employer has a large in-house talent team, or if you work somewhere that uses agency recruiters heavily, you may prefer to leave the feature off entirely and rely on direct applications and outreach instead.

My employer asks everyone to list them as a reference. What do I do?+

Most employers will accept former managers, peers and clients at offer stage and reserve a current-employer check for after you accept, or they will run an employment verification rather than a reference conversation. Say so plainly and early: that your search is confidential and your current employer can be contacted once an offer is signed. If a hiring team refuses that entirely, you are being asked to take all the risk before you have anything in writing, and it is reasonable to decline.

Should I post my resume publicly at all, or only apply directly?+

Public posting generates inbound contact you would not otherwise get, which matters if you are in a niche role. The middle path is a searchable but shielded profile — CareerBuilder's "Hide contact details" option keeps your resume findable while routing employers through a confidential CareerBuilder email address you choose whether to answer (CareerBuilder, undated). If you are in a small industry where your resume would be identifiable even without your name on it, apply directly only.

What if a posting turns out to be from my own employer or a company that shares investors with it?+

Blind postings and group-owned sister companies are a real hazard, so check the description for internal clues — a named applicant tracking system, familiar job-title conventions, a location that matches an office you know. If you only discover it after applying, withdraw in writing with a neutral line and keep the message short. Do not explain yourself at length; brevity reads as professionalism rather than panic.

How do I explain the gaps in my day when interviews stack up?+

Use half-days of annual leave rather than scattered hours, because one booked absence raises fewer questions than three mysterious ones. If your employer requires a reason for leave, give the same mundane answer consistently and do not embellish it. When an onsite is unavoidable, ask the employer whether a first-stage video call can replace it — most will accommodate a candidate who is currently employed, since they deal with it constantly.

Is it worth telling my manager once I'm close to an offer, so they can counter?+

Some managers respond to that information by trying to keep you, and some respond by starting to plan without you — you are the only person who can judge which yours is. If you do want a counter-offer conversation, have the written offer in hand first, and be clear with yourself about what would actually make you stay beyond money. Any pay figures you discuss should come from current published salary data for your role and region rather than from guesswork, so check a reputable source before the conversation.

Sources

  1. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor-sponsored) — 4 tips to help guard your privacy while job searching
  2. Indeed (support.indeed.com) — Profile Settings Menu: Managing Your Privacy
  3. Indeed — FAQ: Indeed's Approach to Privacy
  4. Monster — Resume Security
  5. CareerBuilder — Resume Security
  6. Federal Trade Commission — Fact Sheet on FTC's Proposed Final Noncompete Rule (2024-04)
  7. American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) — FTC vacates noncompete rule, shifts to case-by-case enforcement (2025-09)
  8. JobQuest — LinkedIn Open to Work: who can actually see it?
  9. Contentin — What Does Open to Work Mean on LinkedIn?
  10. MagicPost — LinkedIn Open to Work: What It Means + the Post to Use
  11. CareerBldr — LinkedIn Open to Work (2026): Settings, Privacy & When to Use It

title: The New Hire's Roadmap to Thriving in a Remote or Hybrid Job
dek: Remote onboarding hides the hallway cues that teach you how a team works, so this plan replaces them with scheduled check-ins and written benchmarks.
author: Ingrid Castellanos
body:
Starting a job you can't walk into means nobody sees you struggling, and nobody sees you succeeding either. This roadmap gives you a checklist for the week before you start, hour-by-hour goals for day one and week one, measurable benchmarks a manager can verify at 30, 60 and 90 days, and word-for-word scripts for the conversations most new hires avoid.

It is built for both fully remote and hybrid roles. Where the two differ — office days, equipment, paperwork handoffs — the difference is called out. Details vary by employer and by state, so treat your offer letter and your HR portal as the final word on anything specific to you.

Key takeaways

  • In the week before day one, complete your tax withholding form and gather the ID documents your employer's I-9 instructions list, so paperwork doesn't eat your first morning.
  • By the end of week one, book recurring 1:1s with your manager and 20-minute intro calls with five teammates.
  • By day 30, ship one small deliverable end to end and write down the process you used, so your progress is visible without anyone watching you work.

Before You Start: Pre-Day-One Checklist

Work through these in the week before your start date. Most take under 20 minutes. The goal is that nothing on day one is a logistics problem.

  • Join a test video call with yourself on whatever platform the team uses, and check that your camera, microphone and headset all work without a prompt to install anything.
  • Confirm what hardware the employer is shipping, when it arrives, and whether you are expected to use your own device until it does.
  • Gather the identity and work-authorization documents listed in your employer's Form I-9 instructions and keep them together in one envelope or folder. Your employer must complete and sign Section 2 of Form I-9 within three business days of your first day of work for pay (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, undated), so delays on your side hold up theirs.
  • Complete your Form W-4 if the employer's portal has it open before day one. All new employees first paid after 2019 are required to use the redesigned Form W-4, and an employer who doesn't receive one must withhold as if you were a single filer with no other adjustments (Internal Revenue Service, 14 September 2026).
  • Submit your direct deposit details and note the benefits enrollment deadline on your calendar — enrollment windows are often short and employer-specific.
  • Email your manager or HR contact to confirm your start time, the time zone it refers to, the agenda for day one, and a phone number to call if your login fails.
  • If the role is hybrid, confirm which days you're expected on site, how you get a badge, and where you park or which transit stop you use. Do the commute once at the same hour you'd travel, if you can.
  • Set up a work spot with a door or a wall behind you, a light source in front of your face rather than behind, and your laptop raised so the camera is at eye level.
  • Set up a backup connection — usually your phone's hotspot — and test that your laptop actually connects to it.
  • Write and say out loud a 60-second introduction: your name, what you were doing before, what you've been hired to do, one thing you're looking forward to learning.
  • Write a list of 10 things you'd otherwise guess at: response-time expectations, whether cameras are on by default, who approves expenses, how urgent requests are flagged.
  • Tell anyone you live with your working hours and when you'll be on camera, before the first week rather than during it.

Day 1 to Week 1

Remote and hybrid starts fail quietly. Only about 1 in 10 employees strongly agree their organization does a good job of onboarding new hires (Gallup, January 2019), so assume some of the structure is yours to build.

First morning, before your first meeting

  • Log in 20 minutes early and confirm email, chat, calendar and the video platform all open. Message your HR or IT contact immediately if any one of them doesn't.
  • Set your profile photo, full name, pronouns if you use them, job title and time zone in the chat tool. In a distributed team, your time zone stops people scheduling 7 a.m. calls for you.
  • Hand over your I-9 documents in whatever way HR has specified — in person, or on a video call with a representative.

End of day 1

  • Confirm your payroll and tax forms are submitted and showing as received in the portal.
  • Write down the names and roles of everyone you spoke to, plus one detail about what each person owns. Keep this in one document you'll add to all week.
  • Send your manager three lines at the end of the day: what you set up, what you read, what you're blocked on.

End of day 3

  • Have a recurring 1:1 on the calendar with your manager — weekly or fortnightly, with a start date, not a vague promise.
  • Know the answer to three specific questions: how quickly people are expected to reply to chat messages, what counts as urgent, and which decisions need your manager's sign-off.
  • Complete any required compliance or security training the employer has assigned, rather than letting it sit until week four.

End of week 1

  • Hold 20-minute introduction calls with five people, at least two of them outside your immediate team. Ask each one: what do you work on, what do you need from someone in my role, and what do new people here usually get wrong?
  • Name the three things your manager will judge your first 90 days on, in your manager's own words, written down.
  • Finish one small, real task — a document edited, a ticket closed, a dataset checked — so you've been through the team's review and approval process once while the stakes are low.
  • If the job is hybrid, go in on at least one office day and use it for the conversations that are awkward on video: shadowing, questions you'd feel silly typing, lunch with your team.

30/60/90 Day Benchmarks

Bring this to your first 1:1 and ask your manager to correct it. Written benchmarks are what replace being seen at a desk — and in March 2026, 22.6 percent of workers teleworked or worked at home for pay, a rate that stayed between 21.5 and 23.0 percent over the prior year (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 16 April 2026), so your manager is likely managing several people this way.

Day 30

  • Ship one small deliverable end to end — written, reviewed, approved, released — without your manager chasing you for it.
  • Document one process you had to learn the hard way, in a page your team can actually open, and post the link in the team channel.
  • Hold a 30-minute feedback conversation with your manager where you ask what to keep doing and what to change, and write the answers down.

Day 60

  • Own a recurring piece of work — a weekly report, a support rotation, a standing meeting you run — that was previously someone else's.
  • Close out at least one task that required you to coordinate with a person outside your team, so your manager can see you navigating the organization rather than only your own queue.
  • Raise a problem with a proposed fix attached, in writing, rather than only flagging it.

Day 90

  • Deliver a project your manager assigned at the start of the quarter, on the date agreed, with any slippage flagged at least a week before the deadline.
  • Give a short walkthrough — 10 minutes on a call or a written summary — of what you've shipped, what you've learned, and what you want to take on next.
  • Agree written goals for the following quarter with your manager, including how each one will be measured.

Treat 90 days as the end of the beginning, not the finish line. Gallup found it takes 12 or more months for most people to get fully up to speed in a new job (Gallup, January 2019), so keep asking for feedback past the point where the company's formal onboarding stops.

Scripts for Common Onboarding Conversations

Use these as written, or change the nouns. All of them work on a video call, and the last three work as chat messages too.

Introducing yourself to the team on your first call

"Hi everyone, I'm Priya. I joined on Monday as a support analyst. Before this I spent four years doing customer support at a software company, mostly billing issues. For my first month I'm focused on learning your ticket system and shadowing calls. I'd love 20 minutes with each of you this week — I'll send times. If I ask you something obvious, that's why."

Asking your manager for clearer priorities in week one

"I've got five things on my list and I'm not sure which matters most this week. Could we spend ten minutes ranking them? If I had to drop one, which one should it be?"

Asking a busy teammate for help without apologizing three times

"I'm stuck on the refund report — I've tried pulling it from the dashboard and the numbers don't match the invoice totals. Do you have 15 minutes tomorrow to look at it with me? If not, is there someone else who'd know?"

Requesting feedback at day 30

"I've been here a month. Can I ask two things? First, what's one thing I'm doing that you'd like me to keep doing. Second, what's one thing you'd change about how I'm working. I'd rather hear it now than at the six-month mark."

Flagging that you're behind, before the deadline

"The migration won't be ready Friday. I hit a permissions issue that took two days to resolve. I can have it done Tuesday, or I can hand you the half that's finished on Friday and the rest Tuesday. Which is more useful to you?"

Compare that last script with the alternative: saying nothing on Friday, then explaining on Monday why it slipped. Same delay, completely different impression — one gave your manager a choice, the other gave them a surprise.

Frequently asked questions

What if I forget someone's name on a video call?+

Say it out loud: "Sorry — remind me of your name, I've met about thirty people this week." Nobody in week one is penalized for this. Then add the person to the names-and-roles document you started on day one, with a note about what they own, and check it for 60 seconds before each meeting.

How do I show I'm working when nobody can see me?+

Show output, not activity. Send your manager a short end-of-day note in your first two weeks and a weekly three-line summary after that: what you finished, what's in progress, what's blocked. Post your questions and your finished work in shared team channels rather than only in direct messages, so the work is visible to more than one person.

My manager keeps cancelling our 1:1. What do I do?+

Don't let it lapse silently. After the second cancellation, send one message: "No problem on today — can we move it to Thursday? I have three decisions I need your call on." Naming the specific items makes the meeting worth rescheduling. If it's still not happening by week four, ask who else can approve your work in the meantime.

How many questions is too many in the first week?+

Batch them. Keep a running list and bring five or six to your 1:1 rather than sending fifteen separate messages across a day. For anything blocking you right now, ask immediately — spending three hours guessing costs the team more than a two-minute answer. Most teams expect heavy questioning for the first 30 days.

When should I bring up pay or a promotion?+

Not in the first 90 days unless your offer letter already set a review date. Pay is usually set by a band for your role and location, adjusted at a scheduled review or a promotion cycle, so find out from HR in month one when those cycles fall. For market rates, check your state labor department's wage data and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational wage pages, plus any pay range your state requires in job postings — rules on this vary by state.

Should I go into the office more than required in a hybrid job?+

In the first 30 days, yes if it's practical — go on the days your immediate team goes, not the quietest days. Use office days for shadowing, reviews and the questions that are awkward to type. After day 30, drop back to the required pattern and judge by whether your in-person days are producing conversations your video calls aren't.

Sources

  1. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) — Completing Section 2, Employer Review and Attestation
  2. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — 22.6 percent of workers teleworked in March 2026 (2026-04-16)
  3. Gallup — Essential Ingredients for an Effective Onboarding Program (2019-01)
  4. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — FAQs on the 2020 Form W-4 (2026-09-14)

title: The New Hire's Roadmap to Thriving on a Small Team or Startup
dek: On a team of eight, nobody runs a formal onboarding program for you, so here is how to build one yourself, from first-day paperwork through day 90.
author: Marguerite Dunlevy
body:
Joining a small team or a startup means there is often no onboarding coordinator, no training week, and no printed org chart. What there is instead: a manager who is also doing three other jobs, a product nobody has had time to document, and a seat waiting for someone who can work out what needs doing. This roadmap covers the paperwork to finish before day one, the specific things to accomplish in your first week, what to have shipped by day 30, 60 and 90, and the exact words to use in the conversations that are hardest to start.

Some of what follows depends on your employer and your state — payroll forms, benefits enrollment windows and equipment policies all vary. Where that is the case, the guide says so and tells you who to ask.

Key takeaways

  • Before day one: confirm which ID documents to bring for Form I-9 and complete your Form W-4 so your first paycheck is not delayed.
  • Week 1: book a recurring 1:1 with your manager and write down what 'good work' looks like for your first month in their words.
  • Day 30: ship one small thing end to end — a fixed bug, a published page, a cleaned-up spreadsheet — and send your manager a short written summary.
  • Day 90: document one process you learned the hard way so the next hire does not have to, and ask for direct feedback on two specific pieces of your work.

Before You Start: Pre-Day-One Checklist

Work through these in the week before you start. On a small team, nobody will chase you for most of them, and the ones that affect your pay are your problem if they slip.

  • Email your hiring contact to confirm the start time, the address or video link, who will meet you, and whether the first day is in person. Startups move offices and change plans often.
  • Ask which identity and work-authorization documents to bring for Form I-9. Every employee hired after November 6, 1986 completes Form I-9, with Section 1 done when you start work (Wikipedia, citing federal I-9 requirements, undated). Your employer must complete and sign Section 2 within three business days of your first day (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, 2025-01-20).
  • Complete your Form W-4, the Employee's Withholding Certificate, which your employer uses to withhold the right amount of federal income tax from your pay (Internal Revenue Service, 2022-06-21). All new employees fill one out when starting a job (Paychex, 2025).
  • Ask whether your state requires a separate withholding form, since state payroll paperwork differs from state to state. Your employer's payroll contact will tell you which ones apply.
  • Submit direct deposit details and ask when the first payday falls and which period it covers. Pay schedules vary by employer and some new hires wait longer than they expect for the first deposit.
  • Ask when benefits enrollment opens and when it closes. Enrollment windows are set by the employer and the plan, and missing one can mean waiting months.
  • Turn on your work laptop or accounts before day one if IT allows it. Set up two-factor authentication on your work email and password manager at home, not while three people wait for you in a kickoff meeting.
  • Do a commute dry run at the actual hour you will travel, or, if remote, test your camera, microphone and internet on the company's video tool with a friend.
  • Read everything public about the product: the website, the pricing page, recent blog posts, app store reviews. Write down five questions the public material does not answer.
  • Ask for a list of who works there and what each person does. Teams under about 30 people often have no org chart, and a plain list from your manager saves you a month of guessing who owns what.
  • Create one running notes document for acronyms, customer names, internal tool names and decisions you overhear. You will hear 40 unfamiliar words in week one and remember six.
  • Confirm what people actually wear and whether there is a standing team meeting you are expected to attend on day one.

Day 1 to Week 1

First morning (first three hours)

  1. Hand over your I-9 documents and complete Section 1. Your employer has three business days from your first day to finish Section 2 (U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, 2025-01-20), so do not leave your documents at home.
  2. Get into email, chat and the shared drive, and send one message in the team channel introducing yourself in three sentences.
  3. Write down the first five names you hear with a note about what each person does. Say each name back once in conversation that morning.

End of day 1

  • Payroll paperwork submitted: I-9 Section 1, W-4, direct deposit, and any state form your employer gave you.
  • You can name your manager's top priority for the quarter in one sentence, because you asked and wrote it down.
  • A recurring 1:1 with your manager is on the calendar — weekly is standard on small teams. If your manager does not book it, book it yourself.
  • One question asked out loud in a group setting, so people hear your voice on day one rather than day nine.

End of day 3

  • Ten teammates' names, roles and the thing each one owns, written in your notes doc.
  • You have found where the real work lives: the ticket board, the shared folder, the channel where decisions actually get made rather than the one where they get announced.
  • Access confirmed to every tool you need. On small teams, access is usually granted by whoever has admin rights rather than an IT desk, so ask the person, not a form.
  • One small task completed, however minor — a typo fixed, a document tidied, a customer email answered under supervision.

End of week 1

  • A written list of what your manager expects from you in your first month, in their words, confirmed by email so you both have the same version.
  • Three 20-minute introductory calls held with people outside your immediate function, each ending with the question: "What slows you down that I might be able to help with?"
  • Your own summary sent to your manager on Friday: what you learned, what you are unclear on, what you plan to do next week. Four bullets is enough.

The difference this makes is concrete. One new hire spends week one reading documentation and waiting to be assigned work, then on Friday has nothing to show and no questions. Another finishes the same reading, notices the customer onboarding checklist is six months out of date, asks "Can I update this?", and has a visible contribution by day five. Same information, different ending.

30/60/90 Day Benchmarks

These are things a manager can check without taking your word for it. Adjust the specifics to your role, but keep the shape: by 30 you have produced something, by 60 you own something, by 90 you improve something.

Day 30

  • One piece of work shipped end to end and visible to someone outside your team: a feature released, a campaign sent, a report published, a customer issue resolved from first contact to close.
  • Four weekly 1:1s held with your manager, with notes you keep and refer back to.
  • A written list of every recurring task you now own, shared with your manager so they can correct anything you have wrongly assumed is yours.

Day 60

  • You run at least one recurring responsibility without being asked — the weekly numbers, the support rota, the release checklist — and nobody has had to remind you.
  • One problem you identified yourself turned into a proposal: a short written note with the problem, two options and your recommendation, sent to the person who can decide.
  • You have given useful input in someone else's area at least twice — a review of a colleague's draft, a bug caught before launch — which is how trust gets built on a team of ten.

Day 90

  • One process documented that previously existed only in someone's head, saved where the team can find it. On small teams this is often the single most valued thing a new hire produces.
  • A feedback conversation held with your manager about two specific pieces of your work, with at least one change you will make as a result written down.
  • Agreement in writing on what you own for the next quarter, including what you are deliberately not doing.

If your startup has no formal review at 90 days — many do not — hold the conversation anyway. A 25-minute meeting you request is worth more than a review process that never arrives.

Scripts for Common Onboarding Conversations

Use these close to word for word. They are written to be said out loud, not read.

Asking your manager what to prioritize (week 1)

When you have been given five things and no order

"I've got five things on my list: the onboarding emails, the data clean-up, the two customer calls, and the documentation. If I can only finish two of them this week, which two matter most to you? I'd rather do two properly than four badly."

Introducing yourself to the team (day 1)

Posted in the team chat or said at a standing meeting

"Hi, I'm Dana — I started today on the support side. I came from a smaller agency where I did a bit of everything. For the next couple of weeks I'll be asking a lot of questions, so if I'm interrupting at a bad time, just say so and I'll come back later."

Asking for an introductory chat with someone outside your team (week 1)

Sent as a short message, not a calendar invite with no explanation

"Hi Marcus — I joined on Monday and I'll be working on the billing emails, which I think touch your work. Could I get 20 minutes this week or next to hear how it looks from your side? Happy to work around your calendar."

Asking for feedback at 30 days

Booked as its own conversation, not tacked onto a status update

"I've been here a month and I'd like 20 minutes to check I'm pointed the right way. Two specific things: the pricing page draft and the way I handled the refund request last Tuesday. What would you have done differently in each?"

Admitting you are lost (any time in the first 90 days)

Better said on day three than discovered on day thirty

"I want to flag that I'm stuck on the import script — I've spent about two hours on it and I'm going in circles. Can you point me at someone who's done it before, or tell me if it's fine to park it until next week?"

Asking who decides something (first 60 days)

Useful when a small company has no documented process

"Quick question — if I want to change the wording on the signup form, who needs to say yes before I do it? I'd rather ask now than undo it later."

Frequently asked questions

What if I forget someone's name in the first week?+

Say so immediately rather than avoiding the person for a month: "I'm sorry, I've met about twenty people this week — tell me your name again?" Nobody holds this against a new hire in weeks one and two, and they will hold it against you in week six. Keep a list in your notes with the name, role, and one detail about what they own, and read it before meetings for the first two weeks.

Nobody has time to train me. What do I do?+

This is normal at companies under about 30 people and it is not a sign you were a bad hire. Shift from waiting for training to asking for 20-minute slots with a specific question attached — "Can you walk me through how a refund gets processed?" gets accepted far more often than "Can you train me?". By end of week one, ask your manager directly which two people you should learn the most from, then book time with each.

Am I asking too many questions?+

Batch them. Keep a running list in your notes document and bring five questions to your 1:1 rather than sending five separate messages across a day, and search the shared drive and chat history first so you are not asking about something already written down. Expect your question volume to drop noticeably by week three — if it has not by day 60, say so to your manager rather than hoping it resolves itself.

When should I raise pay or a title change?+

Not in your first 90 days unless your job changed substantially from what you were hired for. Spend those 90 days producing things your manager can point to, then raise it at the first formal review or at a date you agree in advance. Pay structures differ a great deal between small companies — some have salary bands, many do not, and some weight equity heavily — so ask early how pay decisions get made here and check current market rates for your role and state on public salary sources before you open the conversation.

I made a visible mistake in week two. How bad is it?+

Far less bad than hiding it. Tell the person affected within the hour, state what happened, what you have already done, and what you need: "I sent the email to the wrong list. I've paused the sequence and drafted an apology — can you look at it before I send?" Managers judge new hires on how quickly problems surface, not on whether they occur, and a mistake disclosed on day 12 is a story; one discovered on day 40 is a trust problem.

My team is remote or mostly asynchronous. Does this roadmap still work?+

Yes, with two changes. Replace the in-person moments with deliberate ones: a short video introduction in the team channel on day one, and video on for your first few 1:1s so people attach a face to your name. Write more than feels necessary for the first 30 days — a Friday summary of what you did, what you learned and what you are blocked on — because on a remote team, work nobody sees is work nobody knows happened.

Sources

  1. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) — Form I-9 Instructions (2025-01-20)
  2. Wikipedia (citing federal I-9 requirements) — Form I-9
  3. Internal Revenue Service (IRS) — What people new to the workforce need to know about income tax withholding (2022-06-21)
  4. Paychex — What Is a W-4 Form & How to Fill It Out In 2025 (2025)

title: The Ultimate Job Search Tracker Setup for Spreadsheet Beginners
dek: Build a simple spreadsheet that tells you who to contact today, what you promised, and which applications have gone quiet — no formulas required.
author: Desmond Okafor-Lee
body:
A job search tracker is one spreadsheet that answers three questions: what have I applied to, what did I promise someone, and what is due today. You do not need formulas, macros or a paid tool to build one — a blank sheet with the right columns, filled in the same way every time, does the job.

This guide gives you the column list to copy, the daily and weekly habits that keep it accurate, and three follow-up emails you can adapt from it. How employers respond, and how fast, varies enormously by company size, sector and state — the tracker's job is to make sure your side of it never slips.

Key takeaways

  • A **Follow-Up Date** column is the engine of the sheet — sort by it every morning and send only what is due that day.
  • Log each application within one hour of submitting, while the posting, the resume version and the job ID are still in front of you.
  • Use a **Status** column with fixed options (Applied, Screening, Interviewing, Offer, Rejected, No response) so you can filter the dead rows out of your daily view.

Tracker Template Columns

Start a new sheet, put these across row 1, freeze that row, and add one row per application. Both Google Sheets and Excel let you freeze the top row and attach a dropdown list to a column (data validation), which is worth doing for Status so your entries stay consistent enough to filter.

ColumnWhy it matters
Date AppliedEvery follow-up decision is measured from this date, and it tells you at a glance whether a quiet application is two days old or two months old.
CompanyYou will apply to the same company twice without realising it unless you can sort by this column.
Role TitleExact titles differ between postings, and you need the employer's wording when you reply or follow up.
SourceRecords where you found it — a job board, a referral, the company careers page — so you can see which sources actually produce replies.
Job ID or Posting LinkPostings get taken down; the ID or saved link is what lets you reference the right req when someone asks.
Resume Version UsedIf you tailored keywords, job-title wording or metrics for that posting, note which file you sent so an interview question does not catch you out.
Contact NameThe recruiter, hiring manager or referrer attached to that application — without a name, a follow-up has nowhere to go.
Contact Email or ProfileKeeps the actual address or profile URL next to the name so you are not re-searching for it under time pressure.
Follow-Up DateThe one date you act on each morning; set it when you create the row, not later.
StatusA fixed set of values (Applied, Screening, Interviewing, Offer, Rejected, No response) that lets you filter your active pipeline away from the dead rows.
Next ActionOne short phrase plus a date — "send portfolio link, Tue" — so you never reopen a row wondering what you owe.
Interview DatesEach round with its date and the interviewer's name, which is what you need to write a specific thank-you note later.
Posted Pay RangeMany states now require a pay range in the posting; copying what was published gives you a reference point later, and tells you when nothing was published.
NotesAnything that will not fit elsewhere: how you were referred, what the recruiter said about timeline, what you want to ask next.

Add a second tab called Contacts if you are dealing with the same recruiter across several roles, and a third called Archive if the main sheet gets long. Resist adding columns you will not fill in — an abandoned column is worse than no column.

Daily/Weekly Tracking Habits

The tracker only works if updating it is a fixed habit rather than a mood. Pick the cadence below and attach each item to something you already do.

  • Daily, within one hour of submitting: add the row — Company, Role Title, Date Applied, Source, Job ID and resume version — while the posting is still open in front of you.
  • Daily, at the same moment: set a Follow-Up Date 7 calendar days out and type one Next Action phrase in the row.
  • Daily, before closing the tab: paste the full posting text into a notes doc or a hidden column, because postings are removed and you will want the exact requirements before an interview.
  • Daily, first ten minutes of your search block: sort or filter the sheet by Follow-Up Date, send only the follow-ups due today, then push each one's date forward.
  • Daily, immediately after any call or email: update Status, add the interviewer's name and date to Interview Dates, and rewrite Next Action.
  • Weekly, same day each week: change the Status of anything with no reply after 21 days to "No response" and filter it out of your working view.
  • Weekly, same sitting: count how many rows you added, then look at the Source column for which channels produced any reply at all and plan next week's hours around those.
  • Weekly, two minutes: download a copy of the sheet or confirm version history is on, so a bad paste does not cost you the whole search.

Response times vary widely by employer — a small company may reply in days, while large organisations and public-sector hiring in many US states run on fixed review calendars that can take weeks. Treat the 7-day and 21-day marks as your own working rules, not as a prediction of what the employer will do.

Follow-Up Email Templates

Each of these is a skeleton. Fill every bracket from your tracker row, cut anything that is not true for you, and read it aloud once before sending. Sending any of these unedited is obvious to the person receiving it.

One week of silence after applying

Subject: Following up — [Role Title] application

Hi [Contact Name],

I applied for the [Role Title] role on [Date Applied] and wanted to make sure my application reached you. [One sentence naming a specific requirement from the posting and the experience you have with it.]

Happy to send anything else that would help. Thanks for your time.

[Your Name] [Phone] · [Profile or portfolio link]

Personalize before sending: replace the middle sentence with something only you could write about that posting, and use a real name — if your tracker's Contact Name is blank, find one or skip the email rather than writing "Dear Hiring Team" and hoping.

Thank-you after an interview

Subject: Thank you — [Role Title] conversation, [Interview Date]

Hi [Interviewer Name],

Thanks for the time on [Interview Date]. I keep thinking about [specific topic or problem they raised] — [one or two sentences on how you would approach it, or a detail you did not get to mention].

I'd be glad to answer anything else as you decide. Thank you again.

[Your Name]

Personalize before sending: the specific topic must come from that conversation, so write it into your tracker's Notes column the same day. Send within 24 hours, and write separate versions if you met several people.

Status check at three weeks

Subject: [Role Title] — checking in

Hi [Contact Name],

Checking in on the [Role Title] role I applied for on [Date Applied]. I'm still very interested, and I understand timelines move.

If the role is filled or on hold, I'd appreciate knowing so I can plan — and I'd welcome being considered for [related role or team] if something opens there.

Thanks, [Your Name]

Personalize before sending: name a real adjacent team or role rather than asking to be "kept in mind." Log the send date in Notes, and if there is still no reply after this one, change Status to "No response" at your next weekly review.

Frequently asked questions

How many applications should I add to the tracker each week?+

There is no correct number, and anyone quoting you a universal ratio of applications to interviews is guessing — it varies by field, location and how closely you match the postings. Set your own weekly target, write it at the top of the sheet, and use the Source column at your weekly review to judge whether more volume or better-matched roles is the fix.

When should I mark an application dead?+

A practical rule is 21 days with no reply after your one-week follow-up, at which point you change Status to "No response" and filter the row out of your active view. Nothing is lost — the row stays in the sheet with the Job ID and Contact Name, so you can reference it if that employer posts again.

Is a spreadsheet enough, or do I need a dedicated tracking app?+

A spreadsheet with the columns above does everything most searches need, and it never locks your data behind an account. Job boards do keep partial records of their own — LinkedIn and Indeed both have a "My Jobs" area listing roles you saved and applied to through their site — but neither captures applications you made elsewhere, your Follow-Up Date or your Next Action.

title: What Interviewers Really Mean When They Ask 'Why Should We Hire You?'
dek: A plain breakdown of the hiring risk behind the question, three worked answers, and a template you can fill in with your own numbers.
author: Ingrid Castellanos
body:
Interviewers rarely ask "Why should we hire you?" to hear you praise yourself. They ask because they have two or three people who could all probably do the job, and they need a reason to pick one. A strong answer names the employer's problem, attaches your evidence to it, and stops.

Below: what the question is actually screening for, three worked answers for different situations, a template you can fill in with your own facts, and the specific phrases that cost candidates points.

Key takeaways

  • Name the employer's problem first, then your evidence — not your qualities in the abstract.
  • Close with one quantified result; unverifiable self-praise reads as filler.
  • Never answer with what the job would do for you.

Why Interviewers Ask This

By the time this question arrives, the interviewer usually already believes you could do the job. What they are screening for is risk and differentiation: of the people still in play, who is the safest bet to fix the problem that opened the role?

Published interview guidance describes the same underlying checks. Career Sidekick says employers use the question to gauge how confident you are in your own ability to perform the job, and to hear what sets you apart from other candidates (Career Sidekick, undated). Societe Generale's candidate guidance frames it as a test of whether you understand the employer's real needs, and of your motivation for the role (Societe Generale, undated). Naukri's guidance adds a communication test: can you state your value proposition clearly and succinctly (Naukri, undated)?

The red flags are equally specific. An answer built around what the job would give you reads as self-interest — a Seattle Central College career center handout advises treating the answer as a sales pitch summarizing your accomplishments, not a statement of what you want from the job (Seattle Central College Career Center, undated). A generic answer signals you didn't research the employer.

How much the answer counts varies by employer. Structured, scored interviews — common in US federal, state and local government hiring — rate it against fixed criteria. A small-company founder may treat the same question as a gut check.

Strong Sample Answers

Career changer (CAR structure: Challenge, Action, Result)

Retail management into operations coordination

"You said late supplier deliveries keep blowing up the build schedule. At Marrow Lane Outfitters I ran stockrooms for six stores, and two vendors missed their windows most weeks. I rebuilt the reorder calendar, set a standing Monday call with both reps, and tracked every miss on a shared sheet the store managers could see. Late deliveries went from around twelve a month to three over a quarter. The product here is different, but chasing suppliers and protecting a schedule is the same work — I've just been doing it without the title."

Entry-level (Robert Walters' formula)

This one follows the formula in Robert Walters' career guide — "I bring [strengths] that align with [specific job needs], and I'm confident I can [value you'll deliver]" — with the "new to this field, fast learner" framing their guide suggests for candidates without direct experience (Robert Walters, undated).

First job after a two-year program

"I bring solid SQL and a habit of documenting what I build, which lines up with the reporting backlog you described, and I'm confident I can take the weekly dashboards off your analysts within a month. I'm new to insurance, but I'm a fast learner and very motivated — for my capstone I picked up Power BI in three weeks and built a claims dashboard for a fictional insurer, Tamarack Mutual. I'd rather be the person who clears the routine work so your senior people stop doing it."

Senior hire (STAR, with a follow-up)

STAR — Situation, Task, Action, Result — is a structured technique employers use to evaluate responses to behavioral and situational questions (Wikipedia, undated).

Candidate for a support director role

"When I joined Halden Freight, support was running about 900 tickets a month with a four-day first response, and I had a year before I could ask for headcount. I split the queue by issue type, wrote playbooks for the top eight, and put two people on a triage rotation. First response dropped under eight hours in five months, and the headcount we added later came from a business case rather than a panic. You've described the same backlog as your top risk, so that's where I'd start."

Interviewer pushback

"Halden was 200 people. We're 4,000. Why would that scale?"

Your reply

"Unchanged, it wouldn't. The triage split scales; the playbooks would need an owner per region. So the first thing I'd ask for is thirty days to check whether your ticket mix looks like the one I just described — if it doesn't, the plan changes."

Answer Framework You Can Adapt

Indeed's career guide recommends three steps: acknowledge the role's requirements, match your skills to the employer's needs, then give quantifiable achievements (Indeed, undated). Research the employer before you draft anything — CareerOneStop lists researching the employer and job as the first step toward a successful interview (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated), and Novoresume's guidance makes the same point about tailoring your answer (Novoresume, undated).

Core template

"From the posting and what you've described today, the priority is [employer's problem, in their words]. I bring [strength one] and [strength two], which line up with [specific requirement from the job ad]. At [company], I [action you personally took] and [quantified result — a number, percentage, or time saved]. I'm confident I can [specific value in your first 90 days]."

U.S. News & World Report lists presenting yourself as a problem solver as one way to answer this question (U.S. News & World Report, undated) — which is what the first and last lines of that template are doing.

If the honest answer includes a gap

"I'll be straight with you: I haven't [missing requirement]. What I have done is [closest adjacent experience], and I got up to speed on [tool or process] in [timeframe] by [how you did it]. If that gap decides this, I'd rather know now. What you'd get from day one is [strength that is genuinely scarce]."

If they push back

Interviewer: "That's a smaller budget than you'd be handling here."

You: "It is — about [figure] against [their figure]. The part that transfers is [specific skill, e.g. forecasting against an approval cycle]. The part I'd need help with is [honest answer], and I'd want [named person or process] involved for the first quarter."

Write your version out and say it aloud. CareerOneStop recommends writing responses that highlight past experiences, and practicing them with another person or in front of a mirror (CareerOneStop, U.S. Department of Labor, undated). Time it: if you're past 90 seconds and haven't named a result, cut.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Don't open with "I'm a hard worker, I'm passionate, and I'm a people person." Replace each adjective with one dated example that has a number in it.
  • Don't say "because I really need this job" or "it would be a great opportunity for me" — the Seattle Central College handout's point is that this answer summarizes your accomplishments, not your wishes (Seattle Central College Career Center, undated).
  • Don't claim "I'm the best candidate you'll interview." You haven't met the others. Say "here's what I'd bring to the problem you described" instead.
  • Don't say "we" when the question is about your contribution. If the sentence is "we reduced churn," rewrite it as "I wrote the win-back sequence; churn fell from X to Y."
  • Don't retell your resume in chronological order from your first job. Pick the one role that maps to this requirement and skip the rest.
  • Don't name a result you can't source. If asked "where does that number come from?", you need an answer — a dashboard, a report, a manager who signed it off.
  • Don't criticize other applicants or your current employer as your point of difference. Describe what you did, not who was worse.

Frequently asked questions

What if I'm asked this again in a final-round interview?+

Don't repeat the first-round answer word for word — someone in the room has heard it. Use material from the process itself: "Since we spoke, two of your team mentioned the handover between sales and onboarding. That's the gap I'd work on first, and here's what I did about a similar one at [company]." New evidence, same structure.

What if I'd be stepping down a level and they think I'll leave?+

Say the quiet part first, because they're already thinking it. Name why you want a smaller scope — relocation, burnout from managing, wanting hands-on work again — then give a concrete commitment: what you'd want to be doing in two years, and whether that's a promotion track or not. Vagueness here reads as a candidate who'll bolt in six months.

What if I honestly don't think I'm the strongest candidate?+

You don't have to claim you are. Narrow the ground to where you genuinely win: "On [specific requirement], I'd be surprised if you found someone with more direct experience." Then name what you'd need support on. Interviewers who use scored criteria are rating each requirement separately anyway, so an honest strong answer on three of five can still beat a bluff on all five.

  5. CareerOneStop (U.S. Department of Labor) — Practice interview questions
  6. Robert Walters — Why should we hire you? Example interview answers and expert tips
  7. Robert Walters — Why should we hire you? Example interview answers and expert tips

  9. Novoresume — Why Should We Hire You? Answers That Get Job Offers
  10. U.S. News & World Report — 10 Ways to Answer 'Why Should We Hire You?' (With Examples)
  11. Societe Generale — Why should we hire you interview question: tips & samples
  12. Naukri — How to Answer—'Why We Should Hire You?' in 2026!

title: What to Do When Your New Manager Gives You Almost No Feedback
dek: Silence from a new boss usually points to a missing routine or a crowded calendar rather than a verdict on your work — here is how to find out which.
author: Tobias Amarinde
body:
A manager who says almost nothing in your first weeks isn't necessarily unhappy with you. More often the working relationship hasn't been set up yet: no recurring check-in, no agreed definition of "good", no shared list of what you own. The fix is usually a small, specific request you make yourself, within a week of noticing the gap.

Below: why the silence happens, a response you can run inside seven days, and wording you can say out loud without it sounding rehearsed.

Key takeaways

  • If two weeks pass with no comment on your work, assume the check-in routine is missing rather than that your work is bad — ask for a recurring 20-minute slot before you ask for a verdict.
  • Ask about one named piece of work ("was Tuesday's report the right length?") instead of asking for feedback in general; narrow questions get answers, open ones get "you're doing fine."
  • If three specific requests over 30 days produce nothing usable, build your own evidence — written goals, input from the colleagues who review your output, a skip-level conversation — rather than waiting for the formal review.

Understanding the Situation

Most feedback silence in a new job is structural. A manager with twelve direct reports and their own delivery work will default to talking only to whoever has a problem that day. In matrix setups — common in agencies, consultancies and large engineering teams — the person who actually sees your output is a project lead, while your official manager sees a name on a staffing sheet. On hybrid or distributed teams, nobody overhears your calls, and in shift-based work your supervisor may simply not be on the floor when you are.

Timing matters too. Plenty of employers only schedule feedback around formal review cycles, which leaves a new hire in month two sitting between them. SHRM recommends specific one-on-one conversations at 30, 60 and 90 days precisely to catch communication gaps early (SHRM, undated), but whether your employer actually runs those depends on the company — some US employers tie them to a 90-day probationary review, others have nothing until an annual cycle. Gallup's work on effective managers describes regular check-ins, weekly or daily depending on the job, plus formal progress discussions twice a year (Gallup, undated).

And your manager may be new at managing. Harvard Business Review describes two common first-time-manager mistakes: giving feedback before any trust exists, and avoiding or delaying it until something has gone wrong (Harvard Business Review, 2023-09). Silence can mean your manager is waiting until they have something big enough to justify the conversation. That is worth interrupting: employees who say they got meaningful feedback from their manager in the past week are far more likely to be fully engaged (Gallup, 2022-01), and engagement is highest among people who meet their manager at least weekly, though only a minority do (Gallup, 2016-06-02). Early communication gaps also have a cost — SHRM Foundation onboarding guidance cites research that half of senior outside hires fail within 18 months (SHRM Foundation, undated).

Step-by-Step Response

  1. Day 1 of noticing: write down what you want judged. List the three to five things you have finished in the past fortnight and, next to each, the one question you can't answer yourself — right level of detail? right person copied? fast enough? You are not asking for feedback in general; you are asking about these five items.
  2. Day 1-2: request a standing slot, not a one-off chat. Send a short message: "Can I take 20 minutes with you every Thursday for my first three months? I'll bring what I've finished and anything I'm unsure about." A recurring slot removes the need to ask again every week, which is the part most new hires quietly drop.
  3. Day 2-3: ask one narrow question about one named piece of work. In writing, so your manager can answer in ten seconds: "On the client summary I sent Monday — would you have cut it to one page, or was that length right?" Yes/no and either/or questions get replies from managers who never write paragraphs.
  4. Within the first week: get the definition of "good" out of their head and into writing. Ask: "At 90 days, what would make you say this hire worked out?" Then send back what you heard in five bullets and ask them to correct it. Many people who avoid giving feedback will happily correct a written claim.
  5. Within 10 days: widen your sources. Identify the two or three colleagues whose work your output feeds into — the project lead, the editor, the person who presents your numbers to clients. Ask each: "What do you end up fixing in what I send you?" That is the most reliable feedback available to you in month one, because they see the output daily.
  6. By day 30: keep a running agenda in one shared document. Not a productivity system — one page your manager can open before the check-in, with three headings: finished, stuck, needs a decision from you. It turns a vague catch-up into a ten-minute working session and gives you a dated record of what was agreed.
  7. By day 60: escalate quietly if nothing has changed. If three specific requests have produced nothing usable, raise it at a skip-level conversation or with your HR contact as a process question, not a complaint: "I want to make sure I'm calibrated before my 90-day point. What's the normal way people get a read on how they're doing here?" Whether skip-levels are routine or unusual varies a lot by employer and by country, so check what is normal on your team before booking one.

What to Say

Asking for a standing check-in

You

"I'd like 20 minutes with you every Thursday for my first three months — I'll show you what I've finished and you tell me what to change. Does 3pm work?"

Likely response

"Sure, though I'll probably have to move it some weeks."

You

"No problem. If a week gets eaten, I'll send you three bullets Thursday morning and you can just reply to those."

When the answer is "you're doing great"

You

"Good to hear. On the vendor summary from Monday — if you'd written it yourself, what would you have done differently?"

Likely response

"Honestly, it was fine."

You

"Then can I check one thing. Was the detail useful, or do you mostly want the recommendation up top and the rest in an appendix?"

When you need the definition of "good"

You

"At 90 days, what would make you say hiring me worked out?"

Likely response

"Just keep doing what you're doing."

You

"I'll write down what I think the three priorities are and send them over tonight. If any of them are wrong, tell me — I'd rather find out now than in March."

Frequently asked questions

What if I ask three times and still get nothing by day 60?+

Stop asking the same way and change what you ask for. Bring a written self-assessment — three things you think are going well, two you think are weak — and ask your manager to mark anything they disagree with. If that still produces nothing by day 90, treat your colleagues' reactions and your own delivery record as your feedback source, and raise calibration as a question at your skip-level or with HR.

What if the first real feedback arrives in a formal review and it's negative?+

Ask for examples with dates, and ask when each problem was first noticed. Then ask one forward-looking question: "What would the next 30 days need to look like for this to be resolved?" Get the answer in writing in a follow-up email the same day. If a formal performance plan is mentioned, read your employer's handbook on how that process works, because the steps and timelines differ by employer and by state.

My manager is in another country or on a different shift. Does that change things?+

Yes — you need asynchronous feedback rather than meetings. Send a short end-of-week note with two questions that can be answered with a sentence each, and name the deadline: "If I don't hear back by Tuesday I'll go with option A." Also agree with your manager which local colleague can approve routine work, so you are not waiting a day for every decision.

Should I go to HR about this?+

HR is useful here as a source of information about normal practice — whether your employer runs 30/60/90 check-ins, what the probationary review covers, who your skip-level is. Frame it that way rather than as a complaint about your manager. SHRM recommends 30-, 60- and 90-day conversations to catch gaps like this early (SHRM, undated), so asking whether yours exist is a fair question.

What if the check-ins start and then quietly stop after a month?+

That is common when a manager's workload spikes, and it is easier to restart than to start. Within one week of the second cancellation, send the agenda anyway with a line like: "Skipping is fine — here are the two things I need a decision on." If three in a row are cancelled, ask for a shorter slot: ten minutes beats a 30-minute meeting that never happens.

Sources

  1. Gallup — How Effective Feedback Fuels Performance (2022-01)
  2. Gallup — Managers: Millennials Want Feedback, but Won't Ask for It (2016-06-02)
  3. SHRM — Effective Onboarding Should Last for Months
  4. SHRM Foundation — Onboarding New Employees: Maximizing Success (Effective Practice Guidelines Series)
  5. Gallup — Obsolete Annual Reviews: Gallup's Advice
  6. Harvard Business Review — Mistakes First-Time Managers Make When Giving Feedback (2023-09)
